items.model_answer:
If Russia had modernized earlier and more thoroughly, the most likely result is a stronger, richer, and more politically stable Russia—but not necessarily a peaceful or liberal one.

The key issue is what “modernization” means. Russia did modernize in bursts: Peter the Great westernized the army and state; Catherine expanded administration and culture; Alexander II abolished serfdom; Sergei Witte pushed railways and industry. But these reforms were often incomplete, top-down, and uneven. Russia modernized militarily and bureaucratically faster than it modernized socially, legally, or politically. Serfdom lasted until 1861, education remained limited, local self-government was weak, industrialization came late, and the autocracy resisted constitutional limits.

If Russia had abolished serfdom much earlier, expanded mass education, built reliable courts, encouraged private enterprise, developed infrastructure, and created some form of constitutional government, several major outcomes become plausible.

Russia’s economy would likely have grown faster. Earlier emancipation of the peasantry could have created a more mobile labor force, a larger domestic market, and more productive agriculture. Earlier railway construction and industrial investment would have allowed Russia to exploit its enormous resources more effectively. By the late nineteenth century, Russia might have resembled a larger version of Germany or Japan: still authoritarian in some ways, but far more industrial, educated, and militarily efficient.

This would have changed European power politics. A modernized Russia would have been much harder for Napoleon to defeat, though geography already favored Russia in 1812. More importantly, it would have performed better in the Crimean War, the Russo-Japanese War, and World War I. The humiliations that exposed Russia’s backwardness might have been avoided or softened. A stronger Russia could have dominated Eastern Europe and the Balkans more decisively, which might have frightened Britain, Austria, Germany, and the Ottoman Empire even more than historical Russia did.

Domestically, earlier modernization might have reduced the chance of the 1917 revolutions. Much of Russia’s revolutionary crisis came from the combination of autocracy, peasant land hunger, worker exploitation, military failure, and the absence of legitimate representative institutions. If Russia had developed a constitutional monarchy, a broader middle class, and legal political channels earlier, opposition movements might have become parliamentary rather than revolutionary. In that scenario, Bolshevism would probably have remained a fringe ideology rather than taking power.

But modernization could also have made unrest worse in the short term. Industrialization creates urban workers, literacy spreads radical ideas, and national minorities become more politically organized. If the state modernized economically without liberalizing politically, Russia might still have faced revolution—possibly earlier. A more efficient autocracy with factories, railways, schools, and police could have become stronger but also more repressive.

The biggest global consequence would probably be the absence, or major alteration, of the Soviet Union. Without the collapse of the Romanov state in 1917, there may have been no Bolshevik Revolution, no Leninist one-party state, no Stalinist collectivization, and perhaps no Cold War in its familiar form. Russia might instead have become a conservative constitutional empire, a nationalist great power, or a federal monarchy struggling with Poles, Finns, Ukrainians, Caucasian peoples, and Central Asians.

World War I is the major uncertainty. A modern Russia might have deterred Germany and Austria-Hungary from risking war. Or it might have made them feel encircled and strike sooner. If war still came, a better-administered, better-equipped Russia would probably have held the Eastern Front more effectively, making a Central Powers victory less likely and reducing the chance of Russian collapse.

So the most likely answer is: earlier, deeper modernization would have made Russia a much more formidable European and Asian power, reduced the likelihood of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, and possibly produced a more stable constitutional or semi-authoritarian empire. But it would not automatically have made Russia democratic or peaceful. A modernized Russia could have become either a successful constitutional great power—or a stronger, more efficient autocracy with even greater ambitions.

items.question: What If Britain and France made peace in 1811?
human_answers: I definitely agree that the conflict in Spain would continue, and that some form of renewed conflict in Europe down the line is inevitable, but I don’t think Napoleon wouldn’t try to conclude a peace with Britain, so long as it was on terms favourable to him. Now, whether that is possible is a rather different question. The Whigs at least had no interest in continuing to fund the peninsular war regardless, but in negotiations, they are likely to push for a restoration of Portugal and Hannover, and for France to at least withdraw from direct control of the rest of the Hanseatic cities and the Netherlands. It’s quite a lot for Napoleon to be willing to give up, though could possibly be paired with his longstanding designs on Sicily and a British withdrawal from Malta, as well as the return of occupied Dutch and French colonies. Regardless, I don’t think the British could get everything they want.

No mention has been made of the Continental System. I presume it is abolished as part of the peace treaty. And Britain's blockade is lifted. Anything less makes peace a non starter. Predictions from here: Overall peace is going to be short lived. Every one will be watching France waiting for a propitious moment to reduce the almost total hegemony France has. Nap will maintain a large military to enforce his hegemony. I don't know that this is sustainable. Spain will remain a bleeding ulcer. The Spanish people will continue to resist. Nap's best chance at lasting peace is to pull out and return a Bourbon to power. Remaining in a constant state of this kind of war drains resources, but brings no benefits. The best he can hope for (remaining in the conflict) is an uneasy truce where Joseph is somewhat accepted/propped up, while a low level of guerilla warfare continues. The entire Spanish colonial sphere is lost even faster than OTL. Cuba/puerto rico might remain attached, but I doubt it. I don't know whether Britain has destroyed Spain's infrastructure yet, but if not, Spain could actually emerge from the conflict in better shape without Britain's help than with it. Portugal might be able to hold out behind the line of T, as their soldiers have been trained up to a better level than before 1807, but as the British had supplied the top chain of command, they'll be left rudderless. I think their fate lies in how much stomach Nap has for continuing his Iberian adventure. It would be interesting to see what results if Nap simply walks away. OTL, the British acted as a regency while the Braganza court remained in Brazil. Joao did not want to return. Pedro was too young. Portugal is likely to be chaos. Should France manage to take control, Portugal itself may end up in better shape, but the entirety of the colonial sphere attaches to Brazil. I don't think the return of French colonies does much for France. Haiti is finished as a rich colony. Martinique and Guadeloupe, where Britain ironically enforced the status quo maintaining the slave system after capturing the islands, might still hold value. When the Nap Wars resume, Britain faces a hard choice - join in and try to reset the balance of power, or stay on the sidelines and have the European dynamic dictated to them. If they join in, they're quickly going to regret dropping out in the first place. They had France on the ropes in Portugal/Spain, and now they'll have to start all over again. Who knows what has become of Wellington.

The default of the Revolution certainly left its mark, but Napoleon was also ideologically opposed to debt, in part because of fiscal conservatism (there was a hyperinflation crisis during the Revolution), but also because it would have meant making himself dependent on the financial market, and he feared that the banker would try to exert political pressure on him. But I don't think he necessarily tried to raise a large amount of debt from the public market, he preferred to use a sinking fund controlled by one of his appointees for that. For the reparation, he had ways to force the issue, like sending his army in and making the host pay for its quartering. This was the way he was making his puppets, like the Kingdom of Italy, contribute, and alongside their allied contingent, it saved him as much money as the reparations brought him. For Prussia specifically, they were raising a large debt to pay the reparation, with Napoleon himself being one of their creditors, so they probably intended to pay. But you also have to take into account that Napoleon did not hesitate too much to raise taxes (he essentially brought back every indirect tax of the Ancien Régime) or defer payment, after the Restoration, the Bourbons had to pay the equivalent of one year of fiscal revenues in unpaid expenses.
items.original_question: What if Britain and France made peace in 1811? In 1810 King George III suffered a mental breakdown, and in early 1811, his son the Prince of Wales, later to reign as King George IV, was installed as regent by Parliament. The Prince Regent was widely expected to dismiss Spencer Percival’s government, and appoint Lord Grenville as Prime Minister, but was dissuaded from this course by his mother. Unlike the Tories, Grenville and the Whigs were sceptical of the conflict with France, particularly the expense of maintaining Wellington’s army in the Peninsula War, and had they taken power in 1811, whilst Wellesley’s army was holed up behind the lines of Torres Vedras, attempts at negotiating a peace with France are not an unrealistic prospect. Negotiations in 1807 touted an exchange of Sicily for Hannover, and Britain would retain the Cape Colony and Malta, whilst returning other Dutch and French colonial possessions, though these ultimately broke down over Sicily. Talks in 1808 even saw Napoleon offer to concede both Hannover and Portugal, though there is some question of how serious both sides were in this later negotiation. Both of these were also viewed by the Tory governments as a chance for a respite alike to Amiens, rather than to conclude the conflict. The Whigs, less intractable towards the idea of a French dominated Europe would be willing to pursue a long term peace. In addition to questions over Portugal, Hannover and the colonies though, France had by this point annexed the Netherlands and the Hanseatic cities, both of which are likely to be sticking points for British negotiators (although these annexations were in part to enforce the continental system). What terms could realistically be feasibly agreed by both sides at this time? With the end of the war with Britain in 1811, Napoleon’s invasion of Russia appears unlikely to my mind, though relations between the two emperors would undoubtedly continue to deteriorate. The peace would also presumably be unpopular domestically in Britain, where support for the war remained high. Austria, Prussia and Sweden all additionally had cause to want revenge against France and Napoleon, and so it seems unlikely that this peace would be entirely conclusive, and some form of renewed conflict seems eventually likely, even if it only comes with Bonaparte’s death. The aftermath of Amiens however suggests that this might well come sooner. There is however also the question of whether France could afford to maintain their precarious financial situation, and in particular continue to field their army without the subsides of allies, the reparations of former enemies and loot. It seems unlikely France can afford to demobilise in the face of their European rivals, so would this possibly prompt further campaigns? Perhaps against Russia regardless or the Ottomans?
items.model_answer:
If Britain and France made a real peace in 1811, the most likely result is that Napoleon’s empire would have survived much longer, and the dramatic collapse of 1812–1815 probably would not have happened in the same way.

In 1811 Napoleon dominated continental Europe, but Britain still controlled the seas, financed resistance, and kept the Peninsular War alive in Spain and Portugal. Britain could not easily defeat Napoleon on land, and Napoleon could not invade Britain or break British maritime power. A peace would therefore probably have been a compromise: Britain would keep much of its naval and colonial supremacy, while France would receive recognition of its dominance over much of western and central Europe. Napoleon would likely have had to relax or abandon the Continental System, the economic blockade meant to exclude British goods from Europe.

That change would have been decisive. The Continental System was one of the main causes of the worsening quarrel between Napoleon and Russia. Russia was hurt economically by being cut off from British trade and increasingly ignored Napoleon’s restrictions. If Britain and France made peace, Napoleon would have far less reason to punish Russia for trading with Britain. The invasion of Russia in 1812, which destroyed the Grande Armée and triggered Napoleon’s downfall, would therefore become much less likely.

The Peninsular War would also change sharply. If Britain made peace, Wellington’s army would probably withdraw from Portugal and Spain. Spanish guerrilla resistance might continue, but without British money, troops, and naval support, it would be much harder to sustain. Napoleon’s brother Joseph might remain king of Spain, at least formally, though French control there would remain uneasy and expensive.

Without the Russian disaster and without a British-backed coalition forming in 1813, there would probably be no Leipzig, no first abdication in 1814, no Hundred Days, and no Waterloo. The Bourbon restoration in France would likely not occur when it did, and the Congress of Vienna would either not happen or would take a very different form. Europe might instead settle into a tense balance: Britain as the dominant naval, commercial, and colonial power; France as the dominant continental empire.

But this peace would probably not be permanently stable. Britain would remain suspicious of French control over the Low Countries, Antwerp, Italy, and Spain. Austria, Prussia, and Russia would resent French hegemony. National resistance in Spain, Germany, and Italy would keep growing. Napoleon’s empire depended heavily on his personal authority, military prestige, and family rule; after his death or a major succession crisis, it might have fractured.

So the most plausible outcome is not a harmonious Europe, but a prolonged Napoleonic order: France dominant on the continent, Britain dominant at sea, Russia less immediately threatened, and Europe avoiding the catastrophic 1812–1815 sequence. Napoleon likely remains emperor into the 1820s, but the underlying rivalry between Britain and France—and the resentment of French domination across Europe—would make another major conflict quite possible later.

items.model_answer:
If the Mongol Empire had concentrated on Western Europe instead of the Levant, the most likely result would have been a devastating series of invasions and tributary arrangements in parts of Europe, but not a permanent conquest of all Western Europe.

In the short term, the Mongols could probably have inflicted severe defeats on European armies. Their campaigns in Poland and Hungary in 1241 already showed that Western-style knightly forces were vulnerable to Mongol mobility, feigned retreats, coordinated columns, and composite-bow cavalry tactics. If a larger, sustained Mongol army had pushed beyond Hungary into Austria, Germany, northern Italy, or France, it might have destroyed major field armies and forced some rulers to pay tribute. Central Europe, especially Hungary and the Danube basin, was the most plausible area for longer Mongol domination because it had open plains suitable for cavalry.

But conquering and holding Western Europe would have been much harder than conquering steppe regions, Persia, or northern China. Western Europe was densely covered with castles, fortified towns, forests, rivers, mountains, and fragmented local lordships. The Mongols were excellent at siege warfare when they brought engineers, but reducing hundreds of castles and walled towns would have required time, manpower, and supply lines stretching very far from their main bases. Their armies also depended heavily on pasture for huge numbers of horses; western and central Europe had less suitable continuous grazing land than the Eurasian steppe.

Political fragmentation would have cut both ways. It made Europe vulnerable because kings and princes often failed to coordinate, but it also made Europe hard to “decapitate.” Capturing Paris, Rome, or Aachen would not automatically make every count, bishop, town, and castle surrender. England would likely have been safe from full conquest unless the Mongols developed a serious naval strategy, which was not their strength in Europe.

The biggest changes would likely have been indirect. A serious Mongol drive into Western Europe might have weakened the Holy Roman Empire, devastated Hungary and Poland even more deeply, frightened the papacy into diplomacy, and forced France and other kingdoms to centralize military and fiscal systems faster. European fortification, cavalry tactics, missile warfare, and state finance might have evolved more rapidly in response to the Mongol threat.

Meanwhile, if the Mongols did not focus on the Levant, the Mamluks in Egypt and Syria would have faced less pressure. The famous Mongol-Mamluk confrontation, especially Ayn Jalut in 1260, might not have become such a turning point. The Crusader states might have lasted slightly longer or faced a different balance of power, but they were still strategically weak. The Islamic Middle East, especially Syria, may have suffered less immediate Mongol devastation.

Overall, the Mongols could probably have raided and shattered large parts of Europe and perhaps turned some eastern or central European states into tributaries. But a durable Mongol conquest of France, Italy, Iberia, Germany, and England is unlikely. The more plausible counterfactual is not a Mongol-ruled Western Europe, but a traumatized, militarized, and politically altered Europe that survives after absorbing a massive shock.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If the Americans captured and then held Quebec in 1775, Quebec would probably have developed as a French-Catholic region inside the United States rather than as the core of British French Canada. Its culture would survive, but it would be reshaped earlier and more strongly by republican politics, American migration, market capitalism, and English-language institutions.

The first crucial point is that an American victory at Quebec would not automatically mean instant assimilation. The French-speaking Catholic population was large, compact, rural, and socially organized around parish, family, and customary law. The Continental Congress would have had every reason to reassure them. To keep Quebec loyal, American authorities would likely have preserved Catholic worship, tolerated French civil law, and allowed local French-speaking elites and clergy to retain influence, at least initially. A harsh anti-Catholic or anti-French policy would have risked rebellion and made occupation impossible.

So in the short term, Quebec society would probably look surprisingly familiar: French-speaking habitants on farms, Catholic parishes as the center of village life, seigneurial landholding still present, and Montreal and Quebec City as commercial towns with mixed French and English-speaking merchants. But the long-term trajectory would diverge sharply from real history.

Under British rule, the Quebec Act of 1774, later constitutional arrangements, and eventually Canadian federalism gave French Canada a protected but defensive position: Catholic, French-speaking, legally distinct, and politically conscious of being a minority within British North America. Under American rule, Quebec would instead be pulled into the institutions of the early United States. That would mean elected republican government, no established church in the long run, stronger pressure toward individual landownership, and integration into American trade networks.

The Catholic Church would remain powerful for much of the nineteenth century, but probably less dominant than it became in real Quebec. In actual history, the Church became the guardian of French-Canadian identity against British Protestant power, especially after the failed rebellions of 1837–38. In an American Quebec, the clergy would still control much education and parish life at first, but republican disestablishment, religious competition, and American-style public schooling would weaken its authority earlier. Quebec might still be very Catholic, but less clerical and less socially conservative over the long run.

French would survive, especially in rural areas along the St. Lawrence, because the French-speaking population was too large and concentrated to disappear quickly. This would not be like Louisiana, where French declined under heavy Anglo-American settlement and weaker institutional support. Quebec had a much stronger demographic base. However, English would become the language of federal politics, long-distance commerce, higher education, and upward mobility. Montreal would likely become bilingual and perhaps majority English-speaking earlier than in real history, while rural Quebec would remain strongly French-speaking.

Legally, Quebec might develop a mixed system similar to Louisiana: French-derived civil law in private matters, but American constitutional law, criminal law, and political institutions layered above it. The seigneurial system would probably be abolished earlier than it was historically, replaced by freehold property and American-style land markets. This would accelerate social change in the countryside and weaken old elite structures.

Demographically, Quebec would receive more migrants from New England and other American states. The Eastern Townships, Montreal, and commercial corridors would become more Anglophone and Protestant. At the same time, French Canadians would move more easily within the United States—to northern New York, Vermont, the Great Lakes, and later the Midwest—without crossing an international border. Franco-American identity would be much larger and more politically central in U.S. history.

The political identity of French Quebec would also change. There would probably be no Quebec nationalism in the modern Canadian sense, because there would be no British Canada, no Confederation of 1867, and no later struggle between Quebec and Ottawa in its familiar form. Instead, French Quebec would likely develop a regional minority-rights politics inside the United States: defending French-language schools, Catholic institutions, local civil law, and state autonomy. Its politics might resemble a mixture of Louisiana, New Mexico, and later Catholic immigrant politics, but with a much stronger French-speaking majority in its home region.

By the twentieth century, Quebec would probably be a distinctive French-American state or cluster of states: culturally Catholic, historically French-speaking, legally somewhat exceptional, and politically protective of local language rights. But it would also be more Americanized than real Quebec. English would be more dominant in business and federal life; the Catholic Church would likely lose social control earlier; republican and market values would penetrate more deeply; and the dramatic Quiet Revolution of the 1960s would probably not occur in the same way, because the clerical old order would have eroded more gradually.

In short, an American Quebec would probably not become simply “English America.” French language and Catholic culture would persist because of population density and local institutions. But Quebec would become less clerical, more bilingual, more commercially integrated with the United States, and less separatist-nationalist than the Quebec of real history. It would likely emerge as North America’s main French-American society rather than as the heart of French Canada.
