EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

If Napoleon could not make it back to France in 1799, the most likely result is that the Coup of 18 Brumaire either fails or happens under a different general, and France avoids the specific “Napoleonic” path of Consulate, Empire, and continent-wide personal rule.

In real history, Napoleon’s return from Egypt was crucial because France in 1799 was politically unstable but not militarily defeated. The Directory was unpopular, corrupt, and weak. Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès and other political figures wanted to replace it with a stronger executive, but they needed a famous general to give the coup legitimacy and military force. Napoleon was ideal: young, victorious, popular, and politically flexible.

If Napoleon never reaches France, Sieyès has to look elsewhere. His best alternatives are generals such as Jean Victor Moreau, André Masséna, or possibly Bernadotte, though each had problems. Moreau was respected and successful but less politically bold. Masséna was brilliant but less acceptable as a political frontman. Bernadotte had republican sympathies and might not cooperate with Sieyès’ plans. Joubert, another possible candidate, had already been killed at Novi in 1799.

So there are two likely outcomes.

The first and most plausible is that a coup still happens, but under Moreau or another general. In that case, France probably gets a more conservative military-republican government rather than Napoleon’s highly personal dictatorship. Sieyès may have more influence in shaping the new constitution. The result might be a stronger executive than the Directory, but not necessarily an emperor. France continues fighting the Second Coalition, and because French armies were still strong, it probably survives. Masséna’s defense of Switzerland and Moreau’s later campaigns show that France did not depend entirely on Napoleon at that moment.

The second possibility is that the coup fails or is delayed. The Directory limps on, increasingly discredited. Political chaos continues, with royalists, Jacobins, and military factions competing for power. In that case, France might still eventually experience a military coup, but by another commander. The Revolution had already created conditions favorable to military rule: weak civilian institutions, constant war, and generals with independent prestige.

The biggest immediate change would be in the war. Without Napoleon’s return, there is no Napoleon as First Consul, no rapid reorganization of French politics around his authority, and probably no Battle of Marengo in 1800 under his command. However, France might still defeat Austria through Moreau, who historically won the major victory at Hohenlinden in 1800. That means Austria could still be forced into peace, though perhaps under less dramatic circumstances. The Second Coalition was already fragile, and Russia had withdrawn from active cooperation with Austria and Britain.

Napoleon’s army in Egypt would also be doomed more quickly or more completely. In real history, he abandoned it and returned to France; without his successful escape, he might be captured by the British, killed, or trapped in Egypt. The French expedition would likely surrender earlier to the British and Ottomans. This would strengthen Britain’s position in the Mediterranean and remove any lingering French threat to India through the Middle East.

Long-term, Europe changes enormously. Without Napoleon ruling France, there is probably no Napoleonic Empire, no coronation in 1804, no invasion of Spain in 1808, no Continental System in its Napoleonic form, and likely no disastrous invasion of Russia in 1812. The Holy Roman Empire might survive longer, since its abolition in 1806 was directly tied to Napoleon’s victories and reorganization of Germany. German and Italian nationalism would probably develop more slowly, because Napoleon’s conquests helped destroy old structures and spread legal-administrative reforms.

France might still keep some Revolutionary gains: legal equality, secular reforms, the sale of Church lands, and a stronger centralized state. But the Napoleonic Code as we know it may not exist, or it may appear in a less famous and less exportable form. Across Europe, fewer states would be forcibly reorganized along French lines.

Britain remains France’s main rival, but without Napoleon’s aggressive imperial strategy, the war might become less total. A peace between Britain and France is possible, though mistrust would remain. Britain would still dominate the seas and expand its colonial influence, especially if France’s Egyptian adventure ends in humiliation.

In short, if Napoleon could not reach France in 1799, France probably does not collapse, but Napoleon’s personal dictatorship likely never emerges. A different military-backed republic or authoritarian regime may replace the Directory, and France may still remain a major power. But the vast Napoleonic wars, the Empire, the reshaping of Germany and Italy, and the dramatic rise-and-fall story of Napoleon would either not happen or would occur in a much weaker and very different form.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.
items.model_answer:
If the Greek “Great Plan” — the Megali Idea of uniting most Greek-speaking and historically Byzantine lands — had succeeded during the Greek War of Independence, and if that war had helped bring down the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s or 1830s, the eastern Mediterranean would probably have faced an earlier version of the crisis that actually came after 1878–1923: partition, ethnic conflict, Great Power intervention, and the creation of unstable successor states.

The most likely result would not have been a simple rebirth of Byzantium. A large Greek state might have taken the Peloponnese, central Greece, the Aegean islands, Crete, perhaps western Anatolia around Smyrna, and possibly Constantinople if Russia, Britain, and France allowed it. But such a state would have been demographically fragile. Many of the lands claimed by Greek nationalists contained large Muslim Turkish, Albanian, Slavic, Armenian, Jewish, and Arab populations. A “Greater Greece” would therefore have faced the same problem that later destroyed the Megali Idea in 1922: how to rule mixed territories where Greeks were important but not always a majority.

The collapse of the Ottoman Empire that early would have triggered an immediate “Eastern Question” crisis. Russia would have tried to dominate the Straits, protect Orthodox Christians, and expand influence over the Balkans and perhaps eastern Anatolia. Britain would have resisted any Russian control of Constantinople because it threatened the route to India and British naval power in the Mediterranean. France would have sought influence in the Levant and among Catholics. Austria would have feared Balkan nationalism spreading into its own multiethnic empire. So even if the Ottomans collapsed, the Great Powers would almost certainly have imposed a settlement rather than letting Greece or Russia inherit everything.

The Balkans would likely have fragmented sooner. Serbia, the Danubian principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia, and perhaps Bulgaria would have emerged earlier as autonomous or independent states, though under heavy Russian or Austrian influence. Albania and Macedonia would have become contested zones. Without decades of later Ottoman reform and nationalist development, some identities would have been less politically organized, making borders even harder to draw and violence more likely.

In Anatolia, the outcome would have been especially unstable. A Greek occupation of Constantinople and the Aegean coast would probably have provoked Muslim Turkish resistance earlier than in real history. Instead of the Turkish nationalist movement of Mustafa Kemal after World War I, there might have been an earlier Turkish-Muslim successor state in central Anatolia, built around military commanders, provincial notables, and Islamic legitimacy. That state would likely have contested Greek control of western Anatolia and the Straits for generations.

The Arab provinces would probably not have become part of a Greek-led order. Egypt under Muhammad Ali was already powerful and might have become the main successor power in the eastern Arab world, perhaps taking Syria, Palestine, or Arabia if Britain and France did not stop it. North Africa might have fallen sooner under European influence. The Levant could have become a French sphere, while Britain would have sought influence in Egypt, Cyprus, the Gulf, and routes toward India. In other words, European imperial penetration of the Middle East might have begun decades earlier.

For Greece itself, success would have been both a triumph and a burden. It would have gained Constantinople and a much larger population, becoming a major eastern Mediterranean state. But it would also have inherited imperial problems beyond its administrative, military, and economic capacity. The new state would have depended heavily on Britain, France, or Russia for loans, protection, and diplomatic recognition. Internal politics would have been divided between liberal revolutionaries, Orthodox monarchists, local warlords, island shipowners, and foreign patrons. A Greater Greece might have looked impressive on a map but been difficult to govern.

The human cost would likely have been severe. The real Greek War of Independence already involved massacres, reprisals, expulsions, and enslavement. A wider Ottoman collapse would have multiplied these across the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Levant. Population exchanges or mass expulsions might have occurred a century earlier, especially between Orthodox Christians and Muslims. The cosmopolitan character of cities like Constantinople, Smyrna, Salonica, and Alexandria might have been transformed much sooner.

The long-term geopolitical effect would be that the First World War-era settlement of the Ottoman lands would have been anticipated in the early nineteenth century. There might have been no Ottoman Empire left to join World War I, no late Ottoman reforms, no Young Turks, and perhaps no Republic of Turkey in its actual form. But the underlying conflicts over nationalism, empire, religion, and access to the Straits would not have disappeared. They would simply have erupted earlier, under the supervision of the post-Napoleonic Great Powers.

So the most plausible answer is: Greece would have become larger and more prestigious, perhaps even holding Constantinople, but the early Ottoman collapse would have produced a volatile, internationally managed partition of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean. It would have accelerated Balkan nationalism, Russian-British rivalry, European imperialism in the Middle East, and ethnic violence. Rather than creating a stable Greek-led successor to Byzantium, it would probably have produced an earlier and messier version of the conflicts that later culminated in the Balkan Wars, World War I, the Greco-Turkish War, and the post-Ottoman settlement.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.
items.model_answer:
If the French became one of the largest communities in the United States, the impact would depend on how large the community became, where it settled, and whether it remained strongly connected to French language and culture across generations. But broadly, the United States would become more visibly influenced by French culture, politics, education, and international ties.

French would likely become a more common language in American public life, especially in cities or states with large French-speaking populations. Schools might expand French-language programs, bilingual education, and exchange programs with France and other Francophone countries. In some areas, public services, media, newspapers, radio, and local government materials might appear in French more often, similar to how Spanish is used in many parts of the US today.

Culturally, French influence would become more mainstream. French cuisine, fashion, cinema, literature, philosophy, and holidays could become a larger part of American urban culture. Cities with major French populations might develop French-speaking neighborhoods, cultural festivals, schools, churches, and business networks. American food culture, already influenced by France in fine dining, might see broader everyday French influence through bakeries, cafés, markets, and regional French cuisines.

Politically, a large French-American community could become an important voting bloc. Politicians might pay more attention to issues affecting immigrants from France and the wider Francophone world, such as visas, dual citizenship, trade, education, and US-France relations. If the community were concentrated in certain states, it could influence local and national elections. It might also strengthen American support for closer relations with France, the European Union, and Francophone countries in Africa, the Caribbean, and Canada.

Economically, the change could deepen ties between the US and France. French companies might invest more in the US, and American companies might expand operations in France and French-speaking markets. Sectors such as luxury goods, aerospace, energy, technology, tourism, education, wine, agriculture, and design could benefit from stronger transatlantic networks. French professionals, entrepreneurs, and students could contribute to American universities, research institutions, and industries.

Socially, the French would probably become part of the broader American ethnic mosaic, much as earlier European immigrant groups did. Over time, many would assimilate while still keeping elements of French identity. Intermarriage, bilingual households, and mixed cultural traditions would become common. However, if the community remained linguistically distinct, there could also be debates over language, identity, schooling, and immigration policy.

The effect on American identity would be noticeable but not necessarily destabilizing. The US has historically absorbed large communities from Germany, Ireland, Italy, Mexico, China, India, and many other places. A large French community would add another major layer to that pattern. It would make the country more Francophone, more closely linked to France and the wider French-speaking world, and culturally richer in areas such as language, food, arts, and education.

items.question: Independent Naples: What If Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505?
human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.
items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.
items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505, the immediate result would be the removal of Catherine from the English succession game and the creation of a powerful legitimist claim to an independent Kingdom of Naples. The marriage would unite a daughter of Ferdinand the Catholic with the male heir of the dispossessed Aragonese-Neapolitan dynasty, making it possible for Naples to be restored not as a Spanish viceroyalty but as a formally separate kingdom ruled by Ferdinand of Calabria and Catherine.

This is plausible only if Ferdinand the Catholic chose to treat Naples as a client kingdom rather than a directly governed possession. Historically, he did the opposite: after Spain conquered Naples in 1503, he kept Ferdinand of Calabria under control because the duke’s claim was dangerous. So the counterfactual requires a strategic reversal. Ferdinand would be accepting a friendly, dynastically tied Naples in exchange for legitimacy, local stability, and perhaps a diplomatic settlement with France. Naples would be “independent” in name and law, but in practice it would depend heavily on Spanish protection against French ambitions.

For England, the consequences would be enormous. Catherine would not marry Henry VIII in 1509. There would be no Princess Mary born from that marriage, no royal marriage whose validity depended on the Levitical dispensation, and therefore no “King’s Great Matter” in the same form. Henry VIII would still need a wife, probably from the Habsburg, French, or another major European dynasty. If that wife produced a surviving son, the English Reformation as we know it would likely not happen. England might still experience Protestant influence later, but without Henry’s annulment crisis the break with Rome would be delayed, softened, or take a very different political form.

For Naples, Catherine’s marriage would strengthen the native Aragonese claim. Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, had the bloodline; Catherine brought Spanish royal prestige and diplomatic protection. Their court could become a revived Renaissance monarchy in southern Italy, more locally legitimate than the historical Spanish viceroyalty. The Neapolitan barons and urban elites might prefer a resident king and queen to distant rule from Spain. But the kingdom would remain strategically vulnerable. France had not abandoned interest in Italy, and any independent Naples would need Spanish troops, Spanish money, or Spanish alliance to survive.

For Spain and the Habsburgs, this would complicate imperial consolidation. Historically, Naples became a key Spanish-Habsburg possession, central to control of the western Mediterranean and the Italian Wars. If Naples instead passed to Catherine and Ferdinand of Calabria, Charles V would not automatically inherit it in 1516 unless the marriage was arranged to preserve Habsburg succession rights. Charles would probably tolerate an allied Naples if it reliably supported him against France, but he would resist a genuinely neutral or independent policy. Over time, Habsburg pressure would likely pull Naples back into Spain’s orbit through marriage, military dependency, or succession claims.

The most likely long-term outcome is therefore not a fully sovereign Naples able to act like France or Spain, but a semi-independent Aragonese-Neapolitan kingdom: locally ruled, legally separate, Catholic, Spanish-aligned, and militarily dependent on the Habsburgs. If Catherine and Ferdinand produced surviving children, Naples could remain a junior Mediterranean monarchy for several generations. If they failed to produce heirs, or if France successfully exploited the situation, Naples would probably be reabsorbed into the Spanish-Habsburg system.

The biggest global consequence would be in England. Catherine’s absence from Henry VIII’s life removes the central trigger of the Tudor break with Rome. Independent Naples would matter greatly in Italian politics, but the altered fate of England’s Reformation would be the wider historical earthquake.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!
items.model_answer:
If the world had seriously curbed global warming after 1980, the planet today would likely be substantially cooler, cleaner, and less exposed to climate-related disasters, though not free of climate change entirely.

By 1980, enough was known scientifically to justify action: carbon dioxide was rising, fossil-fuel combustion was the main cause, and warming was expected. If governments had responded then with strong policies—carbon pricing, efficiency standards, rapid renewable and nuclear deployment, limits on coal, protection of forests, and international agreements—the rise in greenhouse-gas emissions could have slowed much earlier. Instead of global emissions continuing to climb for decades, they might have peaked in the 1990s or early 2000s.

The most important result would be lower cumulative carbon emissions. Because global warming depends largely on the total amount of carbon dioxide humans emit over time, early action would have mattered greatly. Present-day warming might have been closer to around 1°C or less above preindustrial levels rather than roughly 1.2–1.3°C and rising. That difference sounds small, but it would mean fewer extreme heat waves, less coral bleaching, slower ice loss, reduced sea-level rise, less Arctic warming, and lower risks of severe droughts, floods, and wildfire conditions.

The economic effects would probably have been mixed but manageable. Fossil-fuel industries—especially coal and oil—would have faced earlier decline, causing political conflict and job losses in certain regions. But those losses could have been offset by earlier growth in renewable energy, public transit, building retrofits, electric vehicles, grid modernization, and energy efficiency. Many countries would also have saved money through reduced air pollution, fewer climate damages, and less dependence on imported fuels.

Geopolitically, the world might have been less dependent on oil and gas exporters. Energy security concerns would have developed differently, and some fossil-fuel-rich states might have had less international leverage. At the same time, competition over clean-energy technology, critical minerals, and industrial policy would likely have emerged earlier.

Socially, earlier climate action could have reduced inequality if policies had been designed well: cleaner air in cities, cheaper efficient housing, better transit, and protection for vulnerable communities. But if handled poorly, it could also have produced backlash over energy prices and employment, much as climate policy still does today.

The biggest difference is that the world would have had more time. Acting after 1980 would not have stopped all warming, because oceans, ice sheets, and existing emissions create delayed effects. But it would have made the climate problem far less dangerous and far less expensive. Instead of facing an urgent race to decarbonize in a few decades, humanity might now be managing a slower, more controlled transition with fewer irreversible losses.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini
items.model_answer:
If the seven Marian/Catholic bishops had not died in 1558, Elizabeth I’s religious settlement would probably have been much harder to pass and might have failed in its 1559 form.

The key issue was the House of Lords. Elizabeth’s government could rely more easily on the Commons, but the Lords still contained a strong Catholic-conservative bloc, especially among the bishops. The Elizabethan Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity were already contested, and the Act of Uniformity, which restored an English Protestant prayer book, passed very narrowly. The deaths and resulting vacant bishoprics weakened the Catholic episcopal vote. If those bishops had lived and taken their seats, they likely would have voted against the settlement and could have defeated or forced major changes to it.

The most likely result would not be that England simply remained Catholic permanently. Elizabeth herself was committed to ending papal authority and to a Protestant-leaning national church. But she may have had to accept a slower, more conservative, or more ambiguous settlement: perhaps royal supremacy without such a clearly Protestant liturgy, or a revised prayer book with more Catholic-looking ceremonies and language. Alternatively, she might have delayed Parliament, used political pressure, created or mobilized loyal peers, or waited for vacancies before trying again.

A failed or delayed settlement would have had major consequences. Catholic clergy would have retained more institutional strength for longer. Protestant exiles returning from Geneva and Zurich would have had less immediate influence. The Church of England might have emerged as more conservative and less distinctly Protestant. The later Puritan challenge might also have looked different, because the Elizabethan church would have been less firmly shaped by the 1559 compromise.

Politically, delay would have been dangerous. A stronger Catholic hierarchy could have encouraged domestic resistance, especially in the north, and given foreign Catholic powers more reason to think Elizabeth’s regime was vulnerable. On the other hand, Spain initially preferred a stable Elizabeth to a French-backed Mary, Queen of Scots, so foreign intervention was not automatic.

So the careful answer is: without the deaths of those bishops, the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 probably would not have passed as it did. England would likely still have moved away from Rome under Elizabeth, but more slowly, with a more conservative church settlement and a greater risk of political-religious instability in the early years of her reign.

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." While Rome and Persia lost some cities along the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the Sasanian Empire retains Mesopotamia, and Rome defends the cities on the western coast of the Arabian peninsula, bordering the Red Sea and Judea. The Arabian Empire is then created as a religiously fanatical, militarized, yet mercantile and diplomatic empire. Islam still spreads through Islamic traders, though not as strongly in North Africa or the Mediterranean as a whole thanks to the Roman Tribunal Republic's stability and already existing religions. [By the first millennium CE, Rome's political system works like this:] [Provinces are ruled by Provincial Tribunes, elected by the people of the province from those who have not been in the military for at least four years. Additionally, some large cities, particularly coastal entrepot cities, become provinces in their own right. Each province can pass their own laws and manage their own administration, paying taxes to the Tribunal Treasury in Rome and following senatorial law]. [Each province (plus the city of Rome) elects two senators to represent them in the Tribunal Senate. No senator may have been in the military within the previous four years. The Tribunal Senate has no Consuls, instead having an "Orator," which is basically their Speaker. The longest-serving senator automatically becomes Orator. If the Senate passes a law, it can be vetoed by Provincial Tribunes if at least half of them vote on to veto the Senate law within one year of its passing. Provincial Tribunes may vote to send a law to the Senate for consideration, and if it is sent to the Senate and the Senate approves it, it cannot be vetoed no matter how many tribunes veto it].
