items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?
items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in South Dakota in 2004, the immediate national result would have been modest but important: Republicans would still have controlled the Senate, but with a smaller majority. Instead of a 55–44 Republican Senate with one independent, it would likely have been 54–45 with one independent caucusing with Democrats. George W. Bush still would have had a governing majority after his re-election, but Senate Democrats would have retained their most experienced leader.

The biggest change is that Daschle almost certainly would have remained Senate Democratic leader instead of being replaced by Harry Reid. That would have mattered for the tone and strategy of Democratic opposition during Bush’s second term. Daschle was an institutionalist and a skilled legislative negotiator, but also a symbol of Democratic resistance to Bush’s agenda, especially on taxes, judicial nominations, Social Security privatization, and the Iraq War. His survival would have been read as a major Democratic morale boost, because Republicans had made defeating him a national priority.

On policy, Bush’s second-term agenda probably still would have struggled. Social Security privatization failed in real history even with Daschle gone, so Daschle’s presence would likely have made Democratic resistance even more organized. On judicial nominations, the 2005 filibuster fight might still have happened, though Daschle’s style may have produced a somewhat different negotiation than the one that led to the “Gang of 14” compromise. Bush would still likely have placed John Roberts and Samuel Alito on the Supreme Court, because Republicans had the votes, but the confirmation battles might have been managed differently.

The 2006 midterms become more interesting. If the rest of the election results stayed the same, Democrats would have taken the Senate with a slightly larger margin because Daschle’s South Dakota seat would be Democratic rather than Republican. In that case, Daschle, not Reid, would probably have become Senate Majority Leader in 2007. That would have changed the face of Democratic congressional leadership during the final Bush years and the beginning of the Obama era.

A Daschle-led Senate might have been more policy-oriented and less combative in style than Reid’s Senate, though not necessarily more effective. Reid was exceptionally good at managing narrow majorities, difficult personalities, and procedural warfare. Daschle was also highly capable, but his leadership was more rooted in old Senate relationships and bipartisan negotiation. During 2007–2008, he likely would have pushed hard on Iraq oversight, ethics reform, minimum wage legislation, and opposition to Bush’s domestic agenda, much as Reid did.

The 2008 Democratic presidential race could also have been affected. In real life, Daschle became an important early supporter of Barack Obama and helped give Obama credibility with Democratic insiders. If Daschle were still Senate Majority Leader, he might have been more cautious about openly backing Obama against Hillary Clinton. His private influence could still have helped Obama, but his public role would have been more constrained. That could have slightly weakened Obama’s establishment support early on, though probably not enough by itself to change the nomination outcome.

If Obama still won in 2008, Daschle’s presence would have significantly affected health care reform. In real history, Obama wanted Daschle to be Secretary of Health and Human Services, but Daschle withdrew over tax issues. If he were Senate Majority Leader, he would not have been nominated for HHS. Instead, he would have been central to moving health reform through the Senate. Because Daschle had long studied health policy, he might have pushed for a more technocratic design, possibly including stronger cost-control mechanisms. But the basic constraints would remain: moderate Democrats, the filibuster, industry negotiations, and the need to get 60 votes. The Affordable Care Act, if passed, would probably still have been a compromise bill, not a dramatically more liberal one.

The largest long-term personal consequence is that John Thune would not have entered the Senate in 2005. Thune later became a major Republican leader and eventually one of the party’s most important Senate figures. If he lost again in 2004, his national rise might have been delayed or derailed, though he could still have run for office later.

So the broad answer is: Daschle’s re-election would not have changed control of the Senate in 2005 or stopped Bush’s presidency from moving forward, but it would have preserved a major Democratic leader at a crucial moment. It likely means no Harry Reid as Democratic leader, a stronger Democratic Senate position after 2006, a different internal dynamic around Obama’s rise, and a potentially different Senate strategy on health care reform. The biggest effects would be in leadership, legislative tactics, and party development rather than an immediate transformation of national policy.

items.original_question:
AHC: Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

It's 1930, you're put in charge of the military procurement of a smaller developed nation -- a small or middle/regional power: fairly wealthy, fairly industrialized, fairly well-educated workforce, with robust institutions...etc., but not a major power (think Poland, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Czechoslovakia, or Sweden). Despite the global depression, the government has magically found the funds for a major military expansion. The nation has a small military and professional officer corps to expand on, equipped with a smattering of WW1/post-WW1 weapons, but the point is you basically have nothing in large numbers so you essentially get to start from scratch. There's no massive stock of rifle ammunition forcing you to stick with a specific caliber for cost saving reasons, no huge pile of 2pdr shells in a warehouse forcing you to stay with the pom-pom...etc. Money is not the limiting factor (within reason); it's not infinite, but you're going to hit manpower constraints before budget constraints. In addition to the small professional military, the nation has a small armaments industry (e.g., Czech tanks/small arms, Canadian shipbuilding, Dutch aircraft design/manufacture) -- but not enough to design/build everything you need at scale. So you're going to have to buy/import a lot foreign, at least to start. The goal is a primarily defensive military that still has some expeditionary capability (not independent expeditionary operations, but in support of / in concert with great power allies). You're not aligned with a specific bloc so you can buy/import/adopt from wherever you want. Naval needs are more complicated and specific, so ignoring that to start: how do you equip your army and air force?
items.model_answer:
If you could build the best possible interwar army from scratch, the winning formula would not be “the biggest tank” or “the most men.” It would be a fully integrated combined-arms force: motorized logistics, radio-equipped armor, strong artillery, trained NCOs, tactical air support, and a doctrine built around rapid operational maneuver. In practice it would look like a cleaner, better-equipped version of the late-1930s German army, but with Soviet “deep battle” theory, British/American logistics, and fewer doctrinal blind spots.

The core would be a professional, highly trained army with universal literacy, a strong NCO corps, mission-type command, and extensive field exercises. Every headquarters down to battalion level, and every tank, would have reliable radios. That alone would put it ahead of most real interwar armies, many of which had good weapons but poor coordination.

Its armored force would avoid the interwar mistake of relying on tiny machine-gun tankettes or separate “infantry tanks” and “cruiser tanks.” The ideal main tank, using technology available by the late 1930s, would be a 25–30 ton medium tank with sloped armor, a three-man turret, a good radio, wide tracks, a reliable 400–500 hp engine, and a 50–75 mm dual-purpose gun. In real-world terms, it would be something like a T-34 concept with German crew layout and optics, built before 1939. That was technically plausible, though difficult. It would also need armored recovery vehicles, bridgelayers, fuel trucks, spare parts, and trained mechanics; without those, even the best tank force collapses.

The infantry would be motorized where possible, not merely foot infantry with a few trucks. Standard riflemen could carry bolt-action rifles or early semi-automatics such as the M1 Garand, but the real killing power would come from light machine guns, 50–81 mm mortars, grenades, and excellent communications. Each battalion would have organic mortars, anti-tank guns, engineers, signals troops, and enough trucks or carriers to move quickly behind the armored spearheads.

Artillery would be one of the army’s strongest arms. A best-case interwar force would have masses of 105 mm and 150/155 mm howitzers, modern fire-direction methods, forward observers with radios, sound-ranging and flash-spotting units, and fully motorized gun tractors. Most interwar armies underestimated how decisive fast, accurate artillery could be. This army would not.

Anti-tank and anti-aircraft defenses would be layered. In the late 1930s, 37 mm anti-tank guns were common but becoming marginal, so the ideal army would standardize early on 47–57 mm anti-tank guns and begin developing heavier 75 mm weapons. For air defense it would use 20 mm autocannon, Bofors-type 40 mm guns, and heavy 75/88 mm guns, all tied to early warning, searchlights, and good communications.

It would also need an attached tactical air arm. The best interwar army cannot be separated from air support. It would require modern monoplane fighters comparable to the Bf 109E, Spitfire, or Hurricane; fast reconnaissance aircraft; dive bombers or fighter-bombers for close support; and medium bombers for interdiction. The key would be not just aircraft quality, but air-ground coordination: forward air controllers, radios, preplanned strike procedures, and attacks on bridges, railheads, reserves, and headquarters rather than random battlefield bombing.

Doctrinally, the army would fight by breaking through with concentrated armor, engineers, artillery, and air support, then exploiting deep into the enemy rear to destroy command, supply, and reserves. It would not spread tanks thinly among infantry divisions. Armored and motorized formations would operate in corps-sized groups, while infantry followed to reduce pockets and hold ground.

The main limitation would be cost. Such an army would be smaller than a mass conscript force, and it would consume huge amounts of fuel, rubber, radios, spare parts, ammunition, trained mechanics, and staff officers. It would be devastating in a short campaign against 1930s opponents, but if the war became long and attritional, industrial capacity and access to oil would matter more than clever design.

So the “best possible interwar army” would be a radio-connected, motorized, artillery-heavy, air-supported combined-arms army built around reliable medium tanks and professional command. Against most real armies of 1939, it would be overwhelmingly effective. Its greatest danger would not be battlefield inferiority, but overextension, fuel shortage, and the inability of its economy to sustain such an advanced force over time.

Now, the methods can be as creative as you'd want, was extra development of agriculture/synthetics possible (I know I said breaking of the blockade, but anything that gives the Germans a good food source counts)? items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the war would probably have lasted longer, cost the Allies more, and given Germany a better chance of forcing a favorable settlement in Europe. But it would not automatically have meant German victory.

The biggest change would have been oil. Germany’s war machine was chronically fuel-constrained. Tanks, trucks, aircraft, submarines, pilot training, and operational reserves all depended on fuel Germany never had in sufficient quantity. A reliable oil supply would have made the Wehrmacht more mobile, kept the Luftwaffe flying at a higher tempo, allowed better pilot training, and reduced the catastrophic paralysis Germany experienced in 1944–45 when aircraft, tanks, and vehicles often existed but could not be used effectively.

This could have changed the Eastern Front most dramatically. Germany’s 1942 drive toward the Caucasus was heavily influenced by the need for oil. If Germany already had secure oil, it might not have gambled so heavily on the Caucasus and Stalingrad. It could have concentrated more rationally on destroying Soviet forces, holding defensible lines, or renewing the drive toward Moscow. With adequate fuel and rubber, German logistics would have been stronger: more trucks operating longer, fewer mobility breakdowns, and more sustained armored operations. That might have made Soviet recovery harder and delayed or even prevented some Soviet counteroffensives.

Food would also have mattered. Germany relied heavily on extracting food from occupied Europe and the Soviet territories, often brutally. A sustainable food supply would have reduced pressure on the home front and possibly reduced the economic desperation behind some occupation policies, though it would not have changed the ideological brutality of the Nazi regime. Better food security would have helped civilian morale and labor productivity, making the Allied blockade less strategically effective.

Rubber was less dramatic than oil but still important. Tires, seals, belts, gaskets, aircraft components, vehicle maintenance, and naval equipment all depended on rubber. A secure rubber supply would have improved Germany’s ability to keep vehicles and aircraft operational, especially in a long mechanized war.

The Allied blockade would therefore have lost much of its value. Britain’s strategy depended partly on the assumption that Germany could be strangled economically over time. If Germany could not be starved of food, fuel, or rubber, Britain and later the United States would have had to rely even more heavily on direct military pressure: bombing, invasion, Soviet offensives, and naval containment.

Still, Germany would face enormous structural problems. The United States, Soviet Union, and British Empire together possessed far greater industrial capacity, manpower reserves, shipbuilding ability, and strategic depth. Germany also suffered from poor grand strategy, ideological decision-making, inefficient production priorities, interservice rivalry, and Hitler’s increasingly destructive interference. Secure resources would not solve those problems.

The air war would also remain difficult for Germany. More oil would help the Luftwaffe train pilots and keep fighters in the air, making Allied bombing more costly. But the Allies had immense aircraft production, better long-range strategic reach, radar, intelligence advantages, and eventually overwhelming numbers. Germany could resist longer, but not necessarily regain air superiority over Western Europe.

The most plausible outcome is not that Germany conquers the world, but that the war becomes longer and more uncertain. If Germany used its improved resource position effectively in 1941–42, it might have had a better chance of defeating the Soviet Union or forcing Stalin into a temporary settlement. That would have been the truly dangerous possibility for the Allies: a Germany secure on the continent, supplied with fuel and food, no longer fighting a massive eastern land war, and able to concentrate against Britain and later the United States.

But if the Soviet Union remained in the war and the United States fully mobilized, Germany would still likely lose eventually, though later and at much higher cost. By 1945–46, if Germany were still fighting, the United States might also have considered using atomic weapons against German targets, depending on the state of the war.

So the direct answer is: secure supplies of food, oil, and rubber would have greatly strengthened Nazi Germany and might have prevented some of its worst strategic crises, especially on the Eastern Front. It could have prolonged the war and possibly opened the door to a negotiated or temporary German-dominated Europe if the USSR were knocked out. But unless Germany also solved its manpower, industrial, strategic, and political failures, sustainable resources alone would probably not be enough to defeat the combined power of the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer:
If nuclear fission had been understood early enough for a practical reactor to be built around 1900, the nuclear age would likely have arrived roughly four decades earlier, but it would not have produced an immediate “atomic-powered Edwardian world.” The first effects would have been scientific, military, and geopolitical before they became broadly economic.

A reactor around 1900 would probably have been a crude natural-uranium, graphite-moderated pile, closer in spirit to Chicago Pile-1 than to a modern power plant. Steam turbines, electrical generators, mining, and metallurgy already existed, so converting reactor heat into electricity was not impossible. But the supporting technologies were weak: radiation measurement was primitive, materials science was immature, chemical purification of graphite and uranium would have been difficult, and there was little understanding of long-term radiation sickness, contamination, or reactor safety. Early reactors would likely have been dangerous, inefficient, and built under the control of governments, universities, or large industrial combines rather than as commercial power stations.

The most immediate historical change would be in physics. Nuclear structure, isotopes, neutron behavior, and radioactivity would have advanced much faster. Quantum mechanics might have developed differently or earlier, because unexplained nuclear phenomena would have forced theorists to confront atomic structure sooner. Medicine would also change: radioisotopes for diagnosis and treatment could appear earlier, but so would radiation injuries, contaminated laboratories, and industrial accidents before proper safety standards emerged.

Economically, nuclear power would not instantly replace coal. Around 1900, coal was cheap, abundant, and already integrated into railways, factories, ships, and urban heating. Early reactors would be expensive and unreliable, and electricity grids were still developing. Nuclear energy would likely first be used in specialized roles: research, military production, isotope generation, and perhaps demonstration power stations near major cities or industrial centers. Large-scale civilian nuclear electricity might arrive in the 1920s or 1930s instead of the 1950s and 1960s.

The biggest consequences would be military. A working reactor implies the ability to produce intense neutron fluxes and, eventually, plutonium. Even if no one immediately understood how to make a bomb, the path toward nuclear weapons would become visible much earlier. By World War I, the major powers might have had nuclear research programs, though usable atomic bombs by 1914 would still be unlikely unless the counterfactual includes a very advanced understanding of critical mass, isotope separation, and fast-neutron physics. More plausible is that World War I accelerates reactor and radiochemistry work, leading to nuclear weapons in the 1920s or 1930s.

That would profoundly alter the interwar period. Instead of the Manhattan Project emerging during World War II, Britain, Germany, France, Russia, and the United States might all treat uranium and thorium resources as strategic assets after World War I. Colonial mining regions in Africa, Central Asia, and Canada would become even more geopolitically important. Arms control debates might begin after the First World War, alongside chemical weapons treaties. If atomic bombs were developed by the 1930s, World War II could begin in a world where one or more powers already possessed nuclear weapons—or where fear of them shaped strategy from the start.

The outcome could go in two very different directions. Nuclear weapons might be used earlier, perhaps against cities in a 1930s or 1940s war, with less mature international law and weaker humanitarian norms than existed in 1945. That could make the twentieth century even more catastrophic. Alternatively, if several powers developed nuclear weapons before a major war, deterrence might make leaders more cautious, potentially preventing or limiting a second world war. But early nuclear command systems would be crude, communications unreliable, and political institutions less experienced, so the risk of accidental or panicked use would be high.

Domestic politics would also change. States would become more secretive and technocratic earlier. Nuclear research requires concentrated funding, tight security, specialized expertise, and control over raw materials. This could strengthen centralized governments and military-scientific bureaucracies before World War I. It might also create earlier public fear of “invisible” industrial hazards, especially if early accidents contaminated workers, cities, or rivers. A serious reactor disaster in the 1910s or 1920s could produce a strong anti-nuclear movement long before the real-world Cold War.

Environmentally, the long-term effects are ambiguous. If nuclear power matured earlier and displaced some coal by the mid-twentieth century, global carbon emissions could be lower. Urban air pollution might decline sooner in industrial countries. But early reactors would likely have poor waste handling, weak containment, and little concept of ecological contamination. The world might inherit more badly managed nuclear waste sites from an era with almost no radiation regulation.

So the most likely answer is: fission in 1900 would shift the nuclear timeline forward by decades, transform physics and geopolitics, and make nuclear weapons a central issue before or during World War II. It would not immediately create cheap universal atomic power, because the industrial, safety, and grid technologies were not ready. The world would gain a powerful new energy source earlier, but also face nuclear secrecy, accidents, radioactive contamination, and the possibility of atomic warfare at a less politically mature stage of modern history.

human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!
items.model_answer:
An exotic party system could be imagined as a political system where parties are not permanent ideological blocs, but temporary, issue-based alliances that form and dissolve around specific public problems.

In this system, voters would not choose one party for everything. Instead, each voter could divide their political support across several “policy parties”: for example, an environmental party for climate issues, a labor party for workplace rights, a localist party for regional policy, and a civil-liberties party for rights and justice. Parliament or congress would then be composed not only by general party vote, but also by strength in different policy areas.

The most unusual feature would be that parties would have expiration dates. Every few years, they would need to re-register, prove public support, and clearly define their current goals. This would prevent parties from becoming old machines that survive only through loyalty, money, or identity. New movements could enter more easily, while obsolete parties would disappear.

Government would be formed through “modular coalitions.” Instead of one ruling party controlling all policy, different coalitions could govern different domains. A green-left coalition might control climate policy, a centrist-business coalition might control trade, and a civil-rights coalition might control constitutional issues. The prime minister or executive would coordinate these coalitions rather than command a single majority.

The benefit of such an exotic system would be flexibility. It would better reflect voters who are not purely left-wing, right-wing, liberal, conservative, nationalist, or socialist, but mixed in their views. It could reduce polarization because parties would need to cooperate across issues.

The danger is instability. If parties constantly form and dissolve, voters may become confused, governments may become fragmented, and accountability may weaken. It might be hard to know who is responsible when policy fails. Wealthy groups could also create short-lived parties to influence one issue and then vanish.

So, an exotic party system could be creative and more representative, but it would need strong rules: transparency in funding, clear coalition agreements, independent election supervision, and mechanisms to hold temporary parties accountable. Otherwise, it could become chaotic rather than democratic.

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had kept developing Falcon Heavy and Crew Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions instead of shifting that role to Starship, the most likely result would have been a more modest but earlier commercial lunar capability: crewed lunar flybys and possibly lunar-orbit missions, but not a full reusable Moon-landing system without major additional hardware.

Falcon Heavy could plausibly send a modified Crew Dragon on a free-return trajectory around the Moon. That was the basis of SpaceX’s 2017 plan to fly private passengers around the Moon using Falcon Heavy and Dragon 2. To make that real, SpaceX would have needed to human-rate Falcon Heavy, validate Crew Dragon for deep-space reentry speeds, expand life support duration, improve radiation protection, add deep-space communications and navigation, and certify mission profiles beyond low Earth orbit. None of those are trivial, but they are much less ambitious than building Starship.

The first likely outcome would have been a commercial circumlunar flight sometime in the early-to-mid 2020s, assuming SpaceX prioritized it and NASA or private customers accepted the risk. It would have resembled Apollo 8 in broad outline only in the sense of sending humans around the Moon, but technically it would probably have been simpler: no lunar orbit insertion, no landing, just a free-return loop around the Moon and back to Earth. Dragon’s heat shield technology was probably adaptable to lunar-return speeds, but it would have required testing and certification.

Going beyond a flyby would have been much harder. Crew Dragon does not have the propulsion capability to enter and leave lunar orbit by itself. For a true lunar-orbit mission, SpaceX would have needed an additional propulsion module, a larger service module, or a separately launched stage that Dragon could dock with in Earth orbit. Falcon Heavy could support such an architecture, but it would become a multi-launch mission with orbital rendezvous, docking, and perhaps propellant-management challenges. It would still be feasible in principle, but no longer as clean as “Falcon Heavy launches Dragon to the Moon.”

A crewed lunar landing using Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have required an entirely separate lunar lander. Dragon could perhaps serve as the crew transport from Earth to lunar orbit, while a lander launched separately would handle descent and ascent. That architecture would look more like a commercialized Apollo-style system: Dragon as the command module, Falcon Heavy as the heavy launcher, and another vehicle as the lunar module. SpaceX could have developed or partnered on such a lander, but Falcon Heavy’s payload limits would likely force multiple launches, tight mass constraints, or expendable launch profiles.

The biggest strategic effect is that SpaceX might have become a serious near-term competitor to Orion/SLS for some lunar missions. A Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar flyby would likely have been far cheaper than an SLS/Orion mission, and if demonstrated successfully it would have increased pressure on NASA to buy commercial crewed deep-space transport. However, it probably would not have fully replaced Orion for NASA’s Artemis architecture without extensive redesign, because Orion was built for longer-duration deep-space operations, lunar orbit, and integration with NASA’s broader exploration plans.

The tradeoff is that Starship would likely have been delayed or deemphasized. SpaceX would have gained a more conservative, incremental lunar program, but at the cost of pursuing a less transformative system. Falcon Heavy and Dragon could have delivered impressive “Apollo 8-class” missions and perhaps supported early commercial lunar-orbit operations, but they would not have offered the same payload capacity, reusability, surface cargo delivery, or Mars ambitions that Starship was intended to provide.

So the counterfactual answer is: SpaceX probably could have flown people around the Moon with Falcon Heavy and a modified Dragon earlier than Starship will fly crewed lunar missions, and it might have created a lower-cost commercial alternative for lunar flybys and perhaps lunar orbit. But crewed landings would still have required a separate lander and a more complex multi-launch architecture. It would have been a nearer-term, narrower lunar program—not a full replacement for Starship’s long-term ambitions.

items.original_question: What if the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto? items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a follow-up attack on Taranto soon after the November 1940 raid, the most likely result would have been a larger but still not war-deciding Italian naval disaster.

The first Taranto attack succeeded because it achieved surprise. It damaged three Italian battleships—Conte di Cavour, Littorio, and Caio Duilio—and temporarily shifted the naval balance in the Mediterranean toward Britain. A second raid, especially the following night, might have finished off already damaged ships, hit repair facilities, or possibly damaged one or more of the remaining operational battleships such as Vittorio Veneto or Giulio Cesare. If that had happened, the Regia Marina’s battleship force could have been crippled for many months rather than merely reduced.

That would have made Britain’s position in the Mediterranean stronger. Malta convoys, movements to Greece and Egypt, and Royal Navy operations in the central Mediterranean would have faced less danger from Italian heavy surface forces. Italy might have become even more cautious than it already was, and a later action like Cape Matapan in March 1941 might either not have happened or would have occurred under even worse conditions for the Italians.

But the second attack would also have been much harder. The Italians would no longer have been surprised. Anti-aircraft crews would have been alert, smoke screens and defenses improved, and British aircraft losses probably higher. HMS Illustrious would also have had to remain in dangerous waters longer, increasing the risk from Italian air attack, submarines, or surface forces. The British carrier force in the Mediterranean was too valuable to risk casually.

So the likely answer is: a second Taranto attack might have deepened the Italian defeat and given Britain a stronger short-term naval advantage, perhaps delaying Italian fleet operations for months. But it probably would not have knocked Italy out of the war or solved the wider Mediterranean problem. Axis convoys to North Africa still depended heavily on smaller ships, submarines, destroyers, aircraft, and later German air power. The strategic balance would improve for Britain, but the campaign would not be decided by Taranto alone.

items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow provided 100,000 troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, it probably would have made the Normandy campaign bloodier and possibly slower, but it would not likely have changed the final outcome of the war.

The first issue is plausibility. By 1944 Vichy France no longer had real military independence. After the Allied landings in North Africa in 1942, Germany occupied the previously “unoccupied” zone of France and disbanded most of the Vichy armistice army. Vichy could supply police, militia, labor, and small collaborationist formations, but raising and deploying 100,000 reliable French troops for coastal defense would have required German approval, German equipment, German command integration, and a major political decision to trust French units with weapons. That trust was doubtful, because many French soldiers were anti-German, pro-Allied, or at least unwilling to die defending German occupation.

Assuming the 100,000 troops existed, their effect would depend heavily on where they were placed. If they were spread thinly along the whole Atlantic Wall from the Netherlands to southern France, their impact on D-Day would have been limited. The Atlantic Wall was enormous, and 100,000 men across such a front would mostly improve local garrison strength without solving Germany’s main problems: Allied air superiority, naval gunfire, logistical weakness, poor mobility, and uncertainty about where the invasion would land.

If, however, they were concentrated in Normandy, the effect could have been more serious. One hundred thousand men is roughly the equivalent of several infantry divisions. Additional defenders in the Cotentin, around Caen, or behind Omaha and Juno beaches could have increased Allied casualties, slowed the beachhead expansion, and made German counterattacks more dangerous in the first days after 6 June. Omaha Beach in particular was already a near-run battle; stronger defenses there could have made the landing still more costly and might have forced a local evacuation or temporary failure.

But even in that stronger scenario, the Allies would still have held major advantages. They controlled the air and sea, could bombard coastal positions heavily, and had immense reserves of men, ships, vehicles, and supplies. German armored reserves were constrained by Hitler’s command system, Allied deception, fuel shortages, and air attack. Additional French infantry would not solve those structural problems. Unless those troops were unusually well-trained, well-equipped, highly motivated, and positioned exactly at the decisive points, they would probably delay the Allies rather than defeat them.

Morale and loyalty would be the biggest weakness. Many French soldiers ordered to fight Americans, British, Canadians, and Free French forces on French soil might have surrendered quickly, deserted, passed information to the Resistance, or fought half-heartedly. Allied psychological warfare would have emphasized that they were Frenchmen dying for Germany. The Resistance would likely have targeted them, and German commanders might have distrusted them enough to assign them static or secondary roles, reducing their battlefield value.

Politically, the consequences would have been severe. Vichy’s collaboration would have appeared even more direct and military, not merely administrative or police-based. The postwar reckoning in France would probably have been harsher, with deeper purges, more trials, and a sharper civil conflict between Resistance forces and collaborators. De Gaulle’s claim that Vichy was illegitimate would have been strengthened, while any later attempt to portray Vichy as a shield for French interests would have been much harder to sustain.

So the most likely result is: the Normandy invasion becomes more costly and perhaps slower, especially if the French troops are concentrated near the landing zones, but Germany still loses France. The larger strategic balance in 1944—Allied material superiority, Soviet pressure in the east, Allied air power, and German logistical collapse—would not be reversed by 100,000 Vichy troops. At most, they might have delayed liberation by weeks or possibly a few months; they probably would not have prevented it.

Germany and its friends would be pleased to hear that. As I understand it, the Haber-Bosch process spread more slowly than people often assume. Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. In the 1910s, Germany was the only country in the world capable of doing both. In the OTL, once the Haber process had been developed, the First World War broke out almost immediately. During that period, all resources were directed not toward chemical fertilizer production, but toward the development of explosives. Even afterward, BASF maintained its monopoly over the Haber method.

items.original_question: What if World War I had occurred 9 years earlier? The First Moroccan Crisis occurred between 1905 and 1906 during the Russo-Japanese War. Although this event did not escalate into a full-scale military conflict, it was resolved through the Algeciras Conference. However, tensions between the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente grew stronger. Then, in 1911, the Second Moroccan Crisis took place. At this time, there were talks of a potential war, but ultimately it was resolved through international negotiations. Despite these series of events, in 1914, World War I broke out due to the assassination of the Austrian Archduke and the subsequent invasion of Serbia. This raises an interesting question. During the July Crisis in the OTL, there were numerous efforts to avoid war, but in the end, the arrogance of autocratic monarchs and the complex web of interests caused tensions to escalate and ultimately explode. What if such a chain reaction and explosion had occurred during the First Moroccan Crisis? What if the First Moroccan Crisis had escalated into a full-blown war, leading to World War I happening 9 years earlier than in the OTL? What could have been the consequences of such a scenario? Here are the questions in English: 1. In 1905, how does the military strength of countries such as the United Kingdom, France, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the Kingdom of Italy compare to that of 1914 in OTL? Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? And how would Roosevelt's vision for the post-war world differ from Wilson's? 3. The Russian Empire, after the Russo-Japanese War in OTL, pursued reforms like constitutional monarchy changes and Stolypin’s agricultural reforms. However, in this TL, war breaks out before such reforms happen. What impact do you think this would have on Russia? I believe Russia would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL. However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?
items.model_answer:
If World War I had broken out nine years earlier, in 1905 rather than 1914, it would probably have been a very different war: more favorable to Germany, less globally mobilized, and less likely to produce the exact chain of outcomes that led to the Russian Revolution, Versailles, fascism, and World War II as we know them.

The most plausible spark would have been the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905 or a Balkan crisis involving Austria-Hungary and Russia, not the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Europe already had dangerous alliance structures: Germany and Austria-Hungary were tied together, France and Russia were allied, and Britain had recently reached the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904. But the alliance system was not yet as hardened as it became by 1914. Britain was not as firmly committed to France, Anglo-German rivalry was serious but less intense, and military coordination between Britain and France was less developed. That means a 1905 war might not automatically have become the same full-scale “Triple Entente versus Central Powers” conflict.

Germany would likely have been in a stronger relative position. Russia had just been badly weakened by the Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 Revolution. Its army, navy, finances, and domestic stability were in poor condition. In 1914 Russia was still inefficient but much stronger than in 1905. France, therefore, would have faced Germany with a weaker Russian partner. If Germany attacked France through Belgium, Britain might still have entered the war to defend Belgian neutrality, but British involvement would have been less certain and probably slower. If Britain stayed neutral, France would have been in grave danger.

The war itself would probably have been less technologically advanced but still extremely deadly. Machine guns, rapid-fire artillery, rail mobilization, barbed wire, and modern rifles already existed, so it would not have been a purely nineteenth-century war. However, aircraft, tanks, poison gas, advanced submarines, and the enormous shell-production systems of 1914–1918 were either absent or immature. The conflict might have been somewhat more mobile at first, but trench warfare could still have emerged if offensives failed. The great difference is that governments and economies were less prepared for a long “total war,” so political pressure for a negotiated peace might have come sooner.

A German victory would have been more likely than in 1914, especially if Britain did not intervene decisively. Germany might have defeated France quickly, imposed indemnities or colonial concessions, and strengthened its dominance in continental Europe. Russia, already unstable in 1905, might have been forced into humiliation, deeper revolution, or major internal reform. Austria-Hungary might have survived longer under German protection, though its ethnic tensions would not have disappeared.

If Britain did enter, the war could still have widened into a major European and imperial conflict, but the balance would be different. Britain’s navy was still superior, and Germany’s dreadnought challenge had not yet fully developed. A British blockade would have hurt Germany, but Germany’s submarine campaign would have been far less effective than in the later war. The United States would almost certainly have remained neutral; in 1905 it was less prepared and less politically inclined to intervene in a European war.

The biggest long-term change is that the familiar twentieth century would likely not unfold the same way. A 1905 war would probably not produce the exact conditions of 1917–1919: no identical Russian Revolution, no Versailles settlement in the same form, no Weimar Republic created by defeat in 1918, and therefore no Nazi rise in the same way. Instead, Europe might have seen either an earlier German-dominated order or a shorter, negotiated war that postponed the great reckoning rather than resolving it.

So, if World War I had occurred nine years earlier, it would likely have been less global, less technologically “total,” and more favorable to Germany. It might have prevented the specific disasters that followed the real First World War, but it would not necessarily have made the twentieth century peaceful. The underlying rivalries—German power, Russian weakness and ambition, French revanchism, British fear of continental domination, and Balkan nationalism—would still have remained.

items.original_question: What if A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections I'm trying to create a 1996 US election scenario where the Democrats have the Jay Rockefeller/Henry Cisneros ticket, while the Republicans have the Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander ticket. I have a test map showing which states are likely to be won by each party, but there are some states where I'm not sure who would win. That's why I'm asking for help figuring out how many states the Democrats and Republicans would win. I appreciate any suggestions P.S. I forgot to add Indiana as a Republican.
items.model_answer:
Assuming “Rockefeller” means Senator Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia and the 1996 race is an open contest rather than Bill Clinton seeking reelection, a Rockefeller/Cisneros Democratic ticket would probably defeat a Quayle/Alexander Republican ticket, but by a narrower margin than Clinton/Gore’s real 1996 victory over Dole/Kemp.

Jay Rockefeller would have run as a moderate-to-liberal Democrat with strong credentials on health care, poverty, and social policy, plus personal wealth and establishment credibility. Henry Cisneros, former mayor of San Antonio and Clinton’s HUD secretary, would add urban-policy experience and Latino representation, helping Democrats especially in the Southwest and among Hispanic voters. The ticket would likely emphasize economic stability, welfare reform with a softer edge, health care, education, and continuity with the general direction of the Clinton years, but without Clinton’s personal charisma.

Dan Quayle heading the Republican ticket would be a major liability. Although he had conservative credentials and name recognition as George H. W. Bush’s vice president, by 1996 he was still widely mocked as inexperienced and gaffe-prone. Lamar Alexander as running mate would help somewhat: he was more serious, competent, and associated with education reform and moderate Southern Republicanism. But Alexander probably would not fully neutralize doubts about Quayle at the top of the ticket.

The campaign would likely be less about ideology than competence. Rockefeller would attack Quayle as unready to be president, while Quayle would portray Rockefeller as an out-of-touch liberal heir from one of America’s richest families. Republicans would also likely attack Cisneros over the personal and legal controversies that surrounded him in the mid-1990s. That could damage the Democratic ticket, but probably not enough to make Quayle look like the safer choice.

Regionally, Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely hold most of the Democratic base: the Northeast, the Pacific Coast, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and probably much of the Upper Midwest. Rockefeller would be especially strong in West Virginia and could help in nearby Appalachian or working-class states, though he would not have Clinton’s Southern appeal. Cisneros could help in California, New Mexico, and among Latino voters generally, but Texas would probably still vote Republican.

Quayle/Alexander would likely do better than Dole/Kemp in parts of the South and among social conservatives, and Alexander might help in Tennessee and neighboring states. The GOP would probably carry most of the Great Plains, Mountain West, and Deep South. But Quayle’s weaknesses would make it hard to win enough swing states such as Pennsylvania, Michigan, New Jersey, Wisconsin, or Florida.

A plausible result would be a Democratic victory with something like 300 to 330 electoral votes, rather than Clinton’s real 379. The popular vote might be roughly Rockefeller/Cisneros 49–51%, Quayle/Alexander 42–45%, with Ross Perot or another Reform Party candidate still taking a smaller but meaningful share.

The broader consequences would be significant. Without Clinton’s personal dominance, the Democrats would probably have a less charismatic but more technocratic presidency. A Rockefeller administration might focus more heavily on health care, anti-poverty policy, education, and incremental welfare-state reform. Cisneros could push housing and urban investment higher on the agenda. Republicans, meanwhile, might conclude after a Quayle defeat that the party needed a fresher, more disciplined conservative standard-bearer in 2000, possibly accelerating the rise of George W. Bush or another governor-style Republican.

In short: Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely beat Quayle/Alexander in 1996 because the economy and national mood favored Democrats and because Quayle would be a weak Republican nominee. But the Democratic win would probably be smaller, less personal, and less Southern-based than Clinton’s real-life victory.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and survived, the history of mountaineering would have changed dramatically, though the broader course of world history probably would not.

The immediate result would have been a huge British triumph. In the 1920s Everest was closely tied to imperial prestige: Britain had failed to reach the North Pole and South Pole first, and Everest had become a symbolic “third pole.” A successful Mallory-Irvine ascent would have been celebrated as one of the great achievements of the British Empire. Mallory, already famous, would likely have become a national hero on the scale later occupied by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay.

It would also mean that the first ascent of Everest occurred nearly thirty years earlier than in our timeline, using far more primitive equipment. That would have transformed perceptions of what was possible in high-altitude climbing. Their success would have validated the use of early oxygen apparatus and the northern route from Tibet. The famous question of whether Mallory and Irvine reached the top before dying would never have become one of mountaineering’s great mysteries.

The 1953 ascent by Hillary and Tenzing would still have been important, but it would not have been the first ascent. It might be remembered instead as the first confirmed postwar ascent, the first ascent from Nepal by the South Col route, or the ascent that reopened Everest to the modern era. Tenzing’s role as a Sherpa climber would still have mattered greatly, but the symbolic breakthrough would have been different: less “humanity conquers Everest for the first time,” more “Everest is climbed again by a new route and a new generation.”

Mallory’s survival could also have influenced later climbing culture. He might have written and lectured extensively, shaping mountaineering ethics and technique. Irvine, only twenty-two, might have become a major figure in expedition engineering or high-altitude climbing. Their account would have provided invaluable details about the Second Step, oxygen use, weather, and human performance near 29,000 feet. If they proved that the Second Step could be climbed with 1920s equipment, later debates about the feasibility of their real-life attempt would never have arisen.

There would likely have been fewer British expeditions obsessively focused on “finishing” Everest in the 1930s, since the main prize would already have been won. However, Everest would not have become easy or routine. The mountain would still have killed many climbers, and Himalayan mountaineering would still have developed slowly because of weather, altitude, politics, and limited access to Tibet and Nepal.

Politically, the achievement would have reinforced British imperial confidence in the interwar period, but it would not have stopped the decline of empire, the rise of nationalist movements, or the coming of World War II. Its effects would have been cultural rather than geopolitical: a powerful myth of British courage and endurance, added to the heroic memory of the First World War generation.

In short, if Mallory and Irvine had summited and survived, they would be remembered as the undisputed first conquerors of Everest, the 1953 Hillary-Tenzing ascent would lose its “first ascent” status, and the mythology of Everest would center on a 1924 imperial-era triumph rather than a postwar Commonwealth achievement. The biggest change would be in mountaineering history and national symbolism, not in the fundamental trajectory of the twentieth century.
