items.model_answer:
If the USSR received credible, detailed information about Operation Barbarossa shortly before 22 June 1941 and Stalin actually acted on it, the invasion would still be extremely dangerous, but the opening catastrophe would likely be much less severe.

The biggest change would be in the first days. Historically, Soviet units on the western frontier were caught in a confused half-peace, half-war posture. Aircraft were parked wingtip-to-wingtip, ammunition and fuel were poorly distributed, communications were fragile, commanders were afraid to act without permission, and many forward armies were positioned in ways that made them vulnerable to encirclement. If Moscow had accepted the leak as real, the USSR could have quietly put frontier forces on alert, dispersed aircraft, loaded ammunition, prepared demolitions, moved headquarters, activated air defenses, and warned commanders to expect immediate German attack.

That alone would probably prevent one of the worst historical disasters: the destruction of much of the Soviet air force on the ground. The Luftwaffe would still win air superiority, but not as cheaply. German spearheads would still break through in places, but they would face more organized resistance, more blown bridges, more prepared artillery, and fewer Soviet formations frozen by contradictory orders.

The main strategic effect would be fewer giant encirclements. Historically, the Germans annihilated huge Soviet forces at Białystok-Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, Vyazma-Bryansk, and especially Kiev. If the Soviet leadership were more competent in 1941, it might withdraw from exposed salients earlier rather than ordering doomed stands. Avoiding or reducing the Kiev encirclement alone could preserve hundreds of thousands of men and large amounts of equipment. That would seriously weaken Germany’s chance of reaching Moscow in force.

Germany would probably still advance deep into Soviet territory. The Red Army in 1941 had real structural problems: poor communications, inexperienced officers, incomplete mechanized formations, weak logistics, and the aftereffects of purges and rapid expansion. A warning would not magically fix those. German armored and air doctrine was still superior at the start, and the Wehrmacht would retain the initiative. So this is not a scenario where the USSR easily stops Germany at the border.

But Barbarossa depended on destroying the Red Army quickly. If the Soviets are prepared enough to avoid the worst opening losses, the German plan begins to fail even earlier. Army Group Center might still take Minsk and reach Smolensk, but later and at higher cost. Army Group North might struggle more to isolate Leningrad. Army Group South would have a much harder time achieving a massive Kiev-style victory. By autumn 1941 the Germans would likely be exhausted farther west than they were historically, with fewer Soviet losses and stronger Soviet reserves.

The Battle of Moscow might either not happen in the same form or would be much less favorable to Germany. Instead of German forces reaching the outskirts of Moscow after months of huge encirclements, they might stall earlier, perhaps around Smolensk, the upper Dnieper, or short of the historical Moscow line. If they still tried for Moscow, they would face a larger and less shattered Red Army.

The war would probably still be long, but shorter and less catastrophic for the USSR. A better-prepared Soviet Union in 1941 might save millions of soldiers and civilians, preserve more industry and equipment, and begin counteroffensives from a stronger position in 1942. Germany would have less captured Soviet matériel, fewer prisoners, and less time to exploit Ukraine and western Russia. The Wehrmacht’s failure before winter would be clearer and more damaging.

A plausible outcome is that the Eastern Front turns against Germany earlier, perhaps in 1942 rather than after Stalingrad in late 1942–43. Stalingrad as we know it might not happen, because Germany may never reach the Volga in such strength. The decisive Soviet counteroffensive could occur farther west, or Germany might be forced into a defensive war much sooner.

Politically, the Allies still side with the USSR because Germany still invades. Since there is no Soviet first strike, Hitler cannot credibly claim a defensive war. Japan probably still avoids attacking Siberia, especially if the USSR looks more resilient from the beginning.

The broader consequence is that Nazi Germany likely loses faster. The USSR emerges from the war less devastated and possibly stronger diplomatically. Depending on the timing of Germany’s collapse, Soviet armies might either occupy even more of Eastern and Central Europe, because they advance earlier, or the Western Allies might adjust their plans to land sooner. But the central point is clear: a prepared, competent Soviet response in June 1941 would not stop Barbarossa at the frontier, but it would probably prevent the worst Soviet disasters of 1941 and make Germany’s invasion fail sooner and more decisively.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?
items.model_answer:
Without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, modern popular music would probably still exist in recognizable form, but its development would have been slower, less unified, and shaped by different figures.

Elvis Presley did not invent rock and roll, but he became its first global mass-market symbol. He brought together rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and pop in a way that made rock acceptable to a huge white mainstream audience in the 1950s. Without Elvis, rock and roll would still have emerged through artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others. But its crossover into mainstream American and global youth culture might have been less sudden and less commercially explosive. Black pioneers may have received more direct recognition, though the music industry might also have found another white performer to play a similar crossover role.

Without The Beatles, the biggest change would be in the 1960s transformation of pop music into an album-centered, artist-driven, experimental form. The Beatles helped make it normal for bands to write their own songs, treat studio recording as an art form, explore psychedelia, and present popular music as culturally serious rather than just entertainment. Other artists—Bob Dylan, The Beach Boys, The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, The Who, Motown writers and producers, Jimi Hendrix, and later progressive and psychedelic bands—would still have pushed music forward. But the specific speed and scale of that shift would likely have been reduced.

The “British Invasion” would also have looked very different. British rock may still have reached the United States through The Rolling Stones, The Animals, The Who, or other groups, but The Beatles gave that movement its decisive commercial and cultural force. Without them, American rock, soul, folk, surf, and Motown might have remained more dominant for longer, and British bands may have had a smaller or later global impact.

Pop songwriting would likely be different too. The Beatles helped establish the model of the self-contained band: performers who wrote, arranged, recorded, and evolved their own material. Without them, the industry might have remained more dependent for longer on professional songwriting teams, producers, and label-controlled performers. Singer-songwriters and bands would still have risen, especially through folk and rock traditions, but the prestige attached to the “band as auteur” would be weaker.

Rock’s later genres would still exist, but with different lineages. Hard rock, metal, punk, indie, Britpop, power pop, psychedelic rock, progressive rock, and alternative rock all drew directly or indirectly from The Beatles or from the cultural space they helped create. Those genres would not disappear, because they also came from blues, garage rock, folk, soul, and experimental music. But their sound, mythology, and timing would be noticeably altered.

Popular culture itself would also be less centered on the idea of the pop musician as a generational icon. Elvis helped define the rebellious solo star; The Beatles helped define the band as a cultural movement. Without them, youth culture might have attached itself more strongly to other figures: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Bob Dylan, James Brown, The Rolling Stones, The Beach Boys, Aretha Franklin, Motown groups, or later artists. The energy would still be there, but the symbolic history would be different.

In short, modern music would not be “missing rock” or “missing pop” entirely. The social forces behind them—youth markets, radio, television, racial musical exchange, recording technology, and postwar consumer culture—were too powerful. But without Elvis and The Beatles, rock and pop would likely have become less globally standardized, less quickly dominant, and less focused on the charismatic rock star and the self-writing band. Modern music would still be rich and innovative, but its canon, timelines, and central myths would be radically different.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded genuinely carrier-capable Bristol Sea Beaufort torpedo bombers and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the Fleet Air Arm would have been significantly more dangerous in the first half of the war, especially in the Mediterranean. But it probably would not have transformed the Royal Navy into a Pacific-style fast carrier force or changed the overall outcome of the war by itself.

The biggest change would be that British carriers would have had a modern, fast, twin-engine strike capability much earlier. In reality, the Fleet Air Arm entered the war with aircraft such as the Swordfish, Skua, Roc, Fulmar and later Albacore: useful in some roles, but generally slow, underpowered or obsolescent. A naval Beaufort would have given the RN a faster torpedo bomber with better range, survivability and payload than the Swordfish or Albacore. A naval Beaufighter would have given it a powerful long-range strike fighter with cannon armament, later radar, rockets and anti-shipping capability.

The effect would have been most pronounced in the Mediterranean from 1940 to 1942. British carriers operating from Gibraltar, Alexandria and Malta would have been able to threaten Italian fleet movements and Axis convoys to North Africa more aggressively. A Sea Beaufort force could have made daylight torpedo attacks less suicidal than Swordfish or Albacore attacks, while Sea Beaufighters could have attacked shipping, suppressed flak, escorted strikes at medium range and intercepted bombers. Italian convoys to Libya were already under heavy pressure from submarines, Malta-based aircraft and surface forces; adding carrier-borne Beauforts and Beaufighters would likely have worsened Axis supply losses and made Rommel’s logistics problem bite earlier and harder.

At battles such as Cape Matapan, the result might have been even more decisive. Historically, carrier torpedo aircraft helped cripple the Italian fleet by slowing Vittorio Veneto and Pola. Faster torpedo aircraft would have made those attacks easier to launch in daylight and harder to evade. The Italian fleet might have become even more cautious sooner. British convoy operations to Malta could also have benefited: Sea Beaufighters would have been useful against shadowing aircraft, torpedo bombers and low-level attackers, while Sea Beauforts could threaten Axis surface forces before they closed with a convoy.

Taranto is a more complicated case. The Swordfish was slow, rugged, easy to handle at night and capable of operating in very shallow-water torpedo attacks after special modifications. Sea Beauforts would have been faster and heavier, but not necessarily better for that particular mission. A 1940 Taranto raid by Sea Beauforts might have been more technically difficult, especially at night from carriers, unless the aircraft had excellent low-speed handling and shallow-water torpedo capability. So Taranto might not improve much; it might even remain a Swordfish-style operation.

Against Bismarck in 1941, Sea Beauforts would probably have improved the Royal Navy’s search and strike options. They could have attacked faster, from farther out, and with less vulnerability to anti-aircraft fire than Swordfish. But the historical Swordfish attack succeeded partly because the aircraft were so slow and because one torpedo achieved a lucky but decisive rudder hit. Sea Beauforts might have made the interception more professional and less desperate, but they would not guarantee the same exact disabling hit. The likely broad outcome remains the same: Bismarck is hunted down, though perhaps with less risk and more rapid pressure.

The Sea Beaufighter would have been extremely valuable, but not as a true fleet air-superiority fighter. It was powerful, long-ranged and heavily armed, but it was still a large twin-engine aircraft. It would not have been ideal for dogfighting Bf 109s, Macchis, Zeros or carrier fighters. Its best carrier roles would have been long-range interception, night fighting, anti-shipping strikes, reconnaissance attack, and later radar-equipped convoy defense. In the Mediterranean, a carrier-capable Beaufighter could have been very effective against bombers and torpedo aircraft, especially at night or in poor weather. In the Indian Ocean or Pacific, however, it would not have solved the Royal Navy’s shortage of agile, modern single-seat naval fighters.

This matters because the main weakness of British carrier aviation in 1940–42 was not only the lack of a fast torpedo bomber. It was also limited carrier air group size, shortage of modern fighters, weak early-war fighter direction, and the design trade-off of armored carriers, which were tough but carried fewer aircraft than American or Japanese carriers. Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would have taken up more hangar and deck space than Swordfish, Fulmars or Martlets. So a British carrier might gain quality but lose numbers. On an Illustrious-class carrier, a wing of large twin-engine aircraft would reduce total aircraft capacity unless hangar arrangements, folding wings and deck parks were improved.

There would also be serious technical and logistical costs. Beauforts and Beaufighters were heavy aircraft for carrier work. To be practical from 1940, they would need folding wings, strengthened undercarriages, arrestor hooks, corrosion protection, catapult compatibility and excellent low-speed handling. The Beaufort’s early Taurus engines had reliability problems, and naval service would have made maintenance harder. Carrier accidents would likely have been high at first. Production would also compete with RAF Coastal Command and night-fighter needs. So the RN would be buying a better strike arm at the cost of aircraft numbers, maintenance simplicity and perhaps some land-based RAF capability.

In the Indian Ocean in 1942, these aircraft would help but not reverse the strategic balance. During the Japanese carrier raid, British carriers with Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would have had a longer-range and harder-hitting strike force than historically, but they still would have faced the highly trained Kido Butai, better Japanese carrier doctrine, larger air groups and excellent fighters. Sea Beaufighters would not be an adequate answer to the Zero. The Royal Navy might inflict more damage if it found Japanese ships, but it would still likely avoid a decisive carrier battle until better radar direction, fighters and numbers were available.

In the Atlantic and Arctic, the effect would be useful but narrower. Sea Beaufighters with radar and heavy weapons could have been excellent against reconnaissance aircraft, surface raiders and coastal shipping near Norway. Sea Beauforts could have threatened German naval units and convoys more effectively. But for escort carriers hunting U-boats, these aircraft would be less suitable than Swordfish, Wildcats, Avengers or later smaller carrier aircraft because they were large and demanding to operate from small decks.

Overall, early Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would most likely produce a stronger Royal Navy strike capability, heavier Axis shipping losses in the Mediterranean, better defense of Malta convoys, and greater pressure on the Italian fleet. They might shorten or intensify the Axis supply crisis in North Africa and make some British naval operations less costly. But they would not remove the need for proper carrier fighters, larger air groups, radar fighter direction, reliable torpedoes, and integrated carrier doctrine.

The most realistic conclusion is that they would have made the Fleet Air Arm substantially more effective from 1940 to 1942, especially as an anti-shipping force, but not revolutionary. Britain would gain a dangerous carrier-based maritime strike arm earlier; it would not suddenly become the equal of the U.S. Navy or Imperial Japanese Navy in large-scale carrier warfare.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.
items.model_answer:
If FDR had chosen an openly segregationist vice president in 1944, the main consequence is that when Roosevelt died in April 1945 the United States would have entered the last months of World War II and the early Cold War under a much more conservative, racially reactionary Democratic president than Harry Truman. The closest real-world analogue is James F. Byrnes of South Carolina, a serious 1944 contender who was a capable wartime administrator but also a Southern segregationist.

The immediate military outcome of World War II probably would not change much. Germany was already collapsing when FDR died, and Japan’s defeat was a matter of time. A segregationist Democratic president in 1945 would almost certainly still rely on the same generals, diplomats, and wartime bureaucracy. The atomic bomb would probably still be used against Japan, especially if the president were someone like Byrnes, who in real life favored a hard line toward Japan and the Soviet Union. The timing of Japan’s surrender might be very similar.

The bigger changes would come after the war.

Domestically, civil rights would be set back. Truman was not a civil-rights radical by later standards, but he did take historically important steps: he created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, endorsed a federal civil-rights program, and desegregated the armed forces by executive order in 1948. A segregationist president would almost certainly not do those things. There would likely be no 1948 military desegregation order, no strong presidential civil-rights message, and no symbolic break between the national Democratic Party and the Jim Crow South. Federal judgeships, Justice Department priorities, and executive appointments would probably be more tolerant of segregation.

That could delay the national Democratic Party’s turn toward civil rights. The Black vote, which had been moving toward the Democrats since the New Deal, might shift more heavily toward Republicans or toward third-party liberal movements. Northern liberals, labor unions, and Black voters would be alienated if the Democratic president was visibly aligned with Southern segregationists.

The 1948 election would likely look very different. Truman’s actual 1948 campaign depended on rebuilding the New Deal coalition: labor, urban machines, farmers, Black voters, and enough of the South. A segregationist incumbent might keep the Deep South more unified behind the Democrats, so there might be no Dixiecrat revolt like Strom Thurmond’s. But he would probably lose strength in the North and West. Henry Wallace or another liberal third-party candidate might do better, while Republicans such as Thomas Dewey would have a stronger chance of winning the presidency. In that scenario, the Democrats might preserve the white South but lose the national majority.

On foreign policy, the early Cold War might be at least as hard-line as it was under Truman, possibly more so. A figure like Byrnes was skeptical of the Soviet Union and helped shape the confrontational tone of 1945–46. The Truman Doctrine, containment, NATO, and the Marshall Plan might still emerge, because they were driven by broad geopolitical pressures, not just Truman personally. But the style could be different: less idealistic language about democracy and freedom, more blunt anti-communism, and perhaps less concern about how American racism damaged U.S. credibility abroad.

There might also be changes on specific postwar issues. A segregationist Southern Democrat might be less sympathetic to recognizing Israel quickly in 1948 than Truman was. He might also be more conservative on labor policy and economic reconversion, possibly accepting measures Truman resisted or vetoed, such as stronger anti-union legislation.

The largest long-term effect would be on civil rights and party realignment. Truman’s civil-rights moves helped begin the process by which the national Democratic Party slowly became identified with civil rights and the South began drifting away. A segregationist president in 1945 could delay that split. The Democratic Party might remain longer as an uneasy coalition of Northern New Dealers and Southern segregationists. But the contradiction would not disappear. The civil-rights movement, Black migration to Northern cities, Cold War pressure, and Supreme Court litigation would still force the issue eventually.

So the short answer is: World War II probably ends much the same way, including likely use of the atomic bomb, but the postwar Democratic Party, early civil-rights policy, and perhaps the 1948 election change substantially. A segregationist successor to FDR would probably slow federal civil-rights progress, weaken the Democrats among Northern liberals and Black voters, and make a Republican victory in 1948 more likely.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.
items.model_answer:
If the Allies lost on the Salonica front, the most likely result would be a longer and messier First World War in the Balkans, but not necessarily a Central Powers victory overall.

The Salonica front was strategically secondary for most of the war, but it became important in 1918 because the Allied breakthrough at Dobro Pole knocked Bulgaria out of the war. Bulgaria’s collapse then opened the Balkans, threatened Austria-Hungary from the south, cut the Central Powers’ land connection to the Ottoman Empire, and helped accelerate the general collapse of Germany’s coalition.

So if the Allies instead lost there—meaning their army was driven out of Macedonia or forced to evacuate Salonika—the immediate consequences would be serious. Serbia would remain occupied. Bulgaria would stay in the war. Greece might be intimidated into neutrality or political paralysis, and the Entente would lose its main base in the Balkans. The Central Powers would secure the Berlin–Constantinople land route, making it easier to support the Ottoman Empire. Bulgarian, German, and Austro-Hungarian troops tied down in Macedonia could be shifted elsewhere, perhaps to Romania, Italy, or the Western Front.

The biggest difference would come in 1918. Without the Allied breakthrough in Macedonia, Bulgaria probably would not be the first Central Power to collapse. The Ottoman Empire would be less isolated, Austria-Hungary would not face the same immediate threat from the south, and Germany would have one fewer crisis to manage. This could delay the armistices of Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire, Austria-Hungary, and Germany, perhaps by weeks or months.

But it probably would not reverse the outcome of the war unless the Allied defeat were catastrophic on a much larger scale. By late 1918 Germany was already under immense pressure on the Western Front, the British blockade was strangling the Central Powers, Austria-Hungary was disintegrating internally, and American manpower was arriving in increasing numbers. A Central Powers victory in Macedonia would improve their position, but it would not solve their fundamental strategic problems.

The most plausible counterfactual is therefore: the Central Powers hold the Balkans longer, Bulgaria survives longer, the Ottoman Empire is less quickly isolated, and the war may continue into late 1918 or possibly early 1919. The final Allied victory would likely still come, but the postwar settlement in the Balkans might be different, Serbia’s restoration would be delayed, Greece’s gains could be reduced, and Bulgaria might negotiate from a less disastrous position.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
items.original_question: What if Curtiss P-40 used Merlins? What instead of using Allison V-12's the Curtiss P-40 used the Merlin V-12 instead ? Would this be possible or would it need major airframe development? Would it need a redesigned laminar flow wing to really utilise the engine? How successful would this instillation be? Would it allow the P-40 to be more successful than the later P-51? What boost in combat performance would this instillation allow? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the start around the Rolls-Royce Merlin, it would probably have been a better high-altitude fighter, but it still would not have become a P-51 Mustang.

The main historical weakness of the P-40 was not that it was a bad airplane; it was that its Allison V-1710 engine had a single-stage, single-speed supercharger in most versions. At low and medium altitude the P-40 was sturdy, fast enough, and useful, especially in North Africa, China-Burma-India, and the Pacific. But above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet it lost performance badly compared with Merlin-powered Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later Mustangs.

A Merlin-designed P-40 would have had better altitude performance from the beginning. With a Merlin III, XX, 45, or later Packard-built Merlin, it would have climbed better, retained power higher up, and had a higher service ceiling. It would have been more competitive against the Bf 109E/F and Japanese fighters at medium altitude, and less confined to low-level fighting. In British service especially, it would have been more valuable as a general-purpose fighter rather than mainly as a fighter-bomber and low-to-medium-altitude aircraft.

But the improvement would have had limits. The P-40’s airframe came from the P-36 lineage and had relatively high drag compared with newer designs. Its wing, radiator installation, fuselage shape, and general aerodynamic refinement were not in the same class as the Spitfire or the later P-51. Simply installing a Merlin would not give it the Mustang’s laminar-flow wing, long-range internal fuel capacity, excellent radiator ducting, or low-drag airframe. Historically, the Merlin-powered P-40F and P-40L did exist, and while they were better at altitude than Allison P-40s, they were not revolutionary. They did not turn the P-40 into a first-rank high-altitude escort fighter.

If Curtiss had designed the aircraft around the Merlin from the outset, rather than adapting the engine later, the result would probably have been somewhat better than the real P-40F. The nose, cooling system, center of gravity, and fuselage could have been optimized earlier. It might have been a cleaner, better-balanced aircraft with fewer compromises. Performance might plausibly have landed somewhere between the historical P-40F and early Mustang: useful, rugged, and faster at altitude than the Allison versions, but still not equal to the best contemporary fighters once the war advanced.

The bigger problem would have been production and engine supply. In 1938–1940 the United States did not have large numbers of Merlins available. Britain needed Merlins urgently for Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later bombers. Packard-built Merlin production did not mature until later. If Curtiss had committed the P-40 to the Merlin early, the fighter might have been delayed, produced in smaller numbers, or forced into competition with British priorities. One reason the Allison-powered P-40 mattered historically was that it was available in quantity when the Allies badly needed modern fighters.

So the likely outcome is this: a Merlin P-40 designed from the beginning would have been a more capable aircraft, especially above medium altitude, and it might have had a stronger reputation. It would have been less obviously inferior to the Bf 109 at altitude and more flexible in Allied service. But it would still have been constrained by the basic Curtiss airframe and by Merlin availability. It would not have replaced the Spitfire, and it would not have matched the later P-51 as a long-range escort. Its greatest effect would have been to make the early Allied fighter inventory somewhat stronger, not to change the course of the air war by itself.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? items.model_answer:
Assuming the intended reference is the PT-109 disaster in 1943, the most likely consequence of JFK dying then is that the Kennedy family never produces a president in the 1960s, and several major events of U.S. political history unfold differently.

John F. Kennedy’s death in 1943 would have mattered far beyond the loss of one naval officer because his later political career depended heavily on the PT-109 survival story. That episode became central to his image: courage under pressure, physical endurance despite illness, and youthful heroism in war. Without surviving it, he never becomes a congressman in 1946, never defeats Henry Cabot Lodge for the Senate in 1952, never becomes a national Democratic figure, and never wins the presidency in 1960.

The Kennedy family’s ambitions would probably have been badly damaged. Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. originally expected his eldest son, Joseph Kennedy Jr., to become president, but Joe Jr. died in 1944. If JFK had already died in 1943, the family would have lost both of its plausible presidential heirs within a year. Robert Kennedy was talented but much younger and lacked the independent political base he later gained as JFK’s campaign manager and attorney general. Ted Kennedy was younger still and would not automatically have inherited JFK’s Senate path. The “Kennedy dynasty” might still have existed socially and financially, but probably not as a presidential dynasty.

The immediate military outcome of World War II would not change. PT-109 was a small episode in the Solomon Islands campaign, and JFK’s death would not alter the Pacific war. Its importance is political and symbolic, not strategic.

The biggest change comes in 1960. Without JFK, the Democratic nomination likely goes to someone else: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Stuart Symington, or possibly Adlai Stevenson again. Richard Nixon’s chances of winning the presidency would probably improve. JFK barely beat Nixon in the real 1960 election, and his appeal—youth, television skill, Catholic ethnic urban support, and the Kennedy campaign machine—was crucial. Against a different Democrat, especially one less effective on television or less able to unite northern liberals and urban machines, Nixon may well have won.

If Nixon became president in 1961, U.S. policy would change in several areas, though not always in predictable ways. On Cuba, the Bay of Pigs might either be cancelled, handled with more direct military support, or produce a different crisis. The Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it might not happen, because it depended partly on Khrushchev’s assessment of JFK after the Bay of Pigs and Vienna summit. A Nixon administration might look tougher, which could deter Soviet missiles in Cuba—or provoke a different confrontation.

Civil rights would probably move more slowly. JFK himself was cautious on civil rights until events forced his hand, but his assassination gave Lyndon Johnson a powerful moral and political opening to push the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965. Without JFK’s presidency and martyrdom, and without LBJ inheriting the White House in that exact way, major civil-rights legislation might still pass because the movement was strong and national pressure was rising, but it could be delayed, weaker, or politically configured differently.

Vietnam is uncertain. JFK had expanded the advisory role but had not committed large U.S. combat forces before his death. Nixon was strongly anti-communist, as was nearly every major Cold War politician, so a Nixon presidency could still escalate in Vietnam, perhaps earlier or in a different form. Conversely, Nixon’s later reputation as a hardliner might have given him more political room to avoid a massive ground war. The safest answer is that Vietnam would remain a major danger point, but the exact path of escalation would differ.

The space program would also likely be altered. JFK’s 1961 commitment to land a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was a personal presidential decision shaped by Cold War competition and political theater. Without JFK, the Apollo program might receive less urgency and funding. A Moon landing by 1969 becomes less likely, though U.S.-Soviet space competition would still continue.

So the short answer is: JFK’s death in 1943 would not change World War II, but it would likely prevent the Kennedy presidency, weaken or delay the Kennedy family’s political rise, improve Nixon’s chances in 1960, and significantly alter the timing and shape of civil rights legislation, Cuba policy, Vietnam, and the space race. The United States would still be a Cold War superpower facing the same broad pressures, but the symbolic and political architecture of the 1960s would be very different.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
