items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.
items.model_answer:
If George McGovern had become president in 1968, the largest and most immediate change would have been Vietnam. A McGovern presidency would likely have treated opposition to the war not as disloyalty but as, in his own moral vocabulary, “the highest patriotism.” The United States probably would have moved toward withdrawal years earlier, with fewer American deaths, less bombing of Indochina, and no Nixon-style expansion of the war into Cambodia. But the political cost at home would have been enormous, and McGovern would probably have been blamed by conservatives and many moderates for “losing” Vietnam.

For the scenario to happen, the Democratic convention in 1968 would have had to reject Hubert Humphrey after Robert Kennedy’s assassination and nominate McGovern as an antiwar compromise candidate. He then would have needed to defeat Richard Nixon while George Wallace split the conservative vote. That is unlikely, but not impossible in a very narrow Electoral College outcome.

As president, McGovern would probably have announced a rapid de-Americanization of the war: a bombing halt, direct negotiations with Hanoi, pressure on South Vietnam to accept a political settlement, and a timetable for U.S. troop withdrawal. He would not have invaded Cambodia in 1970, and the Kent State crisis as we know it likely would not have happened. The antiwar movement would have lost some of its central target, though radical unrest would not have disappeared overnight. The war might have ended for the United States by 1970 or 1971 rather than 1973.

The harder question is what happened afterward in Vietnam. McGovern would have hoped for a negotiated settlement, perhaps involving a coalition government or neutralization of South Vietnam. But without continued massive U.S. military support, South Vietnam’s position would likely have deteriorated. A communist victory might have come earlier than 1975. The difference is that it would have come after fewer years of American bombing, fewer U.S. casualties, and probably less destruction in Cambodia and Laos. McGovern’s critics would have called this surrender; his defenders would have called it a necessary end to an unwinnable war.

Domestically, McGovern would have tried to extend the Great Society in a more explicitly egalitarian direction. He cared deeply about hunger, poverty, farm policy, Native American issues, and civil rights. His administration likely would have supported stronger anti-poverty programs, expanded food assistance, national health insurance debates, and campaign-finance reform. But he would have faced a Congress still dominated by Democrats who were not all liberals. Southern Democrats and Republicans would have blocked much of his most ambitious agenda. He would have had moral authority with liberals, but not necessarily the legislative skill or congressional base that Lyndon Johnson had.

Race and law-and-order politics would have been a major problem for him. In 1968, the country was shaken by riots, assassinations, urban crime, and white backlash. Nixon exploited those fears through “law and order” and the Southern Strategy. If McGovern were president instead, that backlash would not vanish; it would probably intensify. Republicans would portray him as soft on crime, soft on communism, and captive to student radicals. The conservative realignment of white working-class and Southern voters might have happened even faster.

The Supreme Court could have changed significantly. Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist. McGovern would almost certainly have chosen more liberal justices. The Warren Court’s liberal direction might have lasted longer, affecting criminal procedure, civil rights, reapportionment, school desegregation, abortion, and executive power. A McGovern Court would likely have been more skeptical of police power and more protective of individual rights than the actual Burger Court became.

Foreign policy beyond Vietnam would have been more complicated. McGovern was not isolationist; he was a World War II bomber pilot and a serious critic of militarized foreign policy. He likely would have pursued détente with the Soviet Union and arms control, perhaps similar in broad direction to Nixon and Kissinger but with less secrecy and less emphasis on great-power manipulation. Opening relations with China might have been delayed, because Nixon’s anti-communist credentials made it easier for him to make that move. McGovern might have wanted engagement with China, but he would have faced harsher domestic attacks for it.

Economically, ending the war earlier might have reduced some federal pressure and social strain, but it would not have eliminated the structural problems of the 1970s. Inflation, the weakening of Bretton Woods, industrial competition, and the coming oil shock would still have posed serious challenges. McGovern was more economically populist than technocratic. He might have expanded social spending while cutting defense, but if inflation worsened, he would have been politically vulnerable. A Republican victory in 1972 or 1976 would have been very likely if the economy weakened and Vietnam ended badly.

The biggest political consequence is that there would be no Nixon presidency as we know it: no Watergate, no Nixon enemies list, no Nixonian Cambodia incursion, and no Nixon appointments reshaping the Court. But there also might be no Democratic recovery. A McGovern presidency beginning in 1969 could have made him, rather than Nixon, the central figure associated with defeat in Vietnam, inflation, racial conflict, and national disorder. The Republican Party might have gained power afterward under someone like Ronald Reagan earlier than in actual history.

So the most likely outcome is a morally clearer but politically fragile presidency. McGovern would have ended or sharply reduced American involvement in Vietnam sooner, saving lives and avoiding some of the darkest escalations of the Nixon years. He would have tried to make American politics more humane, anti-militarist, and egalitarian. But he would have governed a country not yet ready for his kind of liberalism, and the backlash against him might have accelerated the conservative turn of the 1970s and 1980s.

items.question: What If A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)
human_answers: The problem is that everything becomes possible with enough wankium, hence the implied 'it would be best achieved by starting very early on, as per the other thread'; otherwise it's not a Challenge, an exploration of history and factors, rather an exercise in taking OTL and changing it all to successful/lucky/positive events while applying a large butterfly net. No assassination of AII; so he gets scared and Stolypin's reforms are implemented earlier and more decisively; but then, Japan still lucks out in War and so people are angry; WWI however you like, except with less Russian losses; Revolution happens later so Russia wins or at least doesn't lose as much, so the Mensheviks come into power and start building a social democracy in Russia; a couple decades of luck preventing any bad luck until the Nazis go West, while Russia prepares herself for being attacked; so when they come they are pushed back faster and with less losses, leading to a well-integrated post-WWII Russia that can enjoy a few decades of growth, has larger borders, and as a result reaches 300M by 2000 as you asked. But somehow, I don't think that's really what you are after, are you?

I do think early PoDs (which naturally make our world unrecognisable and certainly butterfly the birth of Lenin) are more plausible if you want Russia thoroughly similar to Scandinavia. But the 20th century is a good time for catching up, for radical jumps, for deep transformations, as OTL has also shown, only not in the way the OP desires. Steering a course between Bolshevik tyranny of OTL and its most likely counterpart, continuation of a relatively autocratic tsardom, is not impossible. Neither are the population numbers. A solid multi-party democracy, well, if it works in India, why not in Russia. But you could call what is required for it a good run of sixes, or a healthy dose of wankium. I've dabbled in that in Feeble Constitution , so I'll not dwell on the path of February 1917 consolidating with different policies after the April Days. Instead, I can see both earlier and later PoDs. For a good planning thread on a later PoD (basically SR victory in the Civil War), you could have a look at @galileo-034 's Century of the Common Man . Though this may not entirely fulfill your OP challenge - Lenin would not be an obscure footnote here, and instead die in 1918. So maybe let's go with the one big earlier opportunity - a successful revolution of 1905. @Powdermonkey started a TL on this last year. I'd be thrilled to see where this could go. One could argue that the path towards what the OP describes is still stony and uphill. How one would tackle the Great War problem is still up in the air, among other things. But still probably one path worth exploring more here since it hasn't been done often, I think.
items.original_question:
AHC: A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

The goal is simple - we want to have a 20th century in which Russia avoids the interlocked chain of events leading to a century of trumas as IOTL. In this world, Russia becomes a vibrant multi party democracy, heavily integrated with the rest of Europe and with its intellectual and cultural elites intact. It follows an economic model analogous to the Social Market Economy of post ww2 Germany or even the Nordic Model if things go very positively. Its population is over 300 mln people by 1991 (the year the USSR collapsed IOTL). In this world, Vladimir Lenin is still born (despite the butterfly effect) and still becomes a revolutionary but he dies as an obscure, disillusioned theoretician. His last work, Delusions of the Proletariat , is a scathing critique of the supposed naivety of the working class, lured into capitalism through voting rights and social safety nets. It sells less than 500 copies. When the internet era arrives (either sooner or later than IOTL), Lenin is included in various "10 Failed Radicals You Have Never Heard of" type of articles on various history-related websited but is otherwise a forgotten figure.
items.model_answer:
A drastically better Russian 20th century would most plausibly require Russia to avoid the chain reaction of 1914–1953: World War I collapse, Bolshevik seizure of power, civil war, forced collectivization, Stalinism, the purges, the Nazi-Soviet pact, catastrophic World War II losses, and then the militarized Soviet system. The single best point of divergence is not “a nicer Stalin” or “a more competent USSR,” but an earlier constitutional transformation after 1905.

In this better timeline, the 1905 Revolution forces Nicholas II to accept a real constitutional monarchy rather than a fake one. The Duma gains genuine authority, censorship is relaxed, courts become more independent, and parties such as the Kadets, moderate socialists, and agrarian reformers are allowed to operate legally. Stolypin or someone like him survives long enough to carry out land reform without turning the countryside into a revolutionary pressure cooker. Russia remains unequal, corrupt, and politically tense, but it becomes a flawed parliamentary state rather than an autocracy waiting to explode.

The crucial second improvement is 1914. A better Russia either helps defuse the July Crisis or mobilizes more cautiously and avoids turning the Balkan crisis into a general European war. If World War I is avoided or shortened, the Romanov state is not shattered, the army does not disintegrate, Lenin does not get his revolutionary opening, and the Bolsheviks remain a radical minority rather than rulers of a collapsed empire.

From there, Russia’s 20th century is still difficult, but not apocalyptic. It likely evolves into a constitutional monarchy or republic with a strong parliament, a large peasant electorate, and a contentious debate over federalism, land, labor, and national minorities. Finland, Poland, and perhaps the Baltic states probably become independent or highly autonomous. Ukraine, the Caucasus, and Central Asia either receive federal autonomy or become the central political problem of the state. A genuinely “better” Russian history cannot simply mean a stronger Russian empire; it would also have to mean less repression of non-Russian peoples.

Economically, Russia would probably industrialize more slowly than Stalin’s USSR but far more humanely and efficiently. There would be no forced collectivization, no Holodomor, no mass dekulakization, no Gulag economy, and no Great Terror destroying the administrative, military, scientific, and cultural elite. Russian agriculture would remain inefficient for a while, but peasant property rights, cooperatives, railways, electrification, and foreign investment would gradually raise productivity. By mid-century, Russia could plausibly resemble a very large, rougher-edged Canada, Italy, or Germany: resource-rich, unevenly developed, politically turbulent, but not totalitarian.

The biggest global effect would be on Germany and World War II. Without Bolshevism, European politics change drastically. Fascism might still arise from nationalism, defeat, and economic crisis, but anti-communist panic would be weaker. Hitler’s rise becomes less likely, or at least less explosive. If a Nazi-like Germany still emerges, it faces a Russia that has not murdered its officer corps, starved its countryside, isolated itself diplomatically, or signed a pact dividing Eastern Europe. There is probably no Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, no Soviet occupation of eastern Poland and the Baltic states, and perhaps no German invasion reaching Moscow. A European war might still happen, but it is likely shorter and less catastrophic in the east.

For Russians themselves, the demographic difference would be enormous. Historical Russia and the USSR lost tens of millions through World War I, civil war, famine, terror, World War II, Stalinist repression, emigration, and later Soviet stagnation and post-Soviet collapse. In a better timeline, Russia’s population by 2026 could be dramatically larger, healthier, and less demographically aged. Its cities would still be huge industrial and cultural centers, but without the trauma layers of civil war, Stalinism, and post-Soviet collapse.

Culturally, the consequences would be profound. The Silver Age of Russian culture would not be cut off so violently. Writers, philosophers, scientists, engineers, and artists would not be exiled, shot, censored, or forced into ideological service on the same scale. Russian Orthodoxy would probably decline in political power but not be physically crushed. Jewish life in the former empire would still face antisemitism, but without Stalinism and possibly with less revolutionary/counterrevolutionary violence, its trajectory could be far less tragic—though much would depend on whether a Nazi Germany still appears.

There would probably be no Soviet superpower as we know it. Russia might still become one of the world’s great powers because of its size, resources, population, and scientific talent, but it would not dominate Eastern Europe through communist satellite regimes. The Cold War either does not happen or is far less central. Nuclear weapons may still be invented, but the bipolar U.S.-Soviet arms race would be reduced or replaced by a looser multipolar competition among the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Japan, Russia, and perhaps China.

By 2026, the best-case version of this Russia is a large constitutional federal republic or parliamentary monarchy, wealthy but uneven, conservative in some regions and liberal in major cities, with a strong scientific and literary tradition and a resource-backed industrial economy. It is probably not a perfect liberal democracy; Russia’s geography, security fears, bureaucracy, and imperial legacy would still matter. But it would likely be far freer, richer, less militarized, and less traumatized than the real Russian Federation.

Most importantly, there is probably no Soviet collapse in 1991, no shock-therapy catastrophe on the same scale, no Putinist revanchism, no Chechen wars in their real form, and no full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia’s relationship with Ukraine would be the key test of whether this “better history” is genuinely better or merely more successful imperialism. In the genuinely better version, Ukraine is either independent much earlier or part of a voluntary federation with real language, political, and economic rights.

So the short answer is: a drastically better Russian 20th century requires constitutional reform after 1905, avoidance or limitation of World War I, no Bolshevik dictatorship, no Stalinism, and a gradual transition into a federal parliamentary great power. The result would be a Russia that is still complicated and often troubled, but not devastated by famine, terror, total war, ideological dictatorship, imperial collapse, and renewed authoritarian militarism.

items.question: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?
human_answers: I agree with most of what you said but that’s not quite what happened to Hua - he was backed by Ye Jianying, an ‘elder’, and implemented reforms while publicly proclaiming his support of Mao Zedong Thought. It was Hua who saw the reintroduction of "material incentives". However Hua relied on collective leadership and as Ye's health decline Hua was outflanked by Deng, who took a much harsher stance of de-Maoification despite being economically similar to Hua. I’m going to go on a bit of a tangent to explain why I agree with the rest of what you said and think some equivalent to reform and opening was the most likely outcome - Deng spent the 80s balancing the other “elders” and younger officials. As @Georg von Frundsberg said, other elders were more 'conservative' but generally embraced reform - while younger officials like Hu and Zhao were aggressively reformist. Deng himself was a lot closer to the centre than is remembered - on agriculture for example Zhao Shukai had a good article about how Deng was slow to embrace reform and one of his signature reforms, "household production" (allowing households to dictate production instead of communes) was only adopted by central diktat in 1982 after years of discussion. However throughout the tumultuous 80s political instability remained, culminating in 1989, the removal of Zhao Ziyang and the introduction of martial. Deng was ont he defence for three years until 1992, at which point he returned to power by coordinating “reformist” officials through the southern tour. Deng enjoyed is last five years at his relative peak of influence and admiration since he had outlived everyone else. I mention this to show though that Reform and Opening up was somewhat inevitable. There was a large chunk of the elders that were open to reform and an even larger pool of younger officials. Someone sometime was going to remove the Gang of Four and the only real question left was how much reform and when. To return to OP’s question, the only real alternative to reform and opening up was a coup. People were tired of the stagnant economy and the damage done by the cultural revolution was significant - in certain periods it was closer to a civil war, as PLA and militia fought in the streets. If the government tried to stick with central planning it would be removed by the majority of officials, and if not by them then a popular uprising.

Without reform and opening up in 1978 I think the only alternative would be to chug along with five year plans and central planning. This was attempted immediately after Mao's death, but it failed because everyone believed that continuing that way was a dead end, so it's plausible but unlikely that the Communist Party goes down that path. There's reason to believe that the Cultural Revolution was launched in part as a reaction to the bureaucracy and corruption of the Stalinist party-state, as a way to try and find an alternative to it, which was eventually put to bed in 1968 when Mao sent in the PLA. Broadly, you can characterise the initial years of the Cultural Revolution as the 'left-wing' attempt to find an alternative to the Soviet model, and Reform and Opening up as the 'right-wing' attempt to find an alternative in the wake of the GPCR's failure. Maybe they could've made it work, compared to the post-war Soviet communist party, the Chinese communist party was far more afraid of stagnancy and was far more willing to put themselves behind ambitious economic programmes (this is probably the main the reason they carried out Reform and Opening up and the USSR didn't), and maybe that allows them to pull through and create a creating a working planned economy that marches proudly into the 21st century, avoiding concessions to market economics. Most people will probably dismiss this possibility. It is perhaps more likely that the whole thing ossifies and stagnates at some point, prompting the party to do something like reform and opening up at a later date. If the party has reached Soviet levels of complacency and don't do anything, the system will begin to rot, the black market will explode and you'll get something like North Korea. I don't think Chinese citizens would be as poor as North Koreans are though, considering the collapse of North Korea's living standards was largely caused by the disappearance of Soviet economic aid, something China stopped receiving long before then, but I'm not wholly sure on that one. EDIT: I can't believe I forgot to mention this, but people associated with China's New Left movement often look favourably upon Belarus' Market Socialism as an alternative to what happened in China, with all the social chaos it caused. I am not entirely familiar with how Market Socialism works in Belarus, but in a journal article by Chinese economists praising the Belarusian model they take a liking to the dominance of state-owned companies, central planning, strong leadership and stronger social security and welfare than what exists in China and the rest of the ex-USSR. I don't really know much about how things actually work in practice in Belarus and if it's at all feasible China could copy this economic model, but it gives some pointers.

He was weak. At the time, the Chinese Communist Party was filled with veteran figures who had followed Mao since its early days. In such a situation, Hua Guofeng was merely a novice. As the elders pushed for reform, the young Hua Guofeng could not hold his ground. The Gang of Four, who had driven the Cultural Revolution, were not elders either; they relied on Mao’s personal trust. Hua Guofeng found himself caught between the Gang of Four and the veteran elders. While suppressing the Gang of Four, he also had to confront the elders who were advocating reform. Faced with such an overwhelming burden, Hua Guofeng was simply too young and lacked the political influence to manage it. Unlike the Soviet Communist Party, the Chinese Communist Party had a much stronger tendency to pursue “a today different from yesterday” rather than “a today the same as yesterday.” Even if the result turned out to be disastrous, they were still more inclined to act proactively and at least try to do something. Is this what you mean? If that is true, then it seems that for the PRC, it was ultimately a matter of timing—it would have carried out reform and opening up sooner or later. Then, in your view, is a scenario in which the PRC becomes like North Korea impossible? I mean a situation in which a particular vested elite seizes control of the bureaucracy and the military, crushes all resistance, and pushes for isolation in order to preserve its own power even at the cost of weakening the state’s capabilities. Certainly, the politics of the PRC and North Korea were different. In the PRC, even after Mao had secured absolute power, figures like Deng Xiaoping at least managed to survive by keeping a low profile. As a result, change became possible after Mao’s death. By contrast, in North Korea, Kim Il Sung had already eliminated all alternative forces by the 1960s, and from the 1970s onward he was able to prepare to pass power on to his son.
items.original_question: What if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Unlike in OTL, assume that a POD occurred in the succession struggle after Mao Zedong’s death. Or, if you prefer, assume that the Cultural Revolution itself unfolded differently. In any case, because of this change, Deng Xiaoping either never came to power or was removed partway through. Reform and Opening Up did not take place in the 1980s. Post in thread 'What if succession had occurred in China after Mao's death?' Feb 5, 2025 And I could see Lin being not really into the idea of Mao Anying succeeding Mao lead to a more serious involvement by Lin Biao in Project 571 or an equivalent plot, as opposed to IOTL where his son was the main driving force behind it. Whiteshore (For example, something like this.) What do you think would have happened if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Would the PRC have eventually collapsed under economic crisis, or would it have endured like North Korea? Would the CCP have fallen because its claim to rule lost credibility? Or, like the Kim family and the North Korean ruling elite, could it have remained in power as a poor and isolated dictatorship by maintaining control over the military and political system while eliminating opposition?
items.model_answer:
If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up after 1978, China would almost certainly have remained far poorer, more inward-looking, and much less influential internationally. The most likely result is not simply “China stays the same,” but a long period of economic stagnation followed either by political crisis, forced late reform, or a more repressive socialist command economy.

Without decollectivizing agriculture, allowing private enterprise, creating Special Economic Zones, welcoming foreign investment, and integrating into global trade, China would not have become the “world’s factory.” Rural incomes would have risen much more slowly, food supply would have remained more vulnerable, and hundreds of millions of people would probably not have escaped poverty on the scale they did in real history. Cities such as Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Shanghai, and later many inland industrial hubs would have developed far more slowly. The huge migrant-labor economy, export-manufacturing boom, private property market, and consumer middle class would either not exist or would be much smaller.

Politically, the Communist Party would have faced a serious legitimacy problem. After the Cultural Revolution, the Maoist command economy had limited credibility. In actual history, rapid growth became a major source of regime legitimacy. Without that growth, the Party would have had to rely more heavily on ideology, rationing, surveillance, and coercion. It might have resembled a larger, less isolated version of North Korea, or a stagnant late-Soviet-style system. Alternatively, economic failure could have produced an internal split or a crisis similar to those that hit the Soviet bloc in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The PRC might still have survived, given its strong state apparatus and nationalist legitimacy, but it would have been much less stable and much less confident.

Globally, the effects would have been enormous. The world economy would not have been reorganized around Chinese manufacturing. Foreign companies would have invested more heavily in places such as Southeast Asia, India, Mexico, Turkey, and Eastern Europe. Consumer goods in the United States and Europe would likely have been more expensive, and global supply chains less China-centered. China probably would not have joined the WTO in the same way, would not have accumulated massive foreign-exchange reserves, and would not have become the central trading partner for much of Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

Militarily and diplomatically, China would be far weaker. The modernization of the PLA depended heavily on the economic boom, technology acquisition, and a much larger fiscal base. Without Reform and Opening Up, China would probably not be a near-peer strategic competitor to the United States. It would have less naval reach, weaker aerospace and semiconductor industries, and far less ability to fund initiatives like the Belt and Road. The post-Cold War world would likely have remained more strongly dominated by the United States, with Japan, the EU, and perhaps India or ASEAN playing relatively larger economic roles.

Socially, China would be much less urban, less educated in advanced technical fields, and less connected to the outside world. There would be fewer foreign students, fewer overseas Chinese business networks tied to the mainland, less internet and consumer culture, and a much smaller private sector. At the same time, China might have avoided some costs of rapid development: extreme pollution, land seizures, inequality, speculative real estate growth, and the social dislocation of mass migration. But those avoided costs would come at the price of much lower living standards overall.

The Taiwan and Hong Kong questions would also look different. Hong Kong’s 1997 handover might still have occurred under treaty obligations, but its role as a gateway to a booming mainland would have been much reduced. Shenzhen would not have become a megacity. Taiwan’s economy would have invested elsewhere, and cross-strait economic integration would be far weaker. Beijing would likely have had less capacity to pressure Taiwan militarily, though nationalism might still have kept the issue politically central.

In short, without Reform and Opening Up, the PRC probably would not have become the world’s second-largest economy or a central actor in globalization. It would likely be a poorer, more authoritarian, less technologically advanced, and more internationally isolated state. The biggest uncertainty is whether such a system could have endured indefinitely. A China that never reformed might have survived as a rigid socialist state, but it also might eventually have faced a deep crisis forcing delayed reform or even regime-threatening upheaval.

items.question: What If the Vickers Wellington had been produced with a stressed-skin airframe instead of its geodetic fabric-covered structure?
human_answers: Picked this up from John Dell, whose site is quite often mentioned here, a long time ago. Geodetic structures only show advantages for big aircraft - e.g. a small geodetic fighter would be a non-starter. The advantages of Geodetic aircraft are better the bigger the aircraft - From this point of view it is a shame the Warwick + Windsor were so late. The main Geodetic structures (fuselage + wings) are built as whole units - So it is harder to break up the structure into subassemblies for distributed manufacture. Advantages of Geodetic over steel-tube, wooden formers and fabric covering are... Much greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage, and more g force. No internal bracing - so unobstructed space within for passengers, fuel tanks + other equipment. The potential for cheaper construction if planned + implemented properly and a very large production run with no changes in the primary structure - It may take more people to construct a geodetic aircraft but many more of them will be low-skilled, lower-waged workers. Drag difference between the two types is probably not much. Advantages of Steel tube, wooden formers and fabric covering over Geodetic are... Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Much more cost-effective for short production runs. Advantages of Geodetic over all wood stressed structures (i.e. Mosquito) Potentially greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage. Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production (Wood-workers are some of the most skilled factory workers around and therefore have higher wages and take longer to train) - In actual fact during WWII this was not such a great problem, because so many wood-working companies (i.e. furniture makers) were closed there was a relative glut of wood workers available. Not susceptible to woodworm or termites - a real danger in tropical climates. Advantages of Wooden stressed structures over Geodetic The wooden aircraft should have a lower drag, because of its smooth finish. Wood was more readily available, whereas aviation alloys were in short supply. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make a profit out of a short production run. Advantages of Geodetic over Fully-stressed skin metal aircraft Ability to absorb more battle damage + keep flying (but not necessarily protect the crew) Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production - not actually realised by Vickers. Uses less metal, a particular advantage if aviation alloys are scarce. Advantages of fully stressed metal skin over geodetic Lower drag (smoother skin). More suitable for cabin pressurisation. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make profit out of smaller production run (but still nowhere near that possible with wooden + steel tube structures). Maybe more crew protection. Possibilities for weight saving by integrating structures (eg a fuel tank or firewall could be an integral part of the main structure rather than being something added after the main structure is built - this becomes increasingly important).

Specification B.1/35 was effectively a replacement for the Hampden and Wellington which were designed to meet Specification B.9/32. What became the Halifax began as the HP.55 with 2 Hercules class engines to Spec B.1/35, then the HP.56 with 2 Vultures to Spec. P.13/36, then the HP.57, 59 & 63 with 4 Merlins and the HP.61 with 4 Hercules engines. Handley Page delivered its 500th and last Hampden in July 1940 and its first production Halifax in August 1940. English Electric built 770 Hampdens which were delivered from March 1940 to March 1942. English Electric's Hampden production overlapped with its Halifax production because the first one was delivered in October 1941. The Halifax was also built by Fairey, the London Aircraft Production Group and Rootes. The Warwick was designed to meet Spec. B.1/35 with 2 Hercules class engines too, which was changed to 2 Vulture class engines, but still to B.1/35 rather than the later B.12/36 or P.13/36. If its development had proceeded as smoothly as the Halifax it's likely that this would have happened. Weybridge would have switched from the Wellington to the Warwick in the summer of 1940. Chester may have swiched in August 1940 too, after delivering the 200 Wellingtons ordered 1937-38. The next batch of Wellingtons ordered IOTL (550 in May 1939) would have been the first batch of Warwicks. Blackpool didn't get its first Wellington contract until December 1939 and commenced deliveries in August 1940. Based on the above a contract for 500 Warwicks would have been let instead. 750 Wellingtons were ordered from the Castle Bromwich factory in December 1939 IOTL. It was cancelled before any were built, I don't know when and why, but it was probably so it could concentrate on building Spitfires. The factory also received orders for 650 Lancasters and Lincolns from September 1941 to June 1944 of which 300 were delivered from December 1943 to August 1945. Although the Warwick was only built at Weybridge (first delivery June 1942) it was also ordered from the Blackpool and Chester factories. So contradicting what I wrote in Message 8, if the stressed-skin Warwick is allowed to evolve in the same way that the Halifax did, we may see it built by the thousand at the Vickers factories at Blackpool, Chester and Weybridge instead of most of the OTL Wellingtons and all the OTL Warwicks. Depending upon how the TTL version compares to the Lancaster it might be built at Castle Bromwich too instead of the Lancasters it built IOTL.
items.original_question: What if Vickers Wellington produced with stressed skin? A follow on question from my previous thread about Mosquitoes produced with stress skin production intead of wood. What if the Vickers Wellington was produced with stressed skin production instead of wood and fabric? What would be the pros and cons? What performance advantages if any would the aircraft have e? Would it be able to be produced this way and in thd numbers required? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Vickers Wellington had been built as a conventional stressed-skin aircraft rather than with Barnes Wallis’s geodetic metal lattice and fabric covering, it would probably have been a more ordinary but not necessarily better bomber.

A stressed-skin Wellington would likely have had a smoother exterior, so it might have gained some speed and perhaps a little range through reduced drag. It would also have been easier to weatherproof and less dependent on doped fabric maintenance, which could matter in maritime or tropical service. If redesigned with a more conventional fuselage, it might also have been easier to arrange a cleaner bomb bay or later equipment fits.

But those gains would probably have been modest. The Wellington’s limits were not just its fabric skin; they were its size, twin-engine layout, defensive turrets, bomb load, and the rapid wartime shift toward larger four-engine bombers. A stressed-skin version would not have become a Lancaster-equivalent aircraft.

The largest loss would have been damage tolerance. The geodetic structure was unusually good at redistributing loads after being hit. Wellingtons often came home with huge sections of fabric and structure shot away because the lattice could carry stresses around damaged areas. A conventional stressed-skin aircraft depends more on intact panels, stringers, frames, and spars; battle damage could more easily produce buckling, tearing, or structural failure. So a stressed-skin Wellington might have been cleaner and slightly faster, but probably less survivable.

Production is also ambiguous. In the long run, conventional stressed-skin construction was the direction aircraft manufacturing was going, and it could be well suited to mass production with the right tooling. But in the late 1930s, redesigning the Wellington that way would likely have delayed entry into service and required more conventional aluminium sheet fabrication, riveting, and precision jigs. Britain badly needed available bombers in 1939–41, and a delayed Wellington would have hurt the early RAF bomber force.

The most likely result is that the aircraft would have resembled other contemporary medium bombers: somewhat cleaner aerodynamically, perhaps a little faster, but less distinctive and less rugged. It might have performed slightly better on paper, yet worse in the specific early-war role where the real Wellington’s ability to absorb punishment mattered. Strategically, it probably would not have changed the course of the air war; the RAF would still have moved on to four-engine heavies, and the Wellington would still have ended up in secondary roles such as maritime patrol, training, and special duties.

items.question: What If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power? How would the French Revolution and the wars against the coalitions have unfolded?
human_answers: Alternate-history counterfactuals hinge on small changes producing large downstream effects. Removing Napoleon Bonaparte from the post‑Revolutionary scene doesn’t collapse the French Revolution into a single predictable path; it produces several plausible trajectories shaped by institutional weaknesses, military fortunes, political culture, and international reaction. Below are the most likely variants, their mechanics, and consequences for the war with the Coalition. Summary framing The Revolution’s radical phase (1789–1794) already created durable structural changes: the abolition of feudal privileges, administrative centralization, secular legal reform impulse, and mass mobilization through levée en masse. Those foundations would continue to shape France even without Napoleon. The crucial variables that Napoleon exploited were France’s exhausted but vast manpower, a cohort of competent generals, political instability in Paris, and the European monarchies’ inability to coordinate consistently. Removing Napoleon changes leadership quality and political stability more than the Revolution’s underlying transformations. The outcome of the wars and the Revolution’s political evolution become probabilistic. Two broad families of outcomes dominate: (A) a prolonged Revolutionary/Republican instability with periodic military rule; or (B) an eventual conservative reaction producing a restored monarchy or authoritarian regime under different leaders. Which emerges depends on battlefield results, coalition cohesion, and French political resilience. Probable short‑ to medium‑term scenarios (1797–1815) 1) Revolutionary Directory survives longer but weakens (most likely) With no singular strategic and political talent to convert victories into regime consolidation, the Directory (or a Directory‑like government) would probably limp on. It was already corrupt, factionalized, and unpopular. Military successes would be more uneven. Generals like Moreau, Masséna, Hoche, and Augereau were capable but less politically adroit than Napoleon; they could win theaters but lacked Napoleon’s combination of operational audacity and political ambition. France would likely fight the Coalition to a military stalemate in some theaters, win in others. The levée en masse still supplies manpower: the Republic probably avoids complete defeat but also fails to secure sweeping victories that produce durable peace treaties like those Napoleon negotiated (Amiens/Pressburg/Tilsit analogues would be much harder). Domestic politics: repeated coup attempts, revolts, and coups from both Jacobin and Thermidorian factions. A series of short‑lived regimes and military interventions remain likely until a stronger political solution emerges. 2) A different military strongman rises (plausible) Absent Napoleon, another general could emulate his path. Generals such as Moreau, Masséna, or even Murat might build regional power bases and attempt coups. Any successful military politician would face harder constraints: fewer early spectacular victories (no Italian campaign miracle) and less charisma to exploit domestic exhaustion. But given the Directory’s fragility, a coup‑by‑general remains a strong possibility, producing an authoritarian government similar in form but different in policy from Napoleonic France. If such a figure consolidated power, reforms (legal codification, administrative centralization, meritocratic promotion) could still appear, albeit more modest or delayed. 3) Restoration or conservative stabilization (possible) If the Coalition’s coordination improves and France suffers significant strategic defeats (for instance, if Britain finances continental armies more effectively and Austria/Russia coordinate), royalist and moderate elements could reassert themselves. A negotiated restoration of the Bourbon monarchy or a constitutional monarchy under a conservative regime could occur by the early 1800s. That outcome would reverse some revolutionary gains (partial restoration of elite influence, rollback of some laws) but would struggle to erase deep administrative and social changes already entrenched. Popular resistance would be uneven; rural conservatism in some regions might favor restoration while urban and veteran constituencies resist. Would France win the war against the Coalition? Definitive “win” like the Napoleonic domination of Europe is unlikely without Napoleon’s genius for campaign strategy and diplomacy. France would probably avoid outright conquest by the Coalition but also unlikely to subdue Europe. Most likely military outcome: protracted war with shifting front lines, localized French successes, and negotiated settlements that leave France enlarged territorially in some terms (the Republic might keep some Belgian/Northern Italian gains) but not hegemonic across Europe. If the Coalition obtained decisive coordination and a string of victories (e.g., crushing France in the field and occupying Paris), they could force a restoration. Conversely, if French generals achieve enough operational successes, a compromise peace establishing France as a major but not dominant continental power would follow. Long‑term institutional and global consequences Legal and administrative legacies: the drive for rationalized administration, standardized law, and secular meritocracy likely persists. Even a restored monarchy would inherit the Napoleonic (or proto‑Napoleonic) bureaucracy and many reformist laws because they were efficient and staffed by a new elite. Nationalism and conscription: mass armies and national mobilization create durable national identities and military-industrial practices across Europe. Revolutions and reforms elsewhere accelerate without Napoleon, but not necessarily with the same geopolitical footprint. Colonial and global effects: without the Napoleonic reshuffle (e.g., the sale of Louisiana to the U.S.), colonial transfers follow different paths. Britain remains dominant at sea; colonial contests continue but with alternate timings. Legal codification (Civil Code) may emerge differently or later. The idea of a rational civil code was already present among reformers; in one variant it is completed by another jurist or regime, preserving many modern legal foundations of continental law. Concrete examples and plausible anecdotes Example: A Moreau‑led stabilization. Moreau secures victory over Austrian forces in Germany, returns to Paris, negotiates a constitutional settlement limiting radicalism, and avoids imperial pretensions. France keeps the Rhineland and revenues sufficient to sustain influence but not empire. Example: Coalition success and Bourbon restoration. Improved Anglo‑Austrian‑Russian coordination defeats French armies, occupies Paris, restores the Bourbons with constitutional limits. Local reforms (metric system, secular administration) remain because they are functional; émigrés regain some property through compensation rather than wholesale reversal. Net assessment Napoleon’s absence reduces the likelihood of France conquering Europe and exporting Napoleonic institutions by force. It increases the probability of prolonged internal instability, fragmented military outcomes, and either a delayed authoritarian consolidation under another general or a conservative settlement restoring monarchy with revolutionary reforms partially retained. The Revolution’s social, administrative, and legal transformations mostly survive in adapted form; its geopolitical expansion and specific legacy (Napoleonic Code, Europe‑wide redrawing) are weaker or redistributed differently. Time note: analysis reflects scholarship and primary evidence available through May 2024.
items.model_answer:
If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power, the French Revolution would probably still have overthrown the monarchy, radicalized, fought the First Coalition, and created a mass revolutionary army. Those developments were already driven by deeper forces: fiscal collapse, social conflict, revolutionary ideology, foreign intervention, and the levée en masse. Napoleon did not cause the Revolution, nor did he create France’s military mobilization. But without him, the Revolution’s later course would likely have been less centralized, less expansionist, and less successful militarily.

Up to about 1794, events might have changed relatively little. The fall of the monarchy in 1792, the execution of Louis XVI, the war against Austria and Prussia, the Terror, and the rise and fall of Robespierre were not dependent on Napoleon. France’s survival against the First Coalition was the result of mass conscription, patriotic mobilization, administrative centralization, and the weakness of coalition coordination. France would probably still have pushed back the invaders and occupied Belgium and parts of the Rhineland.

The major divergence comes after 1795. Napoleon’s real historical rise began when he helped suppress the royalist uprising of 13 Vendémiaire in Paris, then won spectacular victories in Italy against Austria. Without him, the Directory would have been more vulnerable. It might still have survived, because other generals such as Hoche, Moreau, Jourdan, Masséna, or Pichegru were capable commanders, but none combined Napoleon’s battlefield brilliance, political instinct, and ambition in quite the same way.

The Italian campaign would probably have been much less decisive. Historically, Napoleon’s victories in northern Italy forced Austria to make peace at Campo Formio in 1797 and gave France enormous leverage. Without him, Austria might not have been knocked out so quickly. The First Coalition war could have dragged on longer, or France might have accepted a more modest peace: recognition of the Republic, control over Belgium, perhaps some influence in the Rhineland, but not the sweeping reorganization of Italy that Napoleon imposed.

The Directory itself would likely have remained unstable. It was corrupt, unpopular, financially weak, and dependent on the army. In real history, Napoleon ended it with the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and created the Consulate, then the Empire. Without him, there are two likely alternatives. Either the Directory limps on and is eventually replaced by a more conservative republican or constitutional regime, or another general seizes power. A military dictatorship was still plausible because the Revolution had militarized French politics, but it probably would not have produced a figure as dominant as Napoleon.

The wars against the coalitions would also have been less sweeping. There would probably have been no Egyptian expedition, no Napoleonic Empire, no Confederation of the Rhine under French control, no invasion of Spain by Napoleon, and almost certainly no invasion of Russia. Those conflicts were closely tied to Napoleon’s personal ambitions and strategic choices. The European powers would still have feared revolutionary France, and France would still have sought defensible “natural frontiers,” especially the Rhine. But the wars would probably have remained more limited: France versus Austria, Britain, Prussia, and Russia over Belgium, the Rhineland, northern Italy, and influence in the Low Countries, rather than a continent-wide Napoleonic struggle.

Britain would likely have remained France’s most persistent enemy. Even without Napoleon, Britain had strong reasons to oppose French control of Belgium, Antwerp, and the Channel coast. Naval and colonial war would therefore have continued. But without Napoleon’s continental system and imperial domination of Europe, Britain might have had less reason to fund repeated grand coalitions on the same scale.

A plausible outcome is that revolutionary France survives but stabilizes earlier and more modestly. It might become a conservative republic, a military republic, or even a constitutional monarchy if royalists gained strength. Some revolutionary reforms would likely endure: abolition of feudalism, secular civil administration, equality before the law, and the sale of church lands. But without Napoleon, those reforms would not have been exported across Europe as systematically through conquest and satellite states. There would also be no Napoleonic Code in its familiar form, though France would probably still have produced some legal consolidation of revolutionary principles.

So the most likely answer is not that the old monarchy simply returns and the Revolution fails. By the time Napoleon rose, the Revolution had already transformed France too deeply. Rather, without him, France would probably have remained a powerful revolutionary state but not become a European empire. The coalition wars would likely have been longer in the 1790s but less vast after 1800. Europe might have reached a compromise peace earlier, with France retaining some revolutionary gains but without the massive Napoleonic reshaping of Germany, Italy, Spain, and central Europe.

items.question: What If the Byzantine Empire successfully contained the Turkish State in Anatolia?
human_answers: I think that, in any case, Constantinople was doomed to fall. The turks were not the only the only threat to the already dying empire. If the Byzantine Empire had successfully contained the Turkish state in Anatolia, the most likely result is that Byzantium would have survived much longer as a major eastern Mediterranean power, and the Ottoman Empire as we know it probably would not have emerged.

The key issue is Anatolia. For Byzantium, Anatolia was not just a frontier; it was the empire’s main source of soldiers, taxes, landholding elites, and strategic depth. After the Turkish victories and migrations of the 11th–13th centuries, especially after Manzikert in 1071, Byzantium lost much of that base. If the empire had contained the Turks—keeping them limited to eastern Anatolia or preventing the rise of powerful Turkish principalities in central and western Anatolia—Constantinople would have had a much stronger military and fiscal foundation.

In that scenario, the Byzantine Empire likely remains a durable regional empire rather than declining into a city-state dependent on Italian merchants and Balkan alliances. Constantinople would be far less vulnerable, and the Ottoman rise from a small frontier beylik in northwest Anatolia would probably never happen. Without an Ottoman state controlling both Anatolia and the Balkans, there would likely be no Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453, no Ottoman domination of southeastern Europe, and no sieges of Vienna in the same form.

The Balkans would have developed very differently. Serbia, Bulgaria, Hungary, and other regional powers would still compete, but without Ottoman conquest their political and religious trajectories would change significantly. Islam would have a much smaller presence in the Balkans, and institutions such as the devshirme and Janissary corps would not exist in the Ottoman form. A stronger Byzantium might reassert influence over parts of Greece, Thrace, Macedonia, and the Black Sea coast, though it probably would not restore the full Roman Empire.

The Crusades would also be affected. A stronger Byzantium holding Anatolia could provide a more secure land route to Syria and Palestine, making cooperation with western crusaders more feasible—or, alternatively, increasing rivalry between Byzantium and Latin powers. The Fourth Crusade’s capture of Constantinople in 1204 might be less likely or less successful if Byzantium retained Anatolian manpower and revenues. If 1204 never happened, Byzantium would avoid one of the most damaging blows in its history.

The eastern Mediterranean balance of power would change sharply. Instead of an Ottoman-dominated region, there might be a three- or four-sided contest among Byzantium, the Mamluks or other Muslim powers in Egypt and Syria, Italian maritime republics such as Venice and Genoa, and later western European monarchies. Trade between Europe and Asia would still be important, but the “Ottoman barrier” often associated with later European efforts to find sea routes to Asia would be reduced or absent. European overseas exploration would still likely occur, driven by profit, technology, Iberian expansion, and competition, but its timing and rhetoric might differ.

Culturally and demographically, Anatolia would probably remain much more Greek-speaking, Armenian, and Christian, though still influenced by Turkic migration, Persianate culture, and Islam along the frontier. Turkish political energy might be redirected toward Iran, the Caucasus, Syria, or Mesopotamia rather than western Anatolia. There could still be powerful Turkic Muslim states, but not an Ottoman Empire centered on Constantinople.

However, this would not mean Byzantium automatically becomes a restored superpower. The empire still faced serious problems: aristocratic factionalism, fiscal weakness, religious tensions with the Latin West, dependence on mercenaries, and pressure from Normans, Bulgarians, Serbs, Crusaders, Venetians, and later Mongol-era disruptions. Containing the Turks would solve Byzantium’s biggest strategic disaster, but it would not remove all causes of decline.

So the most plausible answer is: Byzantium would likely remain a long-lived, stronger Christian empire in the eastern Mediterranean; Constantinople would probably not fall to the Ottomans in 1453; the Ottoman Empire would likely never arise in its historical form; and the political, religious, and cultural map of the Balkans, Anatolia, and the eastern Mediterranean would be profoundly different.

items.question: What If the Byzantine Empire successfully restored the Roman Empire?
human_answers: Scenario overview: a Byzantine restoration of the Roman Empire—meaning the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) state not only survives but reconquers the Western Mediterranean, reclaims Rome and Italy, reunites the Latin West under Constantinople’s rule, and reforms imperial institutions to sustain unity—would reshape geopolitics, religion, culture, economics, technology diffusion, and the timelines of nation-states. Below are the most consequential and plausible ripple effects, organized by theme and time horizon. Immediate (0–75 years after restoration) Political map and administration Reunified imperial bureaucracy centered on Constantinople (or an institutionalized dual-capital system) reasserts provincial governorships in Italy, North Africa, Hispania and possibly parts of Gaul. Roman administrative divisions (themes adapted, praetorian-like prefectures rationalized) combine Eastern fiscal discipline with Western land structures. Local elites in reconquered regions either integrated through pragmatic accommodation—Roman law privileges, land confirmations, local magistracies—or replaced where resistance persists. Latin-speaking elites retain status; Greek becomes an administrative lingua franca alongside Latin. Military and security A larger, more professional imperial army/navy funded by access to Western tax bases. The fleet secures Mediterranean sea lanes, reducing piracy and increasing trade security. Border pressure continues: Lombards in Italy, Visigothic/Frankish polities in Gaul, and rising Islamic powers. Immediate military focus on consolidating reclaimed provinces rather than deep expansion. Religion Imperial policy toward Christianity attempts enforced reconciliation: either a pragmatic tolerance reconciling Chalcedonian and Western rites, or intensified attempts at Byzantine theological leadership. Papal independence is curtailed but papacy remains influential as a regional institution. If imperial policy favors unity through compromise (miaphysite/Catholic balancing or synodal mechanisms), schism is delayed or softened; if it favors central theological control, conflict with the Latin clergy intensifies. Mid-term (75–300 years) Delay or transformation of the East–West Schism A successful restoration likely postpones the formal East–West Schism or transforms it into periodic ecclesiastical tensions rather than permanent rupture. Imperial authority over church councils and bishop appointments reduces papal unilateralism; a Byzantine-style conciliarism could become normative for Western Christianity. Latin liturgical practices persist locally, but doctrinal formulations reflect negotiated compromises. Monastic networks (Benedictine, Eastern counterparts) intermix, accelerating theological exchange. Economic integration and commercial shift Restoration re-links Western agrarian resources, North African grain, Iberian metals and African trade routes into Byzantine commercial networks. Constantinople cements its role as the imperial market hub; Italian port cities (Venice, Amalfi) become institutionalized as imperial trade partners or semi-autonomous city-ports with privileges. Money and taxation: a unified currency standard (solidus or reformed successor) fosters pan-Mediterranean commerce; stronger imperial fiscal capacity funds infrastructure, fortifications and patronage networks. Cultural syncretism and intellectual diffusion Large-scale bilingualism and cross-fertilization: Latin scholarship gains access to Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics earlier and more systematically; Byzantine administrative literacy spreads to the West. Classical texts survive and circulate under imperial patronage, accelerating renaissance-like revivals centuries earlier. Architecture and urbanism combine Roman, Byzantine and local styles—imperial building programs in Rome and Ravenna revive monumental public works, forums, aqueduct repairs and fortified city grids. Technological and institutional consequences Military technology (Greek fire refinement, combined arms doctrine) and shipbuilding spread faster into the West, altering European warfare and naval power balances. Bureaucratic centralization may slow the feudal fragmentation typical of medieval Western Europe; serfdom and decentralized lordship could be less entrenched where imperial authority asserts land law and centralized justice. Long-term (300+ years) Different map of European states Nation-state formation (France, England, Spain, Germany) follows alternative trajectories. Frankish and Anglo-Saxon polities may evolve as semi-autonomous imperial vassals or rival kingdoms constrained by a powerful Mediterranean empire. The Holy Roman Empire as a separate entity may not arise in the same form; imperial legitimacy flows from Constantinople, undermining later Germanic claims to "Roman" succession. Islamic-Christian dynamics If Byzantium retains North Africa and the Iberian frontier, Islamic expansion into the Mediterranean faces a stronger imperial naval and logistical counterweight. Muslim polities in Iberia and North Africa might remain coastal enclaves or be contained, changing the Reconquista narrative and altering Mediterranean cultural exchanges. Alternatively, protracted conflict with Islamic caliphates diverts imperial resources and could prompt military-technological arms races (fortifications, naval arsenals). Economic modernization and global exploration A Mediterranean-centered, bureaucratically coherent empire with strong maritime tradition could sponsor long-distance exploration earlier or in different directions. Imperial control of Atlantic Iberian ports might either accelerate or redirect overseas expansion; exploration initiatives could be state-led rather than the more independent maritime republic model that produced the Age of Discovery. Global trade networks by 1500s could be dominated by an imperial Constantinople–Lisbon axis rather than a fragmented European set of maritime powers, concentrating profits and scientific exchange in imperial hands. Legal and cultural legacy Roman law, updated and imperialized, becomes the predominant legal framework across a larger Europe, reducing customary law diversity. Civic institutions (municipal councils, codified rights) flourish under imperial patronage, producing urban civil service cultures earlier than in our timeline. Latin and Greek literary canons merge into a pan-Roman heritage that influences education, philosophy and sciences; the Renaissance becomes an imperial cultural policy rather than a localized Italian phenomenon. Possible alternate outcomes and caveats Overextension risk: reconquest without sustainable administrative reforms could produce a brittle empire vulnerable to simultaneous pressures—northern Germanic migrations, Slavic expansions, and Islamic incursions—leading to fragmentation similar to historical patterns but delayed. Hybridization vs. dominance: the long-term outcome depends on imperial governance style. A flexible, federated Roman Empire that grants local autonomy and integrates elites will likely endure and produce a cohesive Mediterranean civilization. A rigidly centralized, Hellenizing approach may provoke persistent rebellions and eventual disintegration. Technology and demographic constraints: plague, climate events, and resource limits still shape outcomes. Unity cannot insulate the empire from pan-Eurasian shocks (pandemics, Little Ice Age-style cooling) that alter population and economic productivity. Unpredictable cultural agency: the resilience of local identities (Latin, Germanic, Celtic) and emergent ideologies (nationalism, papal reform movements) could still carve out autonomy over centuries, producing a world less fragmented but not uniformly imperial. Representative alternative timelines (concise sketches) Optimistic durable restoration: Byzantium reforms administratively, integrates Western elites, keeps the papacy as a respected regional institution, and maintains coastal control—result: a Mediterranean superstate fostering an earlier, centralized Renaissance, slower feudalization, limited Islamic maritime dominance, and different colonial patterns. Fragile restoration and rollback: initial reconquest succeeds but fiscal strain, military overstretch and local resistance allow new regional powers (Franks, Normans, later German princes) to erode imperial control—result: a delayed but partial reunification followed by fragmentation, producing a hybrid medieval map. Imperial cold war: a long-term bipolar Europe with a Byzantine-centered Mediterranean superstate and rising independent northern kingdoms; competition fosters accelerated military, navigational and administrative innovation, and a multipolar colonial era. Concluding synthesis A successful Byzantine restoration of the Roman Empire would shift the center of gravity of medieval Europe toward a literate, centralized, Mediterranean polity that blends Greek and Roman institutions with local Western practices. That consolidation would likely delay the doctrinal East–West split, reduce the extent of feudal fragmentation in reconquered regions, alter the pace and agents of exploration and colonization, and produce earlier and broader diffusion of classical learning. Outcomes vary by governance choices and exogenous shocks, but the decisive effect would be a less fragmented, more bureaucratically coherent Europe oriented around an enduring Roman imperial center.

If the Byzantine Empire had successfully restored the Roman Empire, the most important question would be not whether it could reconquer the old western provinces, but whether it could hold and integrate them. A temporary restoration was partly attempted under Justinian in the sixth century, when Byzantium reconquered North Africa, Italy, and parts of Spain. A truly successful restoration would mean those conquests survived, the western Mediterranean was politically reunited with Constantinople, and imperial administration recovered enough tax revenue, military manpower, and local legitimacy to endure.

In that scenario, western Europe would likely have developed very differently. The post-Roman Germanic kingdoms in Italy, Spain, and possibly Gaul would either be absorbed into the imperial system or remain as semi-autonomous client powers. Latin Christian culture would still dominate the West, but it would be tied more closely to Constantinople. The papacy might not become as politically independent as it did historically, because Rome would remain under effective imperial authority. Without a powerful independent papacy and without the same rise of the Frankish kingdom, there may be no Charlemagne-style “Holy Roman Empire,” or it would emerge much later and in a different form.

The Mediterranean would probably remain the central economic and political zone of Europe for longer. A restored empire controlling Italy, North Africa, Egypt, the Balkans, Anatolia, and parts of the western Mediterranean would have enormous fiscal and commercial advantages. Trade between East and West would be more secure, cities such as Rome, Carthage, Ravenna, Alexandria, and Constantinople might remain more integrated, and the sharp economic divergence between the eastern and western Mediterranean could be reduced.

The rise of Islam in the seventh century would be the greatest test. Historically, Byzantium survived but lost Syria, Egypt, and North Africa; a restored empire might have had more manpower and revenue, making it better able to resist early Arab expansion. If it retained Egypt and North Africa, the Islamic caliphates would be less able to dominate the southern Mediterranean, and the later history of Spain, Sicily, and the Crusades could be radically altered. However, a larger empire could also be more overstretched. If plague, fiscal exhaustion, and frontier pressure still occurred, the restored empire might collapse even more dramatically.

Religiously, a durable Roman restoration could reduce or delay the split between Greek East and Latin West. The Great Schism of 1054 was not inevitable; it grew from centuries of political separation, linguistic divergence, papal claims, and theological disputes. If the empire kept both halves under one imperial structure, Christianity might remain institutionally more unified, though tensions between Rome and Constantinople would still exist.

Politically, Europe might remain more Roman, urban, bureaucratic, and imperial, rather than fragmenting into the feudal kingdoms that shaped the medieval West. There would likely be less room for independent kingdoms in France, Germany, and Italy to develop in the same way. Legal and administrative continuity from Roman institutions would be stronger, and Roman law might dominate western Europe earlier and more uniformly.

But even a successful restoration would not simply recreate the empire of Augustus or Trajan. The restored empire would be Christian, Greek-influenced, militarized, and centered on Constantinople. Its western provinces would have changed socially and demographically, and local elites would demand autonomy. The empire would probably resemble a more federated Christian Roman commonwealth rather than a perfectly centralized ancient empire.

So the most likely outcome is a more unified Mediterranean world, a weaker or less independent papacy, a reduced role for the Franks and later medieval kingdoms, a delayed or altered East-West Christian split, and possibly a stronger defense against early Islamic expansion. The long-term survival of such a restored Roman Empire would depend on whether it could avoid overstretch and maintain loyalty across a culturally divided but economically valuable Mediterranean empire.
