Normal reentry gets rid of most of that kinetic energy by using atmospheric drag: the air heats up, the heat shield absorbs and rejects heat, and the spacecraft slows without carrying huge amounts of fuel. A small deorbit burn, often only around 100 m/s, is enough to make the orbit intersect the atmosphere.

If instead the spacecraft tried to use rockets to slow from orbital speed to “a few miles per hour” before or during reentry, the rockets would need to provide nearly the full orbital-speed change: roughly 7.8 km/s of delta-v, plus extra for gravity losses and control. That requires an enormous amount of propellant. With typical chemical rockets, most of the reentering vehicle’s mass would have to be fuel just for braking. And that fuel would first have had to be launched into orbit, making the original launch vehicle much larger.

Also, if the spacecraft slowed to a few mph high in the atmosphere, it would not just stay slow. It would begin falling nearly straight down and accelerate under gravity. To remain at a few mph all the way down, it would need to hover or descend under continuous rocket thrust, like a lander. That is possible, but again propellant-expensive.

If the rockets were fired lower in the atmosphere after most reentry heating had already happened, they could slow the vehicle for landing. That is much more practical. This is essentially what powered landers do. SpaceX Falcon 9 boosters, for example, use rockets to reduce speed during descent and land propulsively, but they still rely heavily on atmospheric drag and do not rocket-brake all the way from orbital speed. Starship’s intended Earth return also uses atmospheric drag for most of the energy loss, then rockets for the final landing burn.

So the direct answer is: yes, rockets could slow a spacecraft to a few miles per hour during reentry, but doing so from orbital speed would require so much propellant that it is usually impractical. The efficient approach is to let the atmosphere remove most of the speed and use rockets only for the final landing or for modest speed reduction during descent.

items.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.
items.original_question: 如果您有整个（例如英文）维基百科的印刷版本，您需要多少台打印机才能跟上对实时版本所做的更改？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to print the entire English Wikipedia “in real time,” the main problem would not be that it is infinitely large; it is that it is constantly changing.

A current English Wikipedia snapshot would be on the order of several million printed pages if formatted like ordinary reference text, excluding most images and page-history data. A single fast office laser printer printing about 60 pages per minute could produce roughly 86,000 pages per day, so printing one full snapshot would take months. It would consume tons of paper, many toner cartridges, and fill thousands of large book volumes.

But during those months, Wikipedia would not stay fixed. English Wikipedia receives roughly one to a few edits per second, or well over 100,000 edits per day. So by the time your printer finished the first volumes, the early pages would already be out of date.

If “real time” means printing every change as it happens, that is actually more manageable: a few fast printers could probably keep up with printing edit diffs or replacement pages, depending on formatting. But if “real time” means maintaining a complete printed copy that is always identical to the live English Wikipedia, then it is effectively impossible. Paper is a static medium, while Wikipedia is a continuously changing database.

So the result would be a huge, expensive, physically impressive encyclopedia that is obsolete almost immediately. You could print a snapshot, or you could print a live stream of updates, but you could not have a fully current printed English Wikipedia in the ordinary sense.

items.question: What If You Jumped from a Plane with Helium Tanks and a Giant Balloon?
human_answers: As ridiculous as it sounds, this is—sort of—possible. Falling from great heights is dangerous.[citation needed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Republic_Presidential_Unit_Citation)] A balloon could actually help save you, although a regular helium one from a party obviously won't do the trick. [Image: image] If the balloon is large enough, you don't even need the helium. A balloon will act as a parachute, slowing your fall to non-fatal speeds. Avoiding a high-speed landing is, unsurprisingly, the key to survival. As one medical paper[1]De Haven H. Mechanical analysis of survival in falls from heights of fifty to one hundred and fifty feet (http://injuryprevention.bmj.com/content/6/1/62.3.long). Injury Prevention. 6(1):62-b-68. put it, It is, of course, obvious that speed, or height of fall, is not in itself injurious ... but a high rate of change of velocity, such as occurs after a 10 story fall onto concrete, is another matter. ... which is just a wordy version of the old saying, "It's not the fall that kills you, it's the sudden stop at the end." To act as a parachute, a balloon filled with air, rather than helium, would have to be 10 to 20 meters across—far too big to be inflated with portable tanks. A powerful fan could be used to fill it with ambient air, but at that point, you may as well just use a parachute. Helium The helium makes things easier. It doesn't take too many helium balloons to lift a person. In 1982, Larry Walters (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters) flew across Los Angeles in a lawn chair lifted by weather balloons, eventually reaching several miles in altitude. After passing through LAX airspace, he descended by shooting some of the balloons with a pellet gun. On landing, Walters was arrested, although the authorities had some trouble figuring out what to charge him with. At the time, an FAA safety inspector told the New York Times, "We know he broke some part of the Federal Aviation Act, and as soon as we decide which part it is, some type of charge will be filed."[2]ARMCHAIR AIRMAN SAYS FLIGHT FULFILLED HIS LIFELONG DREAM (http://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/04/us/armchair-airman-says-flight-fulfilled-his-lifelong-dream.html?pagewanted=all), New York Times, July 4, 1982 A relatively small helium balloon—certainly smaller than a parachute—will suffice slow your fall, but it still has to be huge by party balloon standards. The biggest consumer rental helium tanks are about 250 cubic feet, and you'd need to empty at least 10 of them to put enough air in the balloon to support your weight. You'd have to do it quickly. The compressed helium cylinders are smooth and often quite heavy, which means they have a high terminal velocity. You'll only have a few minutes to use up all the cylinders. (As soon as you emptied one, you could drop it.) You can't get around this problem by moving your starting point higher. Since the upper atmosphere is pretty thin, anything dropped from the stratosphere up will accelerate to very high speeds until it hits the lower atmosphere, then fall slowly the rest of the way. This is true of everything from small meteors[3]By the time meteors hit the Earth, they have slowed down (http://www.geology.wisc.edu/~museum/meteorite.html) to a few hundred miles per hour. to Felix Baumgartner.[4]Jason Martinez, Falling Faster than the Speed of Sound (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/), Wolfram Blog, October 24, 2012 [Image: image] But if you inflated the balloons quickly, possibly by connecting many canisters to it at once, you'd be able to slow your fall. Just don't use too much helium, or you'll end up floating at 16,000 feet like Larry Walters.http://xkcd.com/1110 [Image: image] While researching this article,[5]Additionally, while researching impact speeds for this article, I came across a discussion (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=361878) on the Straight Dope Message Boards about survivable fall heights. One poster compared a fall from height to being hit by a bus. Another user, a medical examiner, replied (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showpost.php?p=7180162&postcount=40) that this was a bad comparison: "When hit by a car, the vast majority of people are not run over; they are run under. The lower legs break, sending them into the air. They usually strike the hood of the car, often with the back of the head impacting the windshield, "starring" the windshield, possibly leaving a few hairs in the glass. They then go over the top of the car. They are still alive, although with broken legs, and maybe with head pain from the nonfatal windshield impact. They die when they hit the ground. They die from head injury." The lesson: Don't mess with medical examiners. They're apparently pretty hardcore. I managed to lock up my copy of Mathematica several times on balloon-related differential equations, and subsequently got my IP address banned from Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=how+many+days+have+i+been+alive) for making too many requests. The ban-appeal form asked me to explain what task I was performing that necessitated so many queries, so this is what I put: [Image: image] I hope they understand.
items.original_question: 如果我带着几罐氦气和一个巨大的未充气的气球从飞机上跳下来怎么办？然后，在下降时，我释放氦气并填充气球。我需要下落多长时间才能让气球减慢我的速度以便我能够安全着陆？
items.model_answer:
If you jumped from a plane with helium tanks and a giant balloon, you would almost certainly not float gently to the ground unless the system had been engineered like a real parachute or balloon. Just carrying tanks and trying to inflate a balloon during free fall would be extremely dangerous and probably fatal.

Helium can lift only about 1 kilogram per cubic meter at sea level. So to support a person plus gear — say 100 kg total — you would need roughly 100 cubic meters of helium, about a sphere 6 meters across. At higher altitude, the balloon would need an even larger volume because the air is thinner. The helium tanks needed to carry that much gas would be very heavy; ordinary compressed-gas cylinders could weigh hundreds of kilograms, which means you would need still more helium to lift the tanks too.

If you jumped and then tried to inflate the balloon, you would be falling at high speed, eventually around 50–60 m/s, or 120 mph, belly-to-earth. The airflow would whip the balloon around, likely tear it, tangle you in it, or cause a violent sudden deceleration if it inflated unevenly. You would also have only tens of seconds from typical skydiving altitude. At commercial-airliner altitude, cold, low oxygen, and low pressure would be immediate additional hazards.

If, by magic, the balloon were already fully inflated, strong enough, correctly attached, and large enough, then yes: it could slow your fall or even make you buoyant. In that case it would behave somewhat like a helium balloon plus a drag device. But it would be hard to control, vulnerable to bursting or collapsing, and dangerous near the aircraft.

The practical answer is: helium lift is far too weak and the tanks/envelope/control problems are too severe. A giant balloon could in principle slow or lift you, but trying to use helium tanks and a balloon as an improvised parachute would almost certainly end badly. A normal parachute is vastly lighter, simpler, and more reliable.

items.question: What If All Digital Data Were Stored on Punch Cards?
human_answers: [Image: image] Google almost certainly has more data storage capacity than any other organization on Earth. Google is very secretive about its operations, so it's hard to say for sure. There are only a handful of organizations who might plausibly have more storage capacity or a larger server infrastructure. Here's my short list of the top contenders: NSA (http://www.nsa.gov/) NRO (http://www.nro.gov/) NGIP (https://www1.nga.mil/Pages/default.aspx) CIA (https://www.cia.gov/index.html) Schlumberger (http://www.slb.com/) Tencent (http://www.tencent.com/en-us/index.shtml) Chevron (http://www.chevron.com/) Honorable mentions: Amazon (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_River) (They're huge, but probably not as big as Google.) Facebook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_book) (They're on the right scale and growing fast, but still playing catch-up.) Microsoft (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Bob) (They have a million servers,[1]Data Center Knowledge: [Ballmer: Microsoft has 1 Million Servers although no one seems sure why.) Let's take a closer look at Google's computing platform. Follow the money We'll start by following the money. Google's aggregate capital expenditures–spending on building stuff[2]I'm excluding the cost of an extremely expensive building they bought in New York.—adds up to somewhere over $12 billion dollars.[3]Data Center Knowledge: Google’s Data Center Building Boom Continues: $1.6 Billion Investment in 3 Months (http://www.datacenterknowledge.com/archives/2013/07/19/google-data-center-spending-continues-to-soar-1-6-billion-in-3-months/) Their biggest data centers cost half a billion to a billion dollars, so they can't have more than 20 or so of those. On their website,[4]Data center locations (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/inside/locations/index.html) Google acknowledges that they have datacenters in the following locations: Berkeley County, South Carolina Council Bluffs, Iowa Atlanta, Georgia Mayes County, Oklahoma Lenoir, North Carolina The Dalles, Oregon Hong Kong Singapore Taiwan Hamina, Finland St Ghislain, Belgium Dublin, Ireland Quilicura, Chile In addition, they appear to operate a number of other large datacenters (sometimes through subsidiary corporations), including: Eemshaven, Netherlands Groningen, Netherlands Budapest, Hungary Wrocław, Poland Reston, Virginia Additional sites near Atlanta, Georgia They also operate equipment at dozens to hundreds of smaller locations around the world. Follow the power To figure out how many servers Google is running, we can look at their electricity consumption. Unfortunately, we can't just sneak up to a datacenter and read the meter.[5]Actually, wait, can we? Somebody should try that. Instead, we have to do some digging. The company disclosed that in 2010 they consumed an average of 258 megawatts of power.[6]Google used 2,259,998 MWh of electricity in 2010 (http://www.environmentalleader.com/2011/09/09/google-reveals-electricity-use-breaking-its-silence/), which translates to an average of 258 megawatts. How many computers can they run with that? We know that their datacenters are quite efficient, only spending 10-20% of their power on cooling and other overhead.[7]Google: Efficiency: How we do it (http://www.google.com/about/datacenters/efficiency/internal/) To get an idea of how much power each server uses, we can look at their "container data center" concept from 2005. It's not clear whether they actually use these containers in practice—it may just have been a now-outdated experiment—but it gives an idea of what they consider(ed) reasonable power consumption. The answer: 215 watts per server. Judging from that number, in 2010, they were operating around a million servers. They've grown a lot since then. By the end of 2013, the total amount of money they've pumped into their datacenters will be three or four times what it was as of 2010. They've contracted to buy over three hundred megawatts of power at just three sites,[8]Google: Purchasing clean energy (http://www.google.com/green/energy/use/#purchasing) which is more than they used for all their operations in 2010. Based on datacenter power usage and spending estimates, my guess would be that Google is currently running—or will soon be running—between 1.8 and 2.4 million servers. But what do these "servers" actually represent? Google could be experimenting in all kinds of wild ways, running boards with 100 cores or 100 attached disks. If we assume that each server has a couple[9]Anywhere from 2 to 5 (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of 2 TB disks attached, we come up with close to 10 exabytes[10]As a refresher, the order is: kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta, exa, zetta, yotta. An exabyte is a million terabytes. of active storage attached to running clusters. 10 Exabytes The commercial hard disk industry ships about 8 exabytes worth of drives annually.[12]IDC: Worldwide External Disk Storage Systems Factory Revenue Declines for the Second Consecutive Quarter (http://www.idc.com/getdoc.jsp?containerId=prUS24302513) Those numbers don't necessarily include companies like Google, but in any case, it seems likely that Google is a large piece of the global hard drive market. To make things worse, given the huge number of drives they manage, Google has a hard drive die every few minutes.[11]Eduardo Pinheiro, Wolf-Dietrich Weber and Luiz Andre Barroso, [Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population This isn't actually all that expensive a problem, in the grand scheme of things—they just get good at replacing drives—but it's weird to think that when a Googler runs a piece of code, they know that by the time it finishes executing, one of the machines it was running on will probably have suffered a drive failure. Google tape storage Of course, that only covers storage attached to running servers. What about "cold" storage? Who knows how much data Google—or anyone else—has stored in basement archives? In a 2011 phone interview with Paul Mah of SMB Tech, Simon Anderson of Tandberg Data let slip[13]SMB Tech: Is Tape Still Relevant for SMBs? (http://www.itbusinessedge.com/cm/blogs/mah/is-tape-still-relevant-for-smbs/?cs=45557) that Google is the world's biggest single consumer of magnetic tape cartridges, purchasing 200,000 per year. Assuming they've stepped up their purchasing since then as they've expanded, this could add up to another few exabytes of tape archives. Putting it all together Let's assume Google has a storage capacity of 15 exabytes, or 15,000,000,000,000,000,000 bytes. A punch card can hold about 80 characters, and a box of cards holds 2000 cards: [Image: image] 15 exabytes of punch cards would be enough to cover my home region, New England, to a depth of about 4.5 kilometers. That's three times deeper than the ice sheets that covered the region during the last advance of the glaciers: [Image: image] That seems like a lot. However, it's nothing compared to the ridiculous claims by some news reports about the NSA datacenter in Utah. NSA datacenter The NSA is building a datacenter in Utah. Media reports claimed that it could hold up to a yottabyte of data,[14]CNET: NSA to store yottabytes in Utah data centre (http://crave.cnet.co.uk/gadgets/nsa-to-store-yottabytes-in-utah-data-centre-49304118/) which is patently absurd. Later reports changed their minds, suggesting that the facility could only hold on the order of 3-12 exabytes.[15]Forbes: Blueprints Of NSA's Ridiculously Expensive Data Center In Utah Suggest It Holds Less Info Than Thought (http://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2013/07/24/blueprints-of-nsa-data-center-in-utah-suggest-its-storage-capacity-is-less-impressive-than-thought/) We also know the facility uses about 65 megawatts of power,[16]Salt-Lake City Tribune: NSA Bluffdale Center won’t gobble up Utah’s power supply (http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/56493868-78/power-center-electricity-utah.html.csp) which is about what a large Google datacenter consumes. A few headlines, rather than going with one estimate or the other, announced that the facility could hold "between an exabyte and a yottabyte" of data[17]Dailykos: Utah Data Center stores data between 1 exabyte and 1 yottabyte (http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/08/05/1228923/-Utah-Data-Center-stores-data-between-1-exabyte-and-1-yottabyte) ... which is a little like saying "eyewitnesses report that the snake was between 1 millimeter and 1 kilometer long." Uncovering further Google secrets There are a lot of tricks for digging up information about Google's operations. Ironically, many of them involve using Google itself—from Googling for job postings in strange cities to using image search to find leaked cell camera photos of datacenter visits. However, the best trick for locating secret Google facilities might be the one revealed by ex-Googler talentlessclown (http://www.reddit.com/user/talentlessclown) on reddit:[18]reddit: Can r/Australia help find Google's Sydney data center? Seems like a bit of a mystery... (http://www.reddit.com/r/australia/comments/1hctj4/can_raustralia_help_find_googles_sydney_data/catef4f) The easiest way to find manned Google data centres is to ask taxi drivers and pizza delivery people. There's something pleasing about that. Google has created what might be the most sophisticated information-gathering apparatus in the history of the Earth ... and the only people with information about them are the pizza delivery drivers. Who watches the watchers? [Image: image] Apparently, Domino's.
items.original_question: 如果所有数字数据都存储在打孔卡上，谷歌的数据仓库有多大？
items.model_answer:
If all digital data had to be stored on punch cards, modern computing would essentially collapse. Punch cards are digital in the sense that holes can represent bits, but their storage density is absurdly low compared with magnetic, optical, or solid-state storage.

A standard 80-column punch card stores about 80 characters, roughly 80 bytes. Even with clever binary encoding, you might only get around 100–120 bytes per card. That is negligible by modern standards. A single 4 GB movie would require about 50 million punch cards. Stacked together, those cards would be several kilometers high. A 1 TB hard drive’s contents would require about 12.5 billion cards.

For global data, the numbers become physically ridiculous. Humanity stores and generates data on the order of 100 zettabytes, or about 10²³ bytes. At 80 bytes per card, that would require roughly 1.25 × 10²¹ punch cards. If each card is about 0.18 mm thick, the stack would be around 20–25 light-years tall. The cards would weigh around 10¹⁸ kilograms, comparable to a large asteroid and far beyond anything the paper industry or Earth’s forests could supply.

Access speed would be another fatal problem. A fast punch-card reader might process a few thousand cards per minute, which is only a few kilobytes per second. Reading a terabyte could take years on one machine. Random access would be terrible: instead of instantly retrieving a file, you would need to locate the correct physical deck, feed it through a reader, and hope the cards were in order and undamaged.

Updating data would also be painful. Punch cards are not conveniently rewritable. Changing a file would mean punching new cards, replacing old ones, and maintaining strict physical organization. Databases, cloud storage, search engines, streaming video, smartphones, AI systems, modern banking, GPS, scientific simulations, and the internet as we know it would be impossible or reduced to tiny, slow, expensive versions of themselves.

Reliability would be poor too. Cards can bend, burn, tear, absorb moisture, get misordered, or be lost. Large-scale error correction and duplication would require even more cards, making the storage problem worse.

So the direct answer is: if all digital data were stored on punch cards, the modern digital world could not function. Storage would require astronomical physical space and material, reading and writing would be millions to billions of times slower, and most data-heavy technologies—video, cloud computing, big data, AI, modern software distribution—would be effectively impossible.

items.question: What If You Began Rising Upward at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: Did you bring a coat? A foot per second isn't that fast—it's substantially slower than a typical elevator.[1]Otis: About Elevators (http://www.otisworldwide.com/pdf/AboutElevators.pdf) It would take you 5-7 seconds to rise out of arms' reach, depending how tall your friends are. [Image: image] After 30 seconds, you'd be 30 feet—9 meters—off the ground. Judging from What-If #44 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/44/), this is getting close to your last chance for a friend to throw you a sandwich or water bottle or something.[2]Not that it will help, ultimately. [Image: image] After a minute or two you would be above the trees. You'd still be about as comfortable as you were on the ground. If it's a breezy day, it will probably get chillier thanks to the steadier wind above the treeline.[3]For this article, I'm going to assume a typical atmosphere temperature profile. It can, of course, vary quite a bit. After 10 minutes you would be above all but the tallest skyscrapers, and after 25 minutes you'd pass the spire of the Empire State Building. [Image: image] The air at these heights is about 3% thinner than it is at the surface. Fortunately, your body handles air pressure changes like that all the time. Your ears may pop, but you wouldn't really notice anything else. Air pressure changes quickly with height. Surprisingly, when you're standing on the ground, air pressure is even measurably lower at your head than at your feet. If your phone has a barometer in it, as a lot of new Android phones do, you can download an app and actually see the pressure difference between your head and your feet. A foot per second is pretty close to a kilometer per hour, so after an hour, you'll be about a kilometer off the ground. At this point, you definitely start to get chilly. If you have a coat, you'll still be ok, though you might also notice the wind picking up. At about two hours and two kilometers, the temperature would drop below freezing. The wind would also, most likely, be picking up. If you have any exposed skin, this is where frostbite starts to become a concern.[4]National Weather Service: Wind Chill Temperature Index (http://www.nws.noaa.gov/om/windchill/images/wind-chill-brochure.pdf) Starting at this point, the air pressure would drop below what you'd experience in an airliner cabin,[5]... which are typically kept pressurized at about 70%-80% of sea level pressure, judging from the barometer in my phone. and the effects would start to become more significant, but unless you had a warm coat, the temperature would be a bigger problem. Over the next two hours, the air would drop to below-zero[6]Either unit.​[7]Not Kelvin, though. temperatures. Assuming for a moment that you survived the oxygen deprivation, at some point you'd freeze to death. But when? The scholarly authorities on freezing to death seem to be, unsurprisingly, Canadians. The most widely-used model for human survival in cold air was developed by Peter Tikuisis and John Frim for the Defence and Civil Institute of Environmental Medicine in Ontario.[8]Prediction of Survival Time in Cold Air (http://cradpdf.drdc-rddc.gc.ca/PDFS/zba6/p144967.pdf)—see page 24 for the relevant tables. According to their model, the main factor in the cause of death would be your clothes. If you were nude, you'd probably succumb to hypothermia somewhere around the five hour mark, before your oxygen ran out.[9]And frankly, this really raises more questions than it answers. If you were bundled up, you may be frostbitten, but you would probably survive ... ... long enough to reach the Death Zone. [Image: image] Above 8,000 meters—above the tops of all but the highest mountains—the oxygen content in the air is too low to support human life. Near this zone, you would experience a range of symptoms, possibly including confusion, dizziness, clumsiness, impaired vision, and nausea. As you approach the Death Zone, your blood oxygen content would plummet. Your veins are supposed to bring low-oxygen blood back to your lungs to be refilled with oxygen. But in the Death Zone, there's so little oxygen in the air that your veins lose oxygen to the air instead of gaining it.[10]Linda D. Pendleton, When Humans Fly High: What Pilots Should Know About High-Altitude Physiology, Hypoxia, and Rapid Decompression (http://www.avweb.com/news/aeromed/181893-1.html) The result would be a rapid loss of consciousness and death. This would happen around the seven hour mark; the chances are very slim that you would make it to eight. [Image: image] And two million years later, your frozen body, still moving along steadily at a foot per second, would pass through the heliopause into interstellar space—the same boundary that Voyager just crossed.[11]Again. Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto, died in 1997. A portion of his remains were placed on New Horizons spacecraft, which will fly past Pluto and then continue out of the Solar System. It's true that your hypothetical foot-per-second trip would be cold, unpleasant, and rapidly fatal. But when the Sun becomes a red giant in four billion years and consumes the Earth, you and Clyde would be the only ones to escape. So there's that. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果你突然开始以每秒一英尺的速度稳定上升，你到底会怎么死？你会先被冻住还是窒息？或者其他什么？
items.model_answer:
If you began rising straight upward at one foot per second, the motion would feel slow at first—about 0.68 mph vertically, or 3,600 feet per hour. But altitude would accumulate quickly enough that the atmosphere would become the main problem.

Assuming you are outdoors, unobstructed, and magically kept moving upward at that constant speed:

After 1 hour, you would be 3,600 feet up. You could still breathe, though it would be cold and windy.

After about 3 hours, you would be around 10,800 feet, where many people start noticing shortness of breath and reduced mental sharpness.

After 4–6 hours, at roughly 14,000–22,000 feet, hypoxia would become dangerous. Without supplemental oxygen, you would likely become confused, lose coordination, then lose consciousness.

After about 8–10 hours, you would be at 29,000–36,000 feet, around Everest-to-airliner cruising altitude. Without oxygen and protection from the cold, you would almost certainly be unconscious or dead. The temperature could be around −40°C to −55°C, and the air pressure would be far too low for normal survival.

After about 17.5 hours, you would reach the Armstrong limit, around 63,000 feet. Above this altitude, water boils at human body temperature unless you are in a pressurized suit or cabin. Exposed skin and fluids in your mouth and eyes would begin to boil, though your blood would not literally boil inside your blood vessels because it is under pressure.

If you somehow had oxygen, thermal protection, and a pressure suit, you would reach the “edge of space” at 100 km altitude after about 3.8 days. But you would not be in orbit. Orbit requires enormous sideways speed—about 7.8 km/s near Earth—not just height. If the upward force stopped, you would fall back down.

So the direct answer is: without special equipment, you would probably die from hypoxia and exposure within several hours, long before reaching space. With a full pressure suit and life support, you could slowly rise into space after a few days, but you would still not be orbiting Earth—you would just be moving upward very slowly.

items.question: What If the Wind Reached 500 Miles per Hour?
human_answers: Absolutely! [Image: image] Some things don't work like they do in the movies. Getting shot doesn't really make someone fly backward. The vacuum of space doesn't make your skin explode. But high wind can definitely pick up a person. In fact, if you were standing in the parking lot, the wind wouldn't just pick you up—it would also peel the pavement from the ground! [Image: image] It wouldn't be strong enough to peel your skin off. Humans can survive blasts of 500 mph wind, which is important because pilots sometimes need to eject from airplanes at those speeds. In the 1940s, the US government put pilots in wind tunnels to learn how they reacted to high winds. Have you ever been curious what happens to a person's face in 457 mph winds? Well, you can watch a video of one of those wind tunnel tests here (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IU4SDDNXuUA). (That test was conducted at NASA Langley Research Center, where I worked before I started drawing internet comics for a living.) It doesn't look very comfortable—I didn't know cheeks could flap like that—but the pilot appears to stay alive. Luckily, he's strapped into that chair. He wouldn't be able to stand up in those winds! If he tried, he would go flying backward down the tunnel. High wind is really powerful. In a paper in the journal Weather, J. F. R. McIlveen showed how to calculate the force of wind on the human body.[1]McIlveen, J. F. R.. "The Everyday Effects Of Wind Drag On People. (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1256/wea.29.02/pdf)" Weather 57, no. 11 (2002): 410-413. The calculations on page 2 show how far you'd have to lean to stay upright in wind of various speeds. [Image: image] When wind speed rises above about 120 mph, it's no longer possible to stay upright no matter how far you lean; you'll start to slide backward across the ground,[2]When Hurricane Isabel hit Virginia in 2003, I had the bright idea of standing on a skateboard with a poncho held up like a sail, so the wind would blow me down the street. But the moment I got the sail up, the wind fell quiet. Later, I learned that people die from doing that (http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-1327705/Kite-surfer-28-dies-gale-drags-100mph-beach-drops-50ft.html). Oops. then quickly go head over heels and start to tumble. You wouldn't necessarily be thrown very high. If the wind were perfectly level, you'd tumble along the surface, bouncing against the ground. However, if there were any updrafts, you could easily be lifted up and carried away. The good news is that 500 mph winds are rare. The strongest hurricanes have wind speeds around 200 mph with gusts up to 250.[3]Courtney, J.; Buchan, S.; Cerveny, R.S.; Bessemoulin, P.; Peterson, T.C.; Rubiera Torres, J.M.; Beven, J.; King, J.; Trerwin, B.; Rancourt, K.. 2012 "Documentation and verification of the world extreme wind gust record: 113.3 m s–1 on Barrow Island, Australia, during passage of tropical cyclone Olivia. (http://www.bom.gov.au/amoj/docs/2012/courtney_hres.pdf)" Australian Meterological and Oceanographic Journal, 62 (1). 1-9. Tornadoes can reach 300 mph.[4]It's difficult to get accurate measurements of surface winds since those tornadoes destroy most measuring equipment (http://www.spc.noaa.gov/faq/tornado/#History)! 300 is a far cry from 500; the force from a 500 mph wind is several times stronger than the force from a 300 mph wind. There are a few ways you could experience wind speeds faster than 500 mph. One is to stand on top of a volcano when it erupts. When Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980, the column of ash was blasted outward at 700 mph, which is close to the speed of sound.[5]Kieffer, S. W., 1981, Fluid dynamics of the May 18 blast at Mount St. Helens, in Lipman, P.W., and Mullineux, D.R., eds., The 1980 Eruptions of Mount St. Helens, Washington: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 1250, p. 379-400. Another way to experience 500 mph winds is to trigger a hypercane.[6]Limits on Hurricane Intensity (http://wind.mit.edu/~emanuel/holem/holem.html) A hypercane is an exotic type of hurricane with 500 mph winds spinning in a very tight vortex just a few miles across. Hypercanes can't exist on Earth right now. To form, they require ocean temperatures of about 50°C. No matter how much we warm the planet, we're not going to get the temperature that high any time soon. However, there's one way these storms might happen. When an asteroid or comet—coincidentally, one about the size of the recently-named 4942 Munroe (http://blog.xkcd.com/2013/09/30/asteroid-4942-munroe/)—hit Mexico 65 million years ago, it punched a hole in the crust and left behind a sea of lava.[7]Christeson, Gail L., Gareth S. Collins, Joanna V. Morgan, Sean P.S. Gulick, Penny J. Barton, and Michael R. Warner. "Mantle Deformation Beneath The Chicxulub Impact Crater (https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/bitstream/10044/1/4214/1/icpub.pdf)." Earth and Planetary Science Letters 284, no. 1-2 (2009): 249-257. When water flowed back in to fill the hole, it would have been heated by contact with the molten rock. This might have created the conditions for hypercanes to form, and one paper suggests that these storms could have lifted a large amount of dust and debris into the upper atmosphere—thus contributing to a global winter and extinction of the dinosaurs.[8]Emanuel, Kerry A., Kevin Speer, Richard Rotunno, Ramesh Srivastava, and Mario Molina. "Hypercanes: A Possible Link In Global Extinction Scenarios (ftp://texmex.mit.edu/pub/emanuel/PAPERS/hypercane95.pdf)." Journal of Geophysical Research 100, no. D7 (1995): 13755-13765. [Image: image] In short, the answer to Grey's question is yes—500 mph winds would send you flying through the air. But don't worry about that. Instead, worry about is the thing that created the 500 mph winds. Odds are, that's what's going to kill you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果风速达到 500 英里/小时，它会卷起人吗？
items.model_answer:
If wind at Earth’s surface reached 500 miles per hour, it would be catastrophically destructive — far beyond any hurricane and stronger than the winds in most measured tornadoes.

At sea-level air density, 500 mph is about 223 m/s, or roughly Mach 0.65. That is below the speed of sound, but still incredibly violent. The dynamic pressure of such wind would be around 30,000 pascals, about 4.4 psi. That may sound small compared with tire pressure, but spread over a wall, roof, vehicle, or human body, it becomes enormous. A 10-square-meter wall could experience hundreds of thousands of newtons of force — enough to rip apart ordinary buildings.

A person caught outside would almost certainly be killed. You would not be able to stand, breathe normally, or protect yourself. The wind itself could throw you like debris, but the bigger danger would be flying objects: wood, glass, metal, gravel, signs, cars, roofing, and tree limbs moving at lethal speeds. Even small particles like sand or rain could cause severe injury at that speed.

Most houses would be destroyed. Roofs would be torn off, walls would fail, windows would explode inward or outward depending on pressure differences, and vehicles could be rolled or lifted. Trees would be shredded or uprooted. Power lines, towers, and weaker steel structures would collapse. Well-built reinforced concrete structures might survive better, but exposed surfaces, doors, windows, and attachments would still take severe damage.

If such winds occurred over the ocean, the sea surface would become chaotic and violently aerated, with extreme spray, waves, and potentially devastating storm surge if the wind persisted over a large area. Ships would be in extreme danger.

A key detail is duration and scale. A brief, narrow 500 mph gust in a tornado-like vortex would cause a trail of extreme destruction. A sustained 500 mph wind over a city or coastline would be an almost unimaginable disaster. On Earth, broad sustained surface winds that fast are not physically plausible under normal weather conditions; hurricanes are limited by ocean heat, atmospheric structure, and energy loss, and even the strongest tornado winds measured or estimated are generally well below 500 mph.

So, in short: a 500 mph surface wind would not just be “very windy.” It would behave like a massive atmospheric battering ram, making outdoor survival nearly impossible and causing near-total destruction of conventional structures in its path.

items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one. [Image: image] The Little Prince, by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, is a story about a traveler from a distant asteroid. It's simple and sad and poignant and memorable.[1]For another take on the Petit Prince, scroll down to the last section of this wonderful piece (http://the-toast.net/2013/08/02/texts-from-peter-pan-et-al/) by Mallory Ortberg. It's ostensibly a children's book, but it's hard to pin down who the intended audience is. In any case, it certainly has found an audience; it's among the best-selling books in history. [Image: image] It was written in 1942. That's an interesting time to write about asteroids, because in 1942 we didn't actually know what asteroids looked like. Even in our best telescopes, the largest asteroids were only visible as points of light. In fact, that's where their name comes from—the word asteroid means "star-like." We got our first confirmation of what asteroids looked like in 1971, when Mariner 9 visited Mars and snapped pictures of Phobos and Deimos.[2]Here's (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/m09_mtvs4109_09.html) a picture of Phobos looking like the archetypical asteroid. The archived images from the mission are at the NASA Space Science Data Center (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?ds=PSPG-00235), but strangely, the NSSDC refers readers to someone's personal Tripod page (http://petermasek.tripod.com/mariner9.html) to browse the actual images. These moons, believed to be captured asteroids,[3]Ironically, while Phobos and Deimos look like asteroids, new research suggests they're not. See Craddock, Robert A.. "Are Phobos And Deimos The Result Of A Giant Impact? (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0019103510004100)". Icarus (2010) solidified the modern image of asteroids as cratered potatoes. [Image: image] Before the 1970s, it was common for science fiction to assume small asteroids would be round, like planets.[4]Not always; plenty of people had a good idea of what they would look like. And there were stranger ideas (http://pencilink.blogspot.com/2010/08/uncle-scrooge-29-carl-barks-art-cover.html) ... The Little Prince took this a step further, imagining an asteroid as a tiny planet with gravity, air, and a rose. There's no point in trying to critique the science here, because (1) it's not a story about asteroids, and (2) it opens with a parable about how foolish adults are for looking at everything too literally. So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果一颗小行星很小但质量却很大，你真的能像小王子一样住在上面吗？
items.model_answer:
You almost certainly couldn’t live there.

A tiny but ultra-massive asteroid would have extremely strong gravity because surface gravity depends on mass divided by radius squared:

\[
g=\frac{GM}{R^2}
\]

So if the object is very small but has a huge mass, its surface gravity becomes enormous.

For example, imagine an asteroid only 1 km in radius but with the mass of Ceres, a dwarf planet. Its surface gravity would be thousands of times stronger than Earth’s. You would be crushed instantly. Even your blood, bones, organs, and spacecraft would be pulled downward with catastrophic force.

There would also be severe tidal forces. Because the asteroid is so small, gravity could be noticeably stronger at your feet than at your head. That difference would stretch and compress your body. On a sufficiently compact object, this “spaghettification” effect could kill you even before simple weight did.

The escape velocity would also be huge. Leaving the surface might require speeds far beyond ordinary rockets. If the asteroid were massive enough, light itself could struggle to escape; if its radius were smaller than its Schwarzschild radius, it would become a black hole. Then there would be no solid surface to live on at all.

Physically, such an object also would not behave like a normal asteroid. Ordinary rock could not support that much mass in such a tiny volume. It would collapse into an exotic compact object, perhaps something like degenerate matter, or if massive and compact enough, a black hole.

So the short answer is: a tiny ultra-massive “asteroid” would be less like a place to live and more like a deadly compact-gravity object. You would be crushed, stretched by tidal forces, unable to escape, and if it were massive enough, you would simply be dealing with a black hole rather than an asteroid.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.
items.original_question: 我心不在焉地搅拌着一杯热茶，心里想：我这不是给杯子里加了动能吗？我知道搅拌确实有助于冷却茶，但如果我搅拌得更快怎么办？我可以通过搅拌来煮一杯水吗？
items.model_answer:
Yes, in principle you can boil water by stirring it, because the mechanical work you do on the water is eventually converted into heat by viscosity and turbulence.

For a mass \(m\) of water, the temperature rise is roughly

\[
\Delta T = \frac{W}{mc}
\]

where \(W\) is the mechanical work put in and \(c \approx 4180\ \text{J/(kg·°C)}\) is water’s specific heat capacity.

For example, to heat 1 liter of water from \(20^\circ\text{C}\) to \(100^\circ\text{C}\):

\[
W = mc\Delta T \approx 1 \times 4180 \times 80 \approx 334{,}000\ \text{J}
\]

So if you could deliver 100 W of stirring power into the water with no heat loss, it would take about

\[
334{,}000/100 \approx 3300\ \text{s}
\]

or roughly 55 minutes just to reach \(100^\circ\text{C}\). To actually vaporize a significant amount of water would require much more energy, because the latent heat of vaporization is about \(2.26 \times 10^6\ \text{J/kg}\).

In practice, stirring water with a spoon would not boil it, because you cannot deliver enough power and the water loses heat to the surroundings. But with a powerful mechanical stirrer or blender in a sufficiently insulated container, yes, stirring can heat water to boiling. This is essentially the same physics as Joule’s paddle-wheel experiment: mechanical work becomes thermal energy.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it. If you're not a physics person, it might not sound odd to you, so here's a little context for why it's such a surprising idea: Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with the world at all. Look at your hand—there are about a trillion neutrinos from the Sun passing through it every second. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the neutrino flood is that neutrinos hardly interact with ordinary matter at all. On average, out of that massive flood, only one neutrino will "hit" an atom in your body every few years.[1]Less often if you're a child, since you have fewer atoms to be hit. Statistically, my first neutrino interaction probably happened somewhere around age 10. In fact, neutrinos are so shadowy that the entire Earth is transparent to them; nearly all of the Sun's neutrino flood goes straight through it unaffected. To detect neutrinos, people build giant tanks filled with hundreds of tons of material in the hopes that they'll register the impact of a single solar neutrino. This means that when a particle accelerator (which produces neutrinos) wants to send a neutrino beam to a detector somewhere else in the world, all it has to do is point the beam at the detector—even if it's on the other side of the Earth! [Image: image] That's why the phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" sounds weird—it mixes scales in an incongruous way. It's like the idiom "knock me over with a feather" or the phrase "football stadium filled to the brim with ants".[2]Which would still be less than 1% of the ants in the world. If you have a math background, it's sort of like seeing the expression "ln(x)e"—it's not that, taken literally, it doesn't make sense, but it's hard to imagine a situation where it would apply.[3]If you want to be mean to first-year calculus students, you can ask them to take the derivative of ln(x)e dx. It looks like it should be "1" or something, but it's not. Similarly, it's so hard to get enough neutrinos to compel even a single one of them to interact with matter, making it hard to picture a scenario in which there'd be enough of them to affect you. Supernovae[4]"Supernovas" is also fine. "Supernovii" is discouraged. provide that scenario. The physicist who mentioned this problem to me told me his rule of thumb for estimating supernova-related numbers: However big you think supernovae are, they're bigger than that. Here's a question to give you a sense of scale: Which of the following would be brighter, in terms of the amount of energy delivered to your retina: A supernova, seen from as far away as the Sun is from the Earth, or The detonation of a hydrogen bomb pressed against your eyeball? [Image: image] Applying the physicist rule of thumb suggests that the supernova is brighter. And indeed, it is ... by nine orders of magnitude. That's why this is a neat question; supernovae are unimaginably huge and neutrinos are unimaginably insubstantial. At what point do these two unimaginable things cancel out to produce an effect on a human scale? A paper by radiation expert Andrew Karam provides an answer.[5]Karam, P. Andrew. "Gamma And Neutrino Radiation Dose From Gamma Ray Bursts And Nearby Supernovae. (http://wayback.archive.org/web/20120313045458/http://www.andrewkaram.com/andy/pdf/HPJ.pdf)" Health Physics 82, no. 4 (2002): 491-499. It explains that during certain supernovae, the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star, 1057 neutrinos can be released (one for every proton in the star that collapses to become a neutron). Karam calculates that the neutrino radiation dose at a distance of one parsec[6]3.262 light-years, or a little less than the distance from here to Alpha Centauri. would be around half a nanosievert, or 1/500th the dose from eating a banana.[7]xkcd.com/radiation (http://xkcd.com/radiation/) A fatal radiation dose is about 4 sieverts. Using the inverse-square law, we can calculate the radiation dose: \[ 0.5\text{ nanosieverts} \times\left ( \frac{1\text{ parsec}}{x}\right )^2 = 5\text{ sieverts} \] \[ x=0.00001118\text{ parsecs}=2.3\text{ AU} \] 2.3 AU is a little more than the distance between the Sun and Mars. Core collapse supernovae happen to giant stars, so if you observed a supernova from that distance, you'd probably be inside the outer layers of the star that created it. [Image: image] The idea of neutrino radiation damage reinforces just how big supernovae are. If you observed a supernova from 1 AU away—and you somehow avoided being being incinerated, vaporized, and converted to some type of exotic plasma—even the flood of ghostly neutrinos would be dense enough to kill you. If it's going fast enough, a feather can absolutely knock you over. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 距离超新星有多近才能获得致命剂量的中微子辐射？
items.model_answer:
A lethal neutrino burst from a supernova would be extraordinarily bad for life but would not “blast” Earth apart. Neutrinos interact so weakly that almost all of them would pass through the planet, the oceans, buildings, and people. But if the supernova were close enough, the sheer number of neutrinos would make even those rare interactions add up to a fatal whole-body radiation dose.

For a core-collapse supernova, the lethal-neutrino distance would be roughly solar-system scale, on the order of a few to a few tens of astronomical units, depending on the assumed neutrino energies and what dose is called “lethal.” At ordinary astronomical distances, even from a nearby star a few parsecs away, the neutrino dose would be negligible. So this scenario requires an impossibly close supernova, essentially a massive star exploding inside or near the outer Solar System.

If it happened, the neutrino pulse would arrive first, lasting about 10 seconds. It would penetrate the whole Earth, so the night side, underground shelters, submarines, and mountains would offer essentially no protection. Everyone and everything would be irradiated nearly uniformly. At a just-lethal dose, humans and many animals would suffer acute radiation sickness and die over days to weeks; at much higher doses, death could occur in hours or less. Microbes and radiation-resistant organisms might survive unless the dose were far above human-lethal levels.

The planet itself would remain mostly intact from the neutrinos alone. A lethal biological dose is only a few joules per kilogram, far too little heat or momentum to crack Earth, boil oceans, or alter its orbit. The danger is molecular and cellular damage, not mechanical impact.

But in any realistic case, the neutrinos would only be the opening act. A supernova close enough for its neutrinos to be lethal would also deliver an immense flash of X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, and later expanding debris. That electromagnetic radiation and ejecta would likely incinerate the surface, strip or heavily damage the atmosphere, and possibly sterilize the planet far more dramatically than the neutrinos. Also, having a massive star that close before it exploded would already be gravitationally and radiatively catastrophic.

So the direct answer is: lethal supernova neutrinos would silently irradiate the entire Earth through all shielding, killing much of life without physically damaging the planet much. But a supernova close enough to do that is not a realistic astronomical threat, and if it occurred, the rest of the supernova would soon be even more destructive.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels. or a quarter of the diameter of the Death Star thermal exhaust port. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. [Image: image] A few months later, the kid would surpass Robert Wadlow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wadlow) to become the tallest human in history. At age 5, the child would be π meters tall (10'4"): [Image: image] At age 7, the child would be 4.2 meters tall, able to stare down a T-rex: [Image: image] By age 10, the child would be 5.8 meters tall (19 feet). If we assume these giants are proportioned like adult humans, this kid would weigh over a metric ton. [Image: image] Actual humans wouldn't be able to grow to such heights. Thanks to the square-cube law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-cube_law), our bones would be too thin to support our weight and our hearts would be unable to pump blood around our bodies. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image] In addition to the insurmountable health problems, someone with this rapid growth rate would face another hardship. To ride roller coasters, you have to be above a certain minimum height. However, they generally also have a maximum height. [Image: image] Bizarro, a coaster at Six Flags New England, has a minimum height of 137 cm (4'6") and a maximum height of 193 cm (6'4"). Our child would be tall enough to ride Bizarro at age 2 ... and too tall by age 3. Their coaster-riding window would last only 387 days. It's a sad truth: Roller coasters just aren't for everyone. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我们在整个发育期（即直到十几岁/二十岁出头）都以与第一个月相同的速度生长，人类会达到什么高度？
items.model_answer:
A one-month-old baby grows roughly 3–4 cm in length per month and gains about 1 kg per month. If humans kept growing at that absolute rate, a person would not merely become a very tall adult; they would become physically impossible.

At about 10 years old, they could be around 4–5 meters tall. By 20, they might be roughly 8–10 meters tall if height kept increasing linearly. By old age, they could be tens of meters tall.

But they would not survive that long. The main problem is the square-cube law: as height increases, body weight rises roughly with volume, proportional to height cubed, while bone and muscle strength rise only with cross-sectional area, proportional to height squared. So a giant human’s weight would increase faster than their bones, joints, and muscles could support. A 9-meter-tall human with normal proportions would likely weigh many tons, not just a few hundred kilograms.

The heart would also struggle to pump blood over such distances, the lungs would have trouble supplying enough oxygen, joints would fail, heat regulation would become difficult, and the calorie requirements would become enormous. Even much smaller “giants” in real life, around 2.5–2.7 meters tall, often suffer severe skeletal and cardiovascular problems.

So if humans kept growing at the rate of a one-month-old baby, they would become gigantic very quickly, but normal human anatomy could not support them. They would likely become disabled and die long before reaching the size predicted by simple extrapolation. If the growth rate were interpreted as a percentage growth rate rather than a fixed number of centimeters per month, the result would be even more extreme: their size would increase exponentially and become impossible within only a few years.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] The 33,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide sell something like 15 billion hamburger patties per year,[5]They stopped reporting the "x billions served" number on their signs, but this website (http://overhowmanybillionserved.blogspot.com/) has some extrapolations. for an average of 1,245 burgers per restaurant per day. 1,245 burgers is about 600,000 calories, which means that each T-rex only needs about 80 hamburgers per day to survive, and one McDonald's could support over a dozen tyrannosaurs on hamburgers alone. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. And then if the T-rex goes for your friend anyway, hey, you have 80 burgers. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果霸王龙被释放到纽约市，它每天需要消耗多少人才能获得所需的卡路里摄入量？
items.model_answer:
If a healthy adult Tyrannosaurus rex were suddenly released in New York City, it would be extremely dangerous but not unstoppable or “Godzilla-like.”

An adult T. rex was roughly 12 meters long, weighed around 6–9 tons, had powerful jaws, strong senses, and enough strength to overturn cars, smash through light structures, and kill people or large animals with ease. In a crowded street, the biggest immediate danger would be panic: stampedes, traffic crashes, blocked exits, and people trying to flee. The dinosaur itself could kill anyone nearby, but it would not be able to chase people through buildings, subways, stairwells, or narrow interiors very effectively.

Its movement would also be limited by the city. Streets are cluttered with vehicles, barriers, signs, glass, wires, and tight turns. Pavement would be hard on its feet. It could move faster than a human over short distances, but it probably would not have great endurance. It could not climb skyscrapers, fit into most buildings, or easily navigate underground stations. If released in Manhattan, authorities could close bridges and tunnels and effectively trap it on the island.

The police would likely establish a large exclusion zone and evacuate nearby blocks. Ordinary police firearms might injure it but would not be a reliable or humane way to stop it quickly. Tranquilizing it would be difficult because the required dose would be enormous, the drug would take time to act, and a panicked multi-ton animal could cause more destruction before collapsing. The response would probably involve helicopters, drones, armored vehicles, wildlife veterinarians, and possibly military support. If it could be lured or driven into an open area such as a park, waterfront, stadium, or industrial zone, containment would become much easier. If public safety were at immediate risk, lethal force would likely be used.

The T. rex would not thrive long-term in New York. It would need large amounts of meat and water, could injure itself on pavement or debris, and would be stressed by noise, lights, crowds, vehicles, and unfamiliar surroundings. It might scavenge from garbage, attack horses, dogs, zoo animals, or people, but it would not have a stable ecological niche.

So the most likely outcome is: severe local chaos, possible deaths and injuries, major property damage, rapid evacuation and lockdown, and then containment or killing of the animal within hours to perhaps a day or two. It would be a major emergency, but modern urban infrastructure and coordinated response would make it a temporary crisis rather than a city-ending disaster.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy.
